oneLiner: Analgesic / antipyretic of choice across all trimesters and during lactation — use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Paracetamol crosses the placenta but has not been shown to increase the risk of major congenital malformations or miscarriage. It is the analgesic / antipyretic of FIRST CHOICE in pregnancy across all trimesters. Recent observational signals (possible association with ADHD, ASD, asthma in offspring with prolonged exposure) have not been replicated in sibling-controlled analyses and remain weak; do not deny clinically indicated paracetamol on this basis. Use lowest effective dose for the shortest duration.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Untreated fever in pregnancy is itself harmful (associated with NTDs in 1st trimester and adverse outcomes throughout). Treating fever with paracetamol is recommended. Pain control with paracetamol is preferred over NSAIDs (3rd trimester contraindicated) and over opioids (neonatal abstinence, sedation).
pregnancy.data: Multiple cohort and case-control studies and a Nordic sibling-controlled study (~ 2.4 million pregnancies) showed no causal link with neurodevelopmental outcomes once familial confounding was adjusted. No animal teratogenicity at clinical doses.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible with breastfeeding. Excreted in milk in small amounts — infant exposure is < 5% of the maternal weight-adjusted dose, well below the paediatric therapeutic dose.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: No specific monitoring required. Use lowest effective maternal dose.
lactation.data: Relative infant dose (RID) approximately 6-25% of the maternal dose adjusted for weight, but absolute infant intake is far below paediatric dosing (15 mg/kg/dose). No adverse effects reported in breastfed infants.

references.label: Ahlqvist VH et al. Acetaminophen use during pregnancy and children's risk of autism, ADHD, and intellectual disability. JAMA 2024;331:1205-1214.

oneLiner: CONTRAINDICATED from 20 weeks gestation onwards (FDA black-box, oligohydramnios + ductal closure). Use paracetamol instead. Acceptable during lactation as occasional short courses.

pregnancy.riskSummary: AVOID NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac, ketorolac, celecoxib) from 20 weeks gestation onwards — FDA-mandated black-box warning (2020). Use causes oligohydramnios (fetal renal hypoperfusion) and, after 30 weeks, premature closure of the ductus arteriosus with persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN). 1st-trimester use is associated with a small increased risk of miscarriage and possibly cardiac septal defects. Paracetamol is the preferred analgesic.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Low-dose aspirin (75-150 mg) is the EXCEPTION — used through pregnancy for pre-eclampsia prophylaxis in high-risk women, with extensive safety data at that dose. Higher analgesic / anti-inflammatory aspirin doses fall under the same NSAID warning.
pregnancy.data: FDA Drug Safety Communication 2020 reviewed > 30 case reports of oligohydramnios and PPHN with second-half-of-pregnancy NSAID exposure, prompting the labelling change. Pre-2020 the cut-off was 30 weeks; the 20-week cut-off was added based on this signal.

trimesterNotes.note: Small increased risk of miscarriage; possible cardiac defects. Use only when paracetamol inadequate AND benefits outweigh risks.
Contraindicated from 20 weeks (oligohydramnios).
Contraindicated (PPHN, premature ductal closure, prolonged labour, increased maternal bleeding at delivery).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible — ibuprofen is the NSAID of choice if NSAID needed during breastfeeding. Minimal transfer into milk; no adverse effects reported in breastfed infants.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Prefer ibuprofen over diclofenac or naproxen for occasional analgesia. For chronic NSAID need (rheumatology) consult specialist — long-half-life NSAIDs (naproxen, piroxicam) less preferred.
lactation.data: RID 0.1-0.7%. Undetectable in breastmilk at therapeutic maternal doses in most studies.

references.label: FDA Drug Safety Communication. NSAID warning at 20 weeks gestation. October 2020.

oneLiner: Low-dose (75-150 mg) ACCEPTABLE through pregnancy — first-line pre-eclampsia prophylaxis from 12-16 weeks. Analgesic doses (≥ 300 mg) follow NSAID rules: avoid from 20 weeks.

pregnancy.riskSummary: DOSE-DEPENDENT. LOW DOSE (75-150 mg/day) is recommended from 12-16 weeks until 36-37 weeks for women at moderate-to-high risk of pre-eclampsia (NNT ~ 20 in high-risk cohorts; supported by USPSTF, NICE, ACOG, WHO). ANALGESIC / ANTI-INFLAMMATORY DOSE (≥ 300 mg) is contraindicated from 20 weeks (same risks as other NSAIDs — oligohydramnios, premature ductal closure, PPHN) and should be avoided 1st trimester (small increased miscarriage risk).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Low-dose aspirin for pre-eclampsia prophylaxis is the EXCEPTION to the general NSAID-in-pregnancy avoidance. It does NOT cause oligohydramnios or ductal closure at 75-150 mg. Stop at 36-37 weeks (some guidelines say 34) to reduce bleeding risk at delivery.
pregnancy.data: ASPRE trial (NEJM 2017): 150 mg aspirin from 11-14 weeks reduced preterm pre-eclampsia by 62% in screened high-risk women. Multiple meta-analyses support low-dose aspirin from before 16 weeks.

lactation.riskSummary: AVOID regular maternal aspirin during breastfeeding (theoretical Reye's syndrome risk in viral infection; reported infant metabolic acidosis with chronic high-dose use). Single occasional low doses are unlikely to harm. For pre-eclampsia prophylaxis, low-dose aspirin (75-150 mg) is commonly continued postpartum with breastfeeding when indicated (e.g. APS); discuss with paediatrics.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Use paracetamol or ibuprofen for postpartum analgesia in preference.
lactation.data: Transferred in low amounts; documented infant salicylate levels with chronic high-dose maternal use.

references.label: USPSTF. Aspirin Use to Prevent Preeclampsia and Related Morbidity and Mortality. 2021.
Rolnik DL et al. ASPRE trial. NEJM 2017;377:613-22.

oneLiner: CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy — warfarin embryopathy (1st trimester) and fetal CNS / haemorrhagic complications (any trimester). Switch to LMWH (enoxaparin) preconception or at first positive pregnancy test.

pregnancy.riskSummary: AVOID warfarin in pregnancy. Crosses the placenta and causes (1) warfarin embryopathy if exposed at 6-12 weeks (nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses; ~ 5-10% incidence with exposure in this window); (2) fetal intracranial haemorrhage at any gestation, particularly during labour; (3) increased miscarriage and stillbirth. ALL women of childbearing potential on warfarin should be on effective contraception and counselled to switch to LMWH BEFORE conception or at the first positive pregnancy test. Mechanical heart valve patients are an EXCEPTION discussed with multidisciplinary specialist input — risk of valve thrombosis on LMWH must be balanced against fetal warfarin risk; some centres continue warfarin 12 weeks to term then switch.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Switch to weight-adjusted therapeutic LMWH (e.g. enoxaparin 1 mg/kg BD) preconception or at first positive pregnancy test. Stop LMWH at onset of labour; restart 4-6 h post vaginal / 6-12 h post Caesarean delivery once haemostasis confirmed. Resume warfarin 24-48 h postpartum if non-breastfeeding context; if breastfeeding, both warfarin and LMWH are compatible.
pregnancy.data: Bates SM et al. ACCP 9th edition — venous thromboembolism in pregnancy. Chest 2012. Multiple registries of warfarin embryopathy.

trimesterNotes.note: Warfarin embryopathy risk at 6-12 weeks. Switch to LMWH BEFORE conception ideally; if exposed, urgent obstetric / haematology / fetal medicine referral.
Fetal intracranial haemorrhage risk — particularly at delivery.

lactation.riskSummary: Warfarin is COMPATIBLE with breastfeeding — does not cross into breast milk in clinically significant amounts (highly protein-bound, weakly acidic). PREFERRED oral anticoagulant during lactation.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Routine monitoring of infant clotting NOT required. Monitor maternal INR as usual.
lactation.data: Warfarin not detected in breast milk in published series; no anticoagulant effect documented in breastfed infants. DOACs in lactation: SAFETY UNKNOWN — limited data; expert consensus advises against DOACs in breastfeeding mothers (use warfarin or LMWH instead).

reproductive.pregnancyTesting: Confirm before initiating warfarin in any patient of childbearing potential; reconfirm if menses missed during therapy.
reproductive.contraception: Effective contraception is mandatory while on warfarin if pregnancy is not desired. Note: warfarin teratogenicity does NOT contraindicate combined oral contraceptive — but estrogen contraceptives increase thrombosis risk and may not be appropriate for the underlying indication. Discuss progestogen-only or non-hormonal options.

references.label: Bates SM et al. VTE, thrombophilia, antithrombotic therapy, and pregnancy. CHEST 2012;141(2 Suppl):e691S-736S.
RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 37b (acute management of VTE in pregnancy).

oneLiner: PREFERRED anticoagulant in pregnancy — does not cross the placenta. Compatible with breastfeeding. Weight-adjusted therapeutic dosing; stop at labour onset; restart 4-12 h post delivery.

pregnancy.riskSummary: LMWH (enoxaparin, dalteparin, tinzaparin) is the anticoagulant of CHOICE throughout pregnancy. Does NOT cross the placenta (too large). Used both prophylactically (high VTE-risk pregnancies, mechanical valves where indicated) and therapeutically (acute VTE, APS, recurrent miscarriage with APS).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Dose is weight-based on booking weight (not adjusted for gestational weight gain in most protocols, but check local guidance). Prophylactic enoxaparin 40 mg OD (BMI < 30); 60 mg OD (BMI 30-39); 80 mg OD (BMI ≥ 40). Therapeutic 1 mg/kg BD (or 1.5 mg/kg OD). Convert to UFH near delivery if planned induction / Caesarean to allow neuraxial anaesthesia. Stop prophylactic at onset of labour; therapeutic 24 h before planned delivery. Restart 4-6 h post vaginal / 6-12 h post Caesarean. Continue at least 6 weeks postpartum.
pregnancy.data: Multiple cohorts; established standard of care in RCOG, ACOG, ACCP guidelines.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Not absorbed orally by the infant; not detected in clinically significant amounts in breastmilk.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: No monitoring required.
lactation.data: Large molecular weight prevents milk transfer; oral bioavailability negligible. Compatible per LactMed.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 37a (reducing risk of VTE during pregnancy and the puerperium).

drug: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers (ACEi / ARB)
oneLiner: CONTRAINDICATED 2nd and 3rd trimester (renal failure, oligohydramnios, fetal hypotension, skull hypoplasia, death). Avoid in 1st trimester if possible. Switch preconception to labetalol or methyldopa.

pregnancy.riskSummary: CONTRAINDICATED in 2nd and 3rd trimesters — fetal renal hypoperfusion and dysplasia, oligohydramnios → pulmonary hypoplasia + limb contractures, fetal hypotension, hypocalvaria (skull hypoplasia), neonatal renal failure and death. 1st trimester exposure may also increase major malformation rate — best to switch BEFORE conception in any woman of childbearing potential on an ACEi / ARB.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Switch preconception (or at first positive pregnancy test) to labetalol, nifedipine MR, or methyldopa for BP control. Sacubitril-valsartan (Entresto) carries the same warning. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone) also avoided.
pregnancy.data: ACOG Practice Bulletin 203 (chronic hypertension in pregnancy).

lactation.riskSummary: Captopril, enalapril, quinapril have published lactation data and are considered ACCEPTABLE with breastfeeding (very low milk transfer). Other ACEi / ARB have less data — prefer captopril or enalapril postpartum if ACEi indicated.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for hypotension, decreased urine output (in premature or low-birth-weight infants particularly).
alternatives: captopril or enalapril (preferred ACEi in lactation if needed)

reproductive.pregnancyTesting: Consider before initiating in patients of childbearing potential.
reproductive.contraception: Effective contraception while on ACEi / ARB if pregnancy is not desired.

references.label: ACOG Practice Bulletin 203 — Chronic Hypertension in Pregnancy.

oneLiner: PREFERRED first-line agent for chronic hypertension and pre-eclampsia in pregnancy — longest safety record. Compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: First-line treatment for chronic hypertension and pre-eclampsia in pregnancy. Decades of safety data showing no adverse fetal effects on growth or neurodevelopment.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Starting dose 250 mg BD-TDS, titrating to 500 mg-1 g BD-TDS (max 3 g/day). Slow onset (1-3 days); not for acute crisis. Maternal side-effects (sedation, postural dizziness, depression, hepatitis) may limit acceptability — labetalol increasingly preferred for tolerability while sharing strong safety profile.
pregnancy.data: 1976 follow-up study (Cockburn et al.) of children exposed in utero showed normal development at 7.5 years.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Low milk transfer; no adverse infant effects reported.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Methyldopa can worsen postpartum depression — consider switching to alternative (labetalol, nifedipine) postpartum if depressive symptoms emerge.
alternatives: labetalol (often preferred postpartum due to depression risk with methyldopa)

references.label: NICE Hypertension in Pregnancy guideline NG133.

oneLiner: Preferred for hypertension in pregnancy (chronic, pre-eclampsia, acute severe). Compatible with breastfeeding. Monitor neonate for hypoglycaemia and bradycardia.

pregnancy.riskSummary: First-line oral and IV agent for hypertension in pregnancy and pre-eclampsia. Combined α- and non-selective β-blockade; preferred over atenolol (which is associated with fetal growth restriction). Crosses placenta.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Oral: 100 mg BD-TDS, titrate to 800 mg TDS (max 2.4 g/day). IV (acute severe hypertension): 20 mg slow IV bolus, doubled every 10 min to max single 80 mg / cumulative 300 mg, or infusion 20-160 mg/h titrated to BP. AVOID in maternal severe asthma, heart block, severely decompensated heart failure. Monitor neonate for hypoglycaemia and bradycardia for 24-48 h post-delivery (placental transfer effect).
pregnancy.data: NICE NG133, ACOG Practice Bulletin 222 (Gestational Hypertension and Preeclampsia).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Low milk transfer; well-tolerated by breastfed infants.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Generally preferred over atenolol (higher milk concentrations and reported infant bradycardia / hypoglycaemia).

references.label: ACOG Practice Bulletin 222 — Gestational Hypertension and Preeclampsia.

oneLiner: HIGHLY TERATOGENIC. Must NOT be used in any woman of childbearing potential unless there is no alternative AND a Pregnancy Prevention Programme is in place. Neural tube defects (10×), major malformations (10%), neurodevelopmental disorders (30-40%).

pregnancy.riskSummary: TERATOGEN — among the most dangerous prescription medicines in pregnancy. (1) Neural tube defects 10× background (~ 1-2% absolute risk). (2) Major congenital malformations ~ 10% (vs ~ 2-3% baseline) — orofacial cleft, hypospadias, cardiac, limb. (3) Neurodevelopmental disorders in 30-40% of exposed children — autism, lower IQ (mean reduction ~ 9 points). Risk is DOSE-DEPENDENT and additive with polytherapy. Switch BEFORE conception. MHRA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Programme is mandatory in the UK/EU for any prescription to a woman of childbearing potential.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: For epilepsy: lamotrigine, levetiracetam, oxcarbazepine are safer first-line options. For bipolar disorder: lithium (own teratogenic profile but lower), lamotrigine, atypical antipsychotics are alternatives. For migraine: propranolol, amitriptyline. ANY woman of childbearing potential on valproate needs: documented annual specialist review, signed Risk Acknowledgement Form, dual contraception (where indicated), pre-pregnancy counselling, folic acid 5 mg/day if pregnancy possible.
pregnancy.data: MHRA Drug Safety Update Jan 2015, Apr 2018 — multiple regulatory actions globally.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible with breastfeeding despite the pregnancy contraindication. Milk transfer is low; serum levels in breastfed infants generally undetectable or very low.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for sedation, poor feeding, jaundice, hepatotoxicity (rare). Avoid in infants with hepatic dysfunction.

reproductive.pregnancyTesting: Mandatory annual pregnancy test (urine or serum); test before each prescription if any concern.
reproductive.contraception: TWO complementary forms (e.g. IUD + condom) per MHRA Pregnancy Prevention Programme. Combined oral contraceptive interacts with some hepatic enzyme-inducing AEDs (not valproate per se but with co-administered AEDs).
reproductive.infertility: Polycystic ovary syndrome features (oligomenorrhoea, hyperandrogenism, weight gain, insulin resistance) are recognised valproate adverse effects.

references.label: MHRA Drug Safety Update: Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Programme. Apr 2018.
Bromley R et al. Treatment for epilepsy in pregnancy: neurodevelopmental outcomes in the child. Cochrane 2014.

oneLiner: Preferred AED in pregnancy — lowest teratogenicity of established AEDs. Compatible with breastfeeding (monitor infant for rash, sedation). Levels DROP in pregnancy; check monthly.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Lamotrigine has the LOWEST major congenital malformation rate of established AEDs (~ 2-3%, near background). Use throughout pregnancy if needed for epilepsy or bipolar disorder. Preconception folic acid 5 mg/day is recommended for any woman on an AED.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Lamotrigine clearance INCREASES during pregnancy (estrogen-induced glucuronidation) — serum level can fall 50-70% by 3rd trimester, requiring dose increases of 50-100% to maintain seizure control. Monitor level monthly through pregnancy, weekly in 3rd trimester. After delivery, reduce dose back to preconception within 1-3 weeks (risk of toxicity / Stevens-Johnson otherwise). Continue folic acid 5 mg/day throughout pregnancy.
pregnancy.data: UK Epilepsy and Pregnancy Register; EURAP registry — major congenital malformation rate 2.0-3.4% across cohorts.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible with breastfeeding. Watch infant for sedation, poor feeding, and rare rash (case reports of Stevens-Johnson in breastfed infants are extremely rare).
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Infant serum levels can reach 20-30% of maternal — higher transfer than most AEDs but generally well tolerated. Monitor infant clinically. Maternal serum level may rise rapidly postpartum due to lost pregnancy-induced clearance — reduce dose to preconception within 1-3 weeks.

references.label: Pennell PB. Use of antiepileptic drugs during pregnancy. NEJM 2020.

oneLiner: Sertraline is the SSRI of choice in pregnancy and lactation — most data, lowest milk transfer. Untreated maternal depression is itself harmful — do not discontinue without specialist input.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Sertraline is the SSRI of CHOICE in pregnancy — extensive safety data; no convincing increase in major congenital malformations. Paroxetine has a small increase in cardiac defects (avoid if alternative possible). Untreated antenatal depression and anxiety are themselves associated with adverse outcomes (preterm birth, low birth weight, postnatal depression, infant behavioural disturbance) — the risk of NOT treating is real.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Neonatal adaptation syndrome (jitteriness, irritability, transient respiratory distress, feeding difficulty) in 15-30% of infants exposed in late pregnancy — usually mild, self-limited within days. Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) — absolute risk small (incidence 1-2 per 1000 exposed, vs 1 per 1000 background). Continue maternal medication through delivery; do not abruptly discontinue (relapse risk).
pregnancy.data: ACOG / APA Joint Practice Guideline: Use of Psychiatric Medications during Pregnancy and Lactation. 2008 (updated).

lactation.riskSummary: Sertraline is the PREFERRED SSRI during breastfeeding — RID < 2%, infant serum levels usually undetectable. Maternal mental health continuity is essential for the infant.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Fluoxetine has higher milk transfer and a long-half-life active metabolite — may accumulate in neonates and breastfed infants (sedation, feeding difficulty reports). If breastfeeding and starting an SSRI fresh, prefer sertraline.
lactation.data: RID for sertraline 0.4-2.2%; fluoxetine 1.6-14.6% (highest of the SSRIs).
alternatives: paroxetine (also low milk transfer; avoid initiation in 1st trimester)

references.label: ACOG Committee Opinion 757: Screening for Perinatal Depression.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy when alternative available (historical cartilage / arthropathy concerns in animal models, not confirmed in human data). Acceptable in lactation in single doses.

pregnancy.riskSummary: AVOID if alternative available, although the historical concern (cartilage arthropathy in juvenile animals) has NOT been confirmed in human follow-up studies of in-utero or paediatric exposure. Use is appropriate when no acceptable alternative exists (e.g. complicated UTI in penicillin-allergic patient, resistant organisms, post-exposure anthrax). Beta-lactams (amoxicillin, cefalexin, nitrofurantoin) and macrolides preferred for routine pregnancy infections.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: First-line pregnancy UTI: nitrofurantoin (1st-2nd trimester only; avoid near term — neonatal haemolysis if G6PD deficient), trimethoprim (avoid 1st trimester — folate antagonist), cefalexin, amoxicillin. Complicated / pyelonephritis: ceftriaxone IV.
pregnancy.data: Multiple cohort studies have not shown increased malformations or musculoskeletal abnormalities with in-utero fluoroquinolone exposure.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible with single doses or short courses; not preferred for long-term use due to theoretical risk of altered infant gut flora and infant joint development concern (mostly theoretical).
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Time feed after dose, or use alternative (cefalexin, nitrofurantoin) for nursing mothers with UTI.
lactation.data: RID 0.4-2.7%; infant serum levels generally undetectable.
alternatives: nitrofurantoin (avoid if infant < 1 month or G6PD deficient)

references.label: Yefet E et al. The safety of quinolones in pregnancy. Obstet Gynecol Surv 2014.

oneLiner: Preferred for uncomplicated UTI in 1st and 2nd trimester. AVOID near term (≥ 38 weeks) and during labour — risk of neonatal haemolytic anaemia, particularly with G6PD deficiency. Avoid in lactation if infant < 1 month or G6PD deficient.

pregnancy.riskSummary: First-line for uncomplicated lower UTI / asymptomatic bacteriuria from 14 weeks to 36 weeks. AVOID at term (≥ 38 weeks) and during labour — risk of neonatal haemolytic anaemia. Also AVOID in 1st trimester if alternative available (small signal for orofacial cleft and cardiac defects, conflicting data) — though acceptable when alternative not safe.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Dose: nitrofurantoin MR 100 mg BD × 5 days for uncomplicated UTI. Confirm sensitivity. Not for pyelonephritis (does not achieve renal tissue concentrations). G6PD: known maternal G6PD deficiency is a contraindication.

trimesterNotes.note: Acceptable when no alternative; theoretical orofacial cleft / cardiac defect signal weak.
Preferred.
Acceptable up to ~ 36 weeks; AVOID ≥ 38 weeks and during labour.

lactation.riskSummary: Avoid if breastfed infant is < 1 month, premature, jaundiced, or G6PD deficient — risk of haemolytic anaemia. Otherwise short courses are acceptable.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Check infant G6PD status if mother of relevant ethnicity. Monitor infant for jaundice / pallor.
alternatives: cefalexin (preferred for breastfeeding UTI with young infants)

references.label: NICE NG109 — Urinary Tract Infection (Lower) in Pregnant Women.

oneLiner: ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy — folate antagonist, abortifacient, teratogenic (methotrexate embryopathy). Mandatory pregnancy exclusion + dual contraception. Compatible-with-caution during lactation only as occasional low-dose rheumatology.

pregnancy.riskSummary: ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED. Folate antagonist → neural tube defects, craniofacial dysmorphism, limb abnormalities, fetal loss. Used clinically to TERMINATE ectopic pregnancy. Stop ≥ 3 months before conception (some guidance now allows 1 month based on EULAR 2016, but local practice may be more conservative). Mandatory pregnancy testing before initiation; dual contraception throughout.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Inadvertent exposure: urgent specialist referral. Folinic acid (calcium folinate) rescue if exposure < 7 days. Discuss therapeutic termination vs continuation based on dose, timing, and parental wishes.
pregnancy.data: Methotrexate embryopathy classic syndrome described from 1970s onwards.

lactation.riskSummary: AVOID — concentrates in tissue and cells; cumulative infant exposure risk. Occasional low-dose oral rheumatology may be considered (RID < 3%, transient milk levels) but most authorities recommend not breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: If essential, time feeds 24 h after a single weekly dose. AVOID if infant has any haematological or hepatic concern.

reproductive.pregnancyTesting: Mandatory monthly during treatment in patients of childbearing potential.
reproductive.contraception: Dual contraception throughout treatment AND for 3 months after stopping (women) / 3 months (men — sperm DNA effects).
reproductive.infertility: Reduces sperm count reversibly in men; advise stopping 3 months pre-conception.

references.label: EULAR points to consider for use of antirheumatic drugs before pregnancy, and during pregnancy and lactation. Ann Rheum Dis 2016.

oneLiner: Compatible with pregnancy — used as first-line for type 2 diabetes and gestational diabetes (NICE / WHO). Compatible with breastfeeding. Crosses placenta but no congenital malformation signal.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Compatible with pregnancy. Used as first-line oral agent for type 2 diabetes and gestational diabetes (GDM) per NICE NG3 and WHO. Crosses placenta; no congenital malformation or growth signal in large meta-analyses. May modestly increase risk of small-for-gestational-age and modestly reduce risk of large-for-gestational-age in GDM.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Insulin is often added when glycaemic targets not met on metformin alone. Pre-existing T2DM on metformin: continue through pregnancy, add insulin when needed. Polycystic ovary syndrome: metformin may be continued in pregnancy if benefit (e.g. reduced miscarriage in some studies — evidence mixed).
pregnancy.data: MIG trial (NEJM 2008) and follow-up: no excess risk of adverse outcomes with metformin vs insulin in GDM.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Minimal milk transfer; no adverse infant effects.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant glucose if mother on combined insulin + metformin and infant has risk factors for hypoglycaemia.

references.label: Rowan JA et al. Metformin versus insulin for the treatment of gestational diabetes (MIG trial). NEJM 2008;358:2003-15.

oneLiner: AVOID from 20 weeks gestation (same NSAID class warning as ibuprofen — oligohydramnios, premature ductal closure). Acceptable in lactation but ibuprofen preferred (shorter half-life).

pregnancy.riskSummary: NSAID class effect — avoid from 20 weeks gestation onwards (FDA black-box). Same fetal renal hypoperfusion / oligohydramnios / ductal closure risks as ibuprofen. 1st-trimester use carries a small increased miscarriage risk. Prefer paracetamol for analgesia in pregnancy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: If chronic NSAID indicated for maternal rheumatic disease, switch BEFORE 20 weeks. Postpartum, naproxen is acceptable but ibuprofen (shorter half-life) is the preferred NSAID for nursing mothers.

lactation.riskSummary: Acceptable for short courses; ibuprofen preferred because of its much shorter half-life (lower infant accumulation).
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Avoid prolonged use in nursing mothers; case reports of infant haemolytic anaemia and prolonged bleeding.

references.label: FDA Drug Safety Communication. NSAID warning at 20 weeks gestation. October 2020.

oneLiner: AVOID from 20 weeks gestation (NSAID class). Acceptable as short-course postpartum analgesia; ibuprofen preferred.

pregnancy.riskSummary: NSAID class effect — avoid from 20 weeks gestation. Same risks as ibuprofen: oligohydramnios, premature ductal closure, PPHN. 1st-trimester use carries small increased miscarriage risk.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Use paracetamol for analgesia in pregnancy. Topical diclofenac has lower systemic absorption but the same class warning is conservatively applied from 20 weeks.

lactation.riskSummary: Acceptable for short courses postpartum; ibuprofen preferred.
lactation.data: RID < 1%; not detected in milk in some studies.

references.label: FDA Drug Safety Communication. NSAID warning at 20 weeks gestation. October 2020.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy and lactation if alternative available — variable maternal CYP2D6 metabolism can produce dangerous infant morphine levels (deaths reported in ultra-rapid metabolisers). Use paracetamol or weak alternatives.

pregnancy.riskSummary: No specific teratogenicity at therapeutic doses, but maternal CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metaboliser phenotype produces high morphine concentrations. Late-pregnancy use risks neonatal respiratory depression and neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS) with chronic exposure.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Use paracetamol first line. If opioid needed, oral morphine (predictable pharmacokinetics) is preferred over codeine.

lactation.riskSummary: AVOID — multiple infant deaths reported with maternal codeine use due to CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metaboliser phenotype producing toxic morphine levels in milk. MHRA / FDA advise against codeine in breastfeeding mothers.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: If unavoidable, use lowest dose for shortest duration (< 3 days); monitor infant for excessive somnolence, poor feeding, limpness.
alternatives: morphine (more predictable than codeine if opioid needed)

references.label: FDA Drug Safety Communication: Codeine and tramadol in nursing mothers. 2017.
MHRA Drug Safety Update: Codeine — restricted use in children and breastfeeding mothers. 2013.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy (neonatal withdrawal, seizure risk) and in breastfeeding (same CYP2D6 metaboliser concern as codeine — FDA contraindicated 2017).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Limited human teratogenicity data; serotonergic activity. Chronic / late-pregnancy use causes neonatal withdrawal and respiratory depression. Lowers seizure threshold.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Avoid if alternative available; use morphine for moderate-severe pain when opioid required in pregnancy.

lactation.riskSummary: AVOID — FDA contraindicated in nursing mothers (2017) due to variable CYP2D6 metabolism producing unpredictable infant opioid exposure.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Same rationale as codeine restriction.

references.label: FDA Drug Safety Communication: Tramadol and codeine in nursing mothers and children. 2017.

oneLiner: PREFERRED opioid in pregnancy and lactation when an opioid is required — predictable pharmacokinetics. Late / chronic use causes neonatal abstinence syndrome — monitor.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Not teratogenic at therapeutic doses. Acute / short-course use (labour analgesia, postoperative) is acceptable. Chronic late-pregnancy use causes neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS) — plan neonatal monitoring and managed withdrawal protocol.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: For acute severe pain in pregnancy, IV/IM/oral morphine is the opioid of choice. Co-prescribe laxative and antiemetic.

lactation.riskSummary: Preferred opioid in lactation if an opioid is required. Single doses produce minimal infant exposure; multiple-day use requires infant sedation monitoring.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: RID ~ 9-35% but oral bioavailability in infant is poor (~ 25%); effective infant exposure low.

references.label: ACOG Committee Opinion 711 — Opioid Use and Opioid Use Disorder in Pregnancy.

oneLiner: Use with caution short-term; morphine preferred when opioid needed. Late / chronic use causes neonatal abstinence syndrome. Acceptable short-course in lactation, monitor infant sedation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Not a known teratogen. Chronic / late-pregnancy use causes NAS. Morphine has more reassurance data; prefer morphine if available.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: If used chronically, plan delivery in unit with neonatal monitoring.

lactation.riskSummary: Short courses acceptable; chronic use poses risk of infant sedation and reported neonatal CNS depression (case reports). Monitor infant for somnolence, poor feeding.

references.label: FDA Drug Safety Communication on opioids in lactation. 2017.

oneLiner: Acceptable for intrapartum / procedural analgesia. Chronic transdermal use causes NAS. Compatible in lactation in single perioperative / labour doses.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Not teratogenic. Widely used intrapartum (epidural / IV) and for perioperative analgesia. Chronic transdermal use (chronic pain) causes NAS.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Intrapartum IV/epidural fentanyl is standard practice and considered safe. Transdermal fentanyl in chronic pain: review necessity preconception.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible — extensively short half-life; single labour / perioperative doses produce negligible infant exposure.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Transdermal chronic dosing in lactation requires individualised assessment.

references.label: ACOG Committee Opinion 766 — Approaches to Limit Intervention During Labor and Birth.

oneLiner: PREFERRED opioid agonist for opioid use disorder in pregnancy (lower NAS severity than methadone). Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Preferred for opioid use disorder (OUD) maintenance in pregnancy alongside methadone. MOTHER trial showed shorter / less severe neonatal abstinence syndrome with buprenorphine vs methadone. Do NOT discontinue OUD treatment in pregnancy — relapse risk is high and harmful.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Use buprenorphine mono-product (not naloxone combination, though combination evidence increasingly reassuring). Continue through pregnancy and postpartum.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Maternal milk transfer is low; breastfeeding is recommended (supports infant bonding and reduces NAS severity).

references.label: Jones HE et al. MOTHER trial. NEJM 2010;363:2320-31.
ACOG Committee Opinion 711 — Opioid Use Disorder in Pregnancy.

oneLiner: Acceptable for opioid use disorder in pregnancy; buprenorphine produces less severe NAS but both are far safer than untreated OUD. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Standard maintenance therapy for opioid use disorder in pregnancy. NAS in 60-80% of exposed neonates; manage with established protocols. Maternal dose may need increases through pregnancy (increased clearance).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Do NOT taper or stop in pregnancy — relapse risk is high. Plan delivery in unit with neonatal NAS protocol.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; recommended to support bonding and ease NAS. Maternal therapeutic doses produce low infant exposure.

references.label: ACOG Committee Opinion 711 — Opioid Use Disorder in Pregnancy.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy — limited human data, placental transfer documented. Switch to LMWH (enoxaparin) preconception or at first positive pregnancy test. Avoid in lactation — limited data, prefer warfarin / LMWH.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Direct factor Xa inhibitor; crosses the placenta. Limited human pregnancy data — animal embryofetal toxicity at high doses. Avoid in pregnancy; switch to LMWH (preferred) or warfarin (mechanical valves discussed separately).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Switch preconception. If conception occurs on apixaban: urgent switch to LMWH, MFM referral.

lactation.riskSummary: AVOID — limited human lactation data; expert consensus recommends LMWH or warfarin during breastfeeding.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 37b — VTE in Pregnancy.
BSH guideline on the use of anticoagulants in pregnancy.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy and lactation — direct factor Xa inhibitor crosses placenta; limited human data; LMWH or warfarin preferred.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Direct factor Xa inhibitor; crosses the placenta. Avoid in pregnancy. Switch to LMWH preconception or at first positive pregnancy test.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Same approach as apixaban.

lactation.riskSummary: AVOID — detected in milk in animals; limited human data. Use warfarin or LMWH during lactation.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy and lactation — direct thrombin inhibitor with limited human data and animal embryotoxicity. LMWH or warfarin preferred.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Direct thrombin inhibitor. Limited human data; animal embryofetal toxicity. Switch to LMWH preconception.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Idarucizumab reversal available if emergency bleeding.

lactation.riskSummary: AVOID — limited data; prefer warfarin or LMWH.

oneLiner: Compatible in pregnancy and lactation. Does not cross the placenta. Used when LMWH unsuitable (severe renal impairment, peri-delivery, rapid reversal need).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Does NOT cross the placenta. Compatible in pregnancy. LMWH usually preferred for convenience (subcutaneous OD/BD; predictable PK; less HIT risk). UFH role: severe renal impairment (CrCl < 30), planned reversal at delivery, prosthetic valve protocols.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Therapeutic IV UFH titrated to APTT 1.5-2.5× control. Stop 4-6 h before regional anaesthesia / delivery. HIT risk higher than LMWH; check platelets day 5-14.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; not absorbed orally by infant, large molecular weight prevents milk transfer.

oneLiner: Use in pregnancy only when LMWH contraindicated (e.g. HIT) — limited data. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Synthetic pentasaccharide factor Xa inhibitor. Small amounts cross placenta (minimal). Reserved for women with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) or LMWH allergy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist (haematology) prescribing.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited data; not orally absorbed by the infant.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy when alternative available — limited data; usually stopped peri-conception unless DAPT mandatory post-PCI. Limited lactation data — use with caution.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Limited human pregnancy data. Animal studies non-teratogenic. If essential (e.g. < 12 months post drug-eluting stent), continue under cardiology/MFM joint care; otherwise transition to aspirin alone.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Stop ≥ 7 days before delivery / neuraxial anaesthesia where possible; restart 24 h post haemostasis.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited lactation data; consensus is to avoid if alternative available.

references.label: ESC Guidelines on Cardiovascular Diseases during Pregnancy. Eur Heart J 2018.

oneLiner: Compatible in pregnancy and lactation. Used for warfarin reversal, neonatal IM prophylaxis, and maternal supplementation on enzyme-inducing AEDs.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Compatible. Maternal oral vitamin K 10-20 mg/day from week 36 is sometimes recommended for women on enzyme-inducing AEDs (carbamazepine, phenytoin) to reduce neonatal haemorrhagic disease risk. IM vitamin K is universal neonatal prophylaxis.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: For warfarin reversal in pregnant patient: IV vitamin K 5-10 mg + 4-factor PCC for major bleeding (specialist input).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Endogenous nutrient; no concern with supplemental doses.

references.label: NICE NG143 — Neonatal jaundice / vitamin K prophylaxis.

oneLiner: Compatible — used for emergent heparin reversal in pregnancy / lactation. No human teratogenicity signal.

pregnancy.riskSummary: No teratogenicity reported. Used in cardiac surgery and emergent heparin reversal. Watch for hypersensitivity / hypotension on rapid administration.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Dose: 1 mg per 100 units of UFH given in last 2-3 h; lower doses if longer interval. Partial reversal of LMWH (~ 60-75%).

lactation.riskSummary: Single-dose IV use compatible; not orally absorbed.

references.label: BSH guideline on the management of bleeding in patients on antithrombotic agents.

oneLiner: Acceptable for hypertension in pregnancy and as tocolytic; modified-release preferred for chronic BP control. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Calcium channel blocker. Widely used in pregnancy for chronic hypertension, severe hypertension of pre-eclampsia, and tocolysis (preterm labour). No teratogenicity signal.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: For severe HTN in pre-eclampsia: nifedipine 10 mg oral, repeat 20 min PRN to 3 doses if BP > 160/110. Tocolysis: 20 mg PO, then 10-20 mg every 6 h. Avoid SUBLINGUAL nifedipine (rapid BP drops / fetal distress).

trimesterNotes.note: Acceptable. Modified-release preparations preferred for chronic BP control.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; low milk transfer.

oneLiner: Limited pregnancy data — switch to nifedipine, labetalol, or methyldopa if chronic hypertension. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Limited human pregnancy data; no teratogenicity signal in small series. Where chronic HTN treatment is needed, switch to a better-studied agent (labetalol, nifedipine, methyldopa).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: If conceived on amlodipine, switching at first prenatal visit is reasonable; abrupt discontinuation risks BP rebound.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited but reassuring lactation data; low transfer expected.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy — associated with fetal growth restriction (worse than other beta-blockers). Switch to labetalol or metoprolol. Avoid in lactation (higher milk transfer than alternatives).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Hydrophilic beta-blocker. Long-standing observational signal for fetal growth restriction (FGR) when used from 1st trimester. Labetalol, metoprolol preferred.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Switch preconception or at first prenatal visit.

lactation.riskSummary: Higher milk concentrations than other beta-blockers; case reports of infant bradycardia, hypoglycaemia, cyanosis. Switch to labetalol / metoprolol / propranolol if breastfeeding.

references.label: Magee LA et al. Beta-blocker use in pregnancy. Cochrane Database. 2003.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation when a cardioselective beta-blocker is needed (e.g. arrhythmia, post-MI). Monitor neonate for bradycardia / hypoglycaemia.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Cardioselective beta-blocker. Used for maternal arrhythmias, post-MI, hyperthyroidism (rate control). Crosses placenta; monitor neonate for bradycardia / hypoglycaemia in first 24-48 h.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Labetalol preferred for chronic HTN in pregnancy; metoprolol reserved for arrhythmia / cardiac indications.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; low milk transfer.

references.label: ESC Guidelines on Cardiovascular Diseases during Pregnancy. 2018.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation. Used for arrhythmia, thyrotoxicosis rate control, and migraine prophylaxis. Monitor neonate for bradycardia and hypoglycaemia.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Non-selective beta-blocker. Long pregnancy experience. Used for migraine prophylaxis, thyrotoxicosis, supraventricular arrhythmia. Avoid in maternal asthma.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor neonate 24-48 h post delivery for bradycardia, hypoglycaemia.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; low milk transfer.

references.label: ESC Guidelines on Cardiovascular Diseases during Pregnancy. 2018.

oneLiner: Limited pregnancy data — switch to labetalol or metoprolol if HTN; bisoprolol reasonable to continue if essential for heart failure / arrhythmia. Limited lactation data.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Cardioselective beta-blocker. Limited human pregnancy data; class-effect monitoring (neonatal bradycardia / hypoglycaemia). Continue if indicated for HFrEF or arrhythmia under cardiology guidance.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: For chronic HTN switch to labetalol / nifedipine.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited lactation data; class-effect approach.

references.label: ESC Guidelines on Cardiovascular Diseases during Pregnancy. 2018.

oneLiner: Acceptable for severe hypertension in pregnancy (IV / oral). Compatible with lactation. Watch maternal reflex tachycardia, headache.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Direct vasodilator. Established IV agent for severe hypertension in pre-eclampsia (alternative to IV labetalol or oral nifedipine). No teratogenicity at therapeutic doses.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: IV bolus 5-10 mg every 20 min PRN. Reflex tachycardia and headache are common.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable second-line for hypertension or pheochromocytoma in pregnancy. Limited lactation data.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Alpha-1 blocker. Used in pheochromocytoma in pregnancy (alpha-blockade before delivery) and occasionally as add-on for refractory HTN. No teratogenicity signal in small series.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: First-dose syncope — initiate at low dose.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited lactation data; expressed in milk.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy for maternal rate control or fetal SVT therapy. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Crosses placenta. Used for maternal atrial fibrillation rate control AND for transplacental therapy of fetal SVT / hydrops. No teratogenicity.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor maternal level; clearance increases in 3rd trimester (may need dose increase).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; infant milk exposure well below paediatric dose.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy if alternative available — fetal hypothyroidism / goitre, neurodevelopmental concerns. AVOID in lactation (high iodine load, accumulates in infant).

pregnancy.riskSummary: High iodine content (37%). Crosses placenta — risk of fetal goitre, congenital hypothyroidism, transient hyperthyroidism, possible neurodevelopmental effects. Use ONLY for life-threatening refractory maternal arrhythmia.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: If used, monitor fetal thyroid (ultrasound) and neonatal TSH/T4.

lactation.riskSummary: AVOID — concentrated in milk; long half-life; infant iodine exposure and thyroid suppression reported.

oneLiner: Use only when clinically indicated (heart failure, pulmonary oedema) — not for routine BP or oedema control in pregnancy. Compatible with lactation but may suppress milk supply.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Crosses placenta. Avoid as routine HTN treatment in pregnancy (intravascular depletion may reduce uteroplacental perfusion). Indicated for maternal heart failure, pulmonary oedema, severe pre-eclampsia with pulmonary oedema.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Not for treatment of dependent oedema of pregnancy or chronic HTN.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible at therapeutic doses; high doses may suppress lactation (diuresis effect).

oneLiner: Avoid initiation in pregnancy; continuation acceptable in selected cases. Compatible with lactation but may suppress supply at high doses.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Thiazide diuretic. Crosses placenta. May reduce plasma volume / uteroplacental perfusion; neonatal thrombocytopenia, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia reported. Not first-line for HTN in pregnancy; if effective preconception some experts continue (e.g. for resistant HTN).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Prefer methyldopa, labetalol, nifedipine for chronic HTN in pregnancy.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible at low doses; may suppress milk supply at higher doses (≥ 50 mg/day).

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy — anti-androgenic activity, theoretical feminisation of male fetus. Limited safety data. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Anti-androgen — theoretical feminisation of male fetal genitalia (no robust human evidence but biological plausibility). Avoid; use other potassium-sparing strategies or different diuretic.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: For primary aldosteronism in pregnancy: specialist endocrine input; eplerenone is the more selective alternative (still limited data).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible — active metabolite excreted in low amounts in milk; no adverse infant effects reported.

oneLiner: Recent FDA / regulatory change (2021): statins no longer broadly contraindicated. Generally STOP preconception or in early pregnancy unless high-risk (e.g. homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia). Avoid in lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Class effect — historically contraindicated; FDA removed the absolute contraindication in 2021 acknowledging that individual high-risk patients (homozygous FH, established ASCVD) may continue under specialist care. For most patients, stop preconception. No reproducible teratogenicity signal in recent meta-analyses but caution maintained.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: For most: discontinue before / at conception; pregnancy is short — atherosclerosis progresses slowly. Discuss high-risk continuation with cardiology / lipidology.

lactation.riskSummary: AVOID — limited data; theoretical concern that cholesterol synthesis inhibition could affect infant CNS development.

references.label: FDA Drug Safety Communication. Statins in pregnancy update. July 2021.

oneLiner: Same class guidance as atorvastatin — stop preconception in most patients; selected high-risk patients may continue under specialist care. Avoid in lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Statin class — see atorvastatin record. Stop preconception in most patients.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: FDA 2021 update removed the absolute contraindication.

lactation.riskSummary: AVOID — limited data.

oneLiner: Same class guidance as atorvastatin — stop preconception in most patients. Avoid in lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Statin class. Hydrophilic — less CNS penetration but pregnancy guidance is the same.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: FDA 2021 update.

lactation.riskSummary: AVOID — limited data.

oneLiner: Most-studied statin in pregnancy contexts (pre-eclampsia prophylaxis trials). Stop preconception in routine lipid management; trials ongoing in high-risk populations. Avoid in lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Hydrophilic statin under active investigation for pre-eclampsia prevention (StAmP, INOVASC, PRAVA-PE trials). Outside trial settings, stop preconception in routine lipid management.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: If patient enrolled in pravastatin pre-eclampsia trial, manage per protocol.

lactation.riskSummary: AVOID outside trial protocols.

references.label: Costantine MM et al. Pravastatin for prevention of preeclampsia. Am J Obstet Gynecol 2021.

oneLiner: PREFERRED in pregnancy and lactation — penicillin class, extensive safety record. First-line for many obstetric infections (GBS prophylaxis, listeria, syphilis-not-penicillin-allergic, etc.).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Penicillin class — extensive pregnancy safety data. Used for GBS prophylaxis (penicillin G is the agent of choice; amoxicillin acceptable alternative), UTI, otitis, sinusitis, Listeria treatment (with gentamicin), and as part of syphilis treatment in non-penicillin-allergic patients (benzylpenicillin preferred).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Dose 500 mg-1 g TDS PO. Allergy: cefalexin or azithromycin alternatives depending on indication.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; minimal milk transfer. Monitor infant for rash, candidiasis, diarrhoea (uncommon).

references.label: NICE NG109 — Urinary Tract Infection (Lower) in Pregnancy.

oneLiner: PREFERRED in pregnancy and lactation — first-generation cephalosporin with extensive safety record. First-line for UTI, mastitis, skin/soft tissue infection.

pregnancy.riskSummary: First-generation cephalosporin. Extensive safety data. First-line for UTI in pregnancy (alongside nitrofurantoin), mastitis in lactating women, and skin/soft tissue infection.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Dose 500 mg QDS PO (UTI 7 days, mastitis 10-14 days).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; minimal transfer.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation — third-generation cephalosporin used for pyelonephritis, severe sepsis, gonorrhoea, meningitis.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Third-generation cephalosporin. Used for pyelonephritis (IV), severe sepsis, gonorrhoea (500 mg-1 g IM single dose), meningitis. Highly protein-bound — theoretical bilirubin displacement in neonate, so avoid in late pregnancy if delivery imminent in jaundiced or preterm neonate.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Cefotaxime is the alternative immediately peri-delivery if concern about neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation. First-line macrolide for chlamydia, syphilis (penicillin allergy alternative — but specialist preferred), atypical pneumonia, pertussis prophylaxis.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Macrolide. Used in pregnancy for chlamydia (1 g PO single dose, first-line), atypical pneumonia, pertussis post-exposure prophylaxis, gastroparesis-MALT considerations. Preferred over erythromycin (less GI toxicity, fewer QT concerns).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: For chlamydia in pregnancy: azithromycin 1 g single dose OR amoxicillin 500 mg TDS × 7 days. Test of cure recommended.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; preferred macrolide in lactation.

references.label: BASHH/CDC guidelines on chlamydia in pregnancy.

oneLiner: Use with caution in 1st trimester (mixed teratogenicity signals); azithromycin preferred. Acceptable in lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Macrolide. Some observational signals for miscarriage and cardiovascular malformations in 1st trimester — overall data conflicting. Azithromycin preferred when a macrolide is needed in pregnancy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: For H. pylori in pregnancy — defer eradication if possible until postpartum.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy (preferred macrolide historically) and lactation. AVOID estolate salt — maternal hepatotoxicity. PPROM standard care (with amoxicillin).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Long-established macrolide. Used in pregnancy for chlamydia, syphilis (penicillin allergy alternative — specialist preferred), and as part of PPROM antibiotic regimen (erythromycin 250 mg QDS for 10 days per RCOG). AVOID erythromycin estolate in pregnancy (cholestatic hepatitis).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: GI intolerance limits compliance.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; small case-series link with infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis with high doses — favour azithromycin.

oneLiner: AVOID 1st trimester (folate antagonist — NTD risk). Acceptable later in pregnancy (with folate supplementation) and in lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Folate antagonist. 1st-trimester exposure associated with neural tube defects and other malformations — avoid 1st trimester. From 2nd trimester onwards, acceptable for UTI in non-G6PD-deficient women; continue folic acid 5 mg/day if used.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: For UTI: trimethoprim 200 mg BD × 3 days (non-pregnant) — in pregnancy preferred alternatives are nitrofurantoin (≤ 36 wk) and cefalexin.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible (acceptable). Avoid in jaundiced, premature, ill, or G6PD-deficient infants.

oneLiner: AVOID 1st trimester (folate antagonist) and near term (sulfa — neonatal kernicterus, haemolysis if G6PD). Use only when no alternative (PCP prophylaxis in HIV; resistant pathogens).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Folate antagonist (trimethoprim) + sulfonamide. AVOID 1st trimester (NTD, cardiac defects) and near term (sulfonamide displaces bilirubin → kernicterus risk; risk in G6PD-deficient neonate). Used in HIV for PCP prophylaxis — continue under specialist care with folate supplementation.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: If essential, co-prescribe folic acid 5 mg/day.

lactation.riskSummary: Avoid in jaundiced, premature, ill, or G6PD-deficient infants. Otherwise acceptable for short courses.

references.label: BHIVA Guidelines for the management of HIV in pregnancy.

oneLiner: AVOID from 15 weeks gestation (tooth discoloration, bone growth). Short courses pre-15 weeks acceptable when no alternative. Avoid prolonged use in lactation; short courses acceptable.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Tetracycline class. Deposits in developing teeth and bone after ~ 15 weeks gestation — yellow-brown tooth discoloration of deciduous dentition. Avoid from 15 weeks. Before 15 weeks, no teratogenic signal in human data; acceptable for short courses if no alternative (e.g. rickettsial / atypical infection, malaria prophylaxis where no alternative).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: For chlamydia in pregnancy use azithromycin or amoxicillin instead.

trimesterNotes.note: Acceptable for short courses when no alternative.
Avoid from 15 weeks.
Avoid.

lactation.riskSummary: Short courses (< 21 days) acceptable — calcium in milk chelates doxycycline reducing absorption. Avoid prolonged courses (theoretical infant tooth/bone effects).

references.label: CDC Yellow Book — Doxycycline in pregnancy and lactation.

oneLiner: AVOID from 15 weeks gestation (tooth discoloration, bone growth, maternal hepatotoxicity in high IV doses). Same lactation considerations as doxycycline.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Same class effects as doxycycline. Maternal high-dose IV tetracycline historically associated with acute fatty liver of pregnancy — IV formulations no longer used.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Use alternatives.

lactation.riskSummary: Short courses acceptable.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy (all trimesters per WHO / NICE — older 1st-trimester avoidance no longer supported by data) and lactation. Used for BV, trichomonas, anaerobes, C. difficile.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Nitroimidazole. Crosses placenta. Older texts advised 1st-trimester avoidance — extensive subsequent data (meta-analyses) show no teratogenicity. Acceptable in all trimesters per current NICE / WHO.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: For BV in pregnancy: metronidazole 400 mg BD × 7 days OR 2 g single dose (treat symptomatic women; reduces preterm birth in selected high-risk women). Avoid alcohol (disulfiram-like reaction).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; some authorities advise withholding breastfeeding for 12-24 h after a single 2 g dose because of bitter taste / theoretical mutagenicity. Routine multi-dose courses are compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable for serious infection in pregnancy and lactation. Monitor levels; theoretical fetal ototoxicity/nephrotoxicity but not seen at standard short courses.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Aminoglycoside. Crosses placenta. Theoretical fetal ototoxicity / nephrotoxicity (well-documented with streptomycin / kanamycin; less clear for gentamicin at standard doses). Used for chorioamnionitis, pyelonephritis sepsis, listeria, intrapartum endometritis.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Use therapeutic drug monitoring. Short courses for clear indications.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible — orally not absorbed by infant; milk concentrations low.

oneLiner: Acceptable IV in pregnancy and lactation for serious gram-positive infection / MRSA. Oral vancomycin (C. difficile) compatible.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Glycopeptide. Crosses placenta in 3rd trimester. Used for MRSA, severe gram-positive sepsis, GBS prophylaxis in penicillin-anaphylaxis. Monitor levels to avoid fetal ototoxicity / nephrotoxicity.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Oral vancomycin (for C. difficile) has negligible systemic absorption.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; not absorbed orally.

oneLiner: Use only when no alternative (resistant gram-positive, drug-resistant TB) — limited human data. Limited lactation data.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Oxazolidinone. Limited human pregnancy data. Used in MDR-TB and resistant gram-positive infection. Reversible myelosuppression and peripheral / optic neuropathy with prolonged use.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist (ID / TB) prescribing.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited lactation data; transferred in milk; monitor infant for GI upset.

references.label: WHO Consolidated Guidelines on Drug-Resistant TB Treatment. 2022.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation. Useful for BV, skin/soft tissue infection (MRSA option), penicillin-allergic GBS prophylaxis (only if susceptibility confirmed).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Lincosamide. Long pregnancy safety record. Used for BV (vaginal cream or oral), MRSA SSTI, anaerobic infection, GBS prophylaxis in severe penicillin allergy (CHECK susceptibility — increasing resistance).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: C. difficile colitis risk with oral courses.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; small case reports of infant bloody stools (resolves on stopping).

oneLiner: AVOID high-dose / chronic in 1st trimester (teratogenic). Single low-dose 150 mg for thrush is generally avoided in pregnancy — use topical clotrimazole/nystatin instead. Acceptable in lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Triazole. HIGH-DOSE chronic use (400-800 mg/day for coccidioidomycosis) in 1st trimester causes a recognised teratogenic syndrome (craniofacial, cardiac, limb). Single low-dose (150 mg) for vulvovaginal candidiasis: associations with miscarriage (Danish registry 2016) — UK and US guidance advises topical antifungal (clotrimazole, nystatin) in pregnancy where possible. For invasive candidiasis or cryptococcal disease, benefit may outweigh risk in 2nd/3rd trimester.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: For vulvovaginal candidiasis in pregnancy: topical clotrimazole 7 days first line.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; transferred in milk at concentrations similar to maternal serum, but well-tolerated.
lactation.data: RID 16-22%; comparable to therapeutic neonatal dose.

references.label: FDA Drug Safety Communication: Fluconazole and miscarriage. 2016.
BASHH National Guideline for the Management of Vulvovaginal Candidiasis.

oneLiner: Compatible in pregnancy and lactation — minimal systemic absorption. First-line topical antifungal for thrush in pregnancy.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Polyene antifungal. Negligible systemic absorption from topical/oral application. First-line for oral / vaginal candidiasis in pregnancy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Vaginal pessaries; oral suspension for thrush.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible — minimal absorption.

oneLiner: Compatible in pregnancy and lactation — topical use only; negligible systemic absorption.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Topical imidazole. First-line for vulvovaginal candidiasis in pregnancy (7-day pessary regimen). Negligible absorption.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Avoid concurrent topical steroid combinations unless indicated.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation — extensive safety record. First-line for genital HSV in pregnancy (treatment and 36-week suppression).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Nucleoside analogue. Extensive pregnancy safety registry data (> 1000 1st-trimester exposures) without malformation signal. Used for primary genital HSV (treat at presentation), recurrences, and suppression from 36 weeks to reduce shedding at delivery.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: For genital HSV suppression from 36 weeks: aciclovir 400 mg TDS until delivery.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; appears in milk but RID < 1%.

references.label: RCOG / BASHH guidelines on Genital Herpes in Pregnancy. 2014.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation; prodrug of aciclovir with better oral bioavailability. Used for HSV/VZV.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Valine prodrug of aciclovir. Better oral bioavailability allows BD dosing. Same safety profile as aciclovir. Investigated for CMV prevention (high-dose valaciclovir in primary maternal CMV infection — emerging evidence).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Suppression dose 500 mg BD from 36 weeks.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy (recommended for influenza — pregnant women are at high risk of severe disease) and lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Neuraminidase inhibitor. Pregnant women are at HIGH risk of severe influenza — treat empirically without waiting for lab confirmation, ideally within 48 h of symptom onset, irrespective of trimester. No teratogenicity signal across pandemic and seasonal cohorts.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Dose: 75 mg BD × 5 days. Influenza vaccination (inactivated) in pregnancy strongly recommended.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; very low milk transfer.

references.label: CDC. Influenza Antiviral Drugs and Pregnancy.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation for active TB treatment or latent TB treatment. Co-prescribe pyridoxine 50 mg/day.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Long pregnancy experience as part of TB treatment. No teratogenicity. Co-prescribe pyridoxine (B6) 50 mg/day (maternal peripheral neuropathy; neonatal pyridoxine deficiency risk).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Standard adult dose 5 mg/kg/day (max 300 mg). Hepatotoxicity monitoring.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; co-prescribe pyridoxine to mother. Monitor infant for hepatotoxicity (rare).

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation for TB. Vitamin K to mother (late pregnancy) and neonate (after delivery) for haemorrhagic disease prevention.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Standard component of TB treatment. No teratogenicity signal. Enzyme inducer — reduces efficacy of combined oral contraceptives. Late-pregnancy use depletes vitamin K → maternal supplementation week 36 onwards and neonatal vitamin K at delivery.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Significant DDI: reduces apixaban, warfarin, oestrogen contraceptives, antiretrovirals (consult specialist).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; very low milk levels.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy for TB (WHO recommended). Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: WHO recommends inclusion in 1st-line TB regimen in pregnancy; historically excluded in US guidance but international experience extensive.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Hyperuricaemia, hepatotoxicity monitoring.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation for TB.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Standard 1st-line TB drug. No teratogenicity. Optic neuropathy is the maternal concern (visual monitoring).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Standard 15 mg/kg/day.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: PREFERRED first-line antiretroviral in pregnancy (WHO, BHIVA, DHHS). Initial 2018 neural tube defect signal not confirmed in updated Tsepamo data. Compatible with breastfeeding decisions made jointly under HIV specialist.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI). First-line ART in pregnancy. The 2018 Tsepamo (Botswana) NTD signal (0.94% vs 0.12% baseline) has NOT been confirmed with longer follow-up (final 2022 analysis: 0.19%, no significant increase). Folic acid 5 mg/day periconceptionally for all women of childbearing potential.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: WHO and DHHS recommend dolutegravir-based ART preconception and throughout pregnancy. Monitor maternal weight gain (DTG associated with greater weight gain).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible in resource-limited settings where breastfeeding recommended; in higher-income settings formula feeding is generally recommended for HIV-positive mothers (decision under HIV specialist).

references.label: Zash R et al. Neural tube defects with dolutegravir treatment from conception (Tsepamo). NEJM 2019; final analysis 2022.
BHIVA Guidelines for the management of HIV in pregnancy. 2024.

oneLiner: PREFERRED NRTI backbone in pregnancy. Used in HIV ART and chronic hepatitis B in pregnancy. Compatible with breastfeeding per HIV-context guidance.

pregnancy.riskSummary: NRTI. TDF (tenofovir disoproxil fumarate) has the largest pregnancy safety dataset; used in HIV ART backbone and to prevent vertical transmission of hepatitis B (from 28-30 weeks in HBeAg+ women with high viral load). TAF (tenofovir alafenamide) has less but reassuring pregnancy data.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Maternal renal monitoring; minimal effect on fetal growth in registry data.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible (HIV decision is context-specific; HBV mothers do breastfeed).

references.label: BHIVA Guidelines for the management of HIV in pregnancy. 2024.

oneLiner: PREFERRED NRTI in pregnancy as part of HIV ART. Compatible with hepatitis B treatment if not on tenofovir.

pregnancy.riskSummary: NRTI. Extensive pregnancy safety record. Standard backbone (with tenofovir or abacavir).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Active against HBV — caution at lamivudine cessation in HIV/HBV coinfected (HBV flare).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy (initial 1st-trimester concern not confirmed in human registries). Dolutegravir-based regimens preferred. Compatible with lactation in HIV setting.

pregnancy.riskSummary: NNRTI. Earlier signal (1st-trimester neural tube defects in non-human primates) NOT confirmed in human registries. Dolutegravir preferred for new starts. Continue if virologically suppressed.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Maternal CNS side-effects (vivid dreams, depression).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible in HIV-context.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy — INSTI with extensive safety data; useful for rapid viral load reduction in late presentation. Compatible with lactation in HIV setting.

pregnancy.riskSummary: INSTI. Rapid VL reduction makes it useful for women presenting late in pregnancy with detectable VL. No teratogenicity signal.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: BD dosing (vs OD dolutegravir).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy as part of ART (HLA-B*5701 negative). Compatible with lactation in HIV setting.

pregnancy.riskSummary: NRTI. Test HLA-B*5701 before initiation (hypersensitivity reaction risk). Pregnancy safety extensive.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Alternative to tenofovir in renal disease.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy; IV intrapartum used for women with detectable HIV viral load near delivery. Compatible with lactation in HIV setting.

pregnancy.riskSummary: First antiretroviral with proven reduction in vertical HIV transmission (ACTG 076). IV intrapartum AZT recommended when maternal VL > 1000 copies/mL near delivery. Maternal anaemia / neutropenia monitoring.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Used in combination ART, not monotherapy.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible (HIV-context decisions).

oneLiner: Acceptable for uncomplicated falciparum malaria in 2nd / 3rd trimester (WHO). 1st trimester: WHO 2022 updated to allow ACT when quinine+clindamycin unavailable. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Artemisinin combination therapy (ACT). First-line in 2nd/3rd trimester for uncomplicated falciparum. 1st trimester: WHO 2022 guidance now recommends ACT as first-line if quinine+clindamycin not available, on basis of accumulated reassuring registry data.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Severe malaria in pregnancy: IV artesunate (preferred over quinine in all trimesters per WHO 2015 update).

trimesterNotes.note: WHO 2022: ACT acceptable if quinine+clindamycin not available.
First-line.
First-line.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; low transfer.

oneLiner: Acceptable for malaria in pregnancy (with clindamycin). Maternal hypoglycaemia monitoring. Avoid high-dose in lactation (G6PD-deficient infants).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Used for uncomplicated falciparum + clindamycin × 7 days, historically the 1st-trimester choice (now superseded in many WHO contexts by ACT). Maternal hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia is a recognised complication.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: For severe malaria: IV artesunate preferred. Quinine reserved for ACT-resistance or specific contexts.

lactation.riskSummary: Acceptable in single therapeutic doses; avoid in G6PD-deficient infants (haemolysis).

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation for chloroquine-sensitive malaria prophylaxis / treatment. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Used where Plasmodium remains chloroquine-sensitive (rare for P. falciparum; relevant for P. vivax / ovale in selected regions). Long pregnancy safety record.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Most regions require alternative agents due to resistance.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy for malaria prophylaxis in chloroquine-resistant areas. Compatible with lactation. Neuropsychiatric side-effects.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Used for malaria prophylaxis when travelling pregnant women to chloroquine-resistant areas. No teratogenicity in registry data. Caution with maternal history of psychiatric illness, seizures.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Weekly dosing; start 2-3 weeks before travel.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy (G6PD status of fetus unknown — haemolysis risk). Acceptable in lactation if maternal AND infant G6PD normal. Used for P. vivax/ovale radical cure.

pregnancy.riskSummary: 8-aminoquinoline used for radical cure of P. vivax / ovale (eliminates hypnozoites). Causes haemolysis in G6PD-deficient individuals — defer until after delivery and confirm fetal/infant G6PD status.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Delay radical cure until postpartum; use chloroquine prophylaxis through pregnancy.

lactation.riskSummary: Acceptable only if both mother and infant G6PD normal.

oneLiner: Used for intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp) in malaria-endemic Africa from 13 weeks. AVOID 1st trimester (folate antagonist). Compatible with lactation in 2-week intervals.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Folate antagonist + sulfa. Used as IPTp (intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy) from 13 weeks gestation, monthly until delivery, in sub-Saharan Africa per WHO. AVOID 1st trimester. Continue periconceptional folic acid 5 mg/day.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Concurrent cotrimoxazole prophylaxis (HIV): do NOT give IPTp-SP (overlapping mechanism / toxicity).

lactation.riskSummary: Acceptable.

oneLiner: PREFERRED for severe malaria in pregnancy (all trimesters) per WHO. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: WHO recommends IV artesunate over IV quinine for severe malaria in pregnancy in ALL trimesters (2015 onwards). Maternal mortality benefit; no excess fetal loss vs quinine.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Dose: 2.4 mg/kg IV at 0, 12, 24 h then daily; switch to oral ACT once tolerating.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: PREFERRED AED in pregnancy with lamotrigine — low teratogenicity. Compatible with lactation (very low milk transfer). Clearance increases — monitor levels.

pregnancy.riskSummary: One of the safest AEDs in pregnancy alongside lamotrigine. Major congenital malformation rate ~ 2-3% (near background). Clearance increases through pregnancy (renal); seizure breakthrough is common — monitor monthly serum level and adjust.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Continue folic acid 5 mg/day. Reduce dose back to preconception within 1-2 weeks postpartum.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; low milk transfer.

references.label: Pennell PB. Use of antiepileptic drugs during pregnancy. NEJM 2020.

oneLiner: Use only when better-studied alternatives unsuitable — 1st-trimester NTD risk (~ 1%), spina bifida. Maternal vitamin K from week 36. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Major congenital malformation rate ~ 5%; specifically NTD (spina bifida) ~ 1%. Enzyme inducer — reduces hormonal contraception efficacy; depletes vitamin K (give maternal vitamin K 10 mg/day from week 36; infant IM vitamin K at birth). Lamotrigine, levetiracetam preferred.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Folic acid 5 mg/day periconceptionally and through pregnancy.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; well-tolerated by breastfed infants.

oneLiner: Avoid initiation in pregnancy — fetal hydantoin syndrome (~ 10%), enzyme induction. Continue if essential, with vitamin K supplementation. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Fetal hydantoin syndrome (craniofacial dysmorphism, distal phalanx hypoplasia, growth restriction, mild cognitive deficit) in ~ 10% of exposed. Enzyme inducer (contraception, vitamin K, vitamin D depletion). Use only if other AEDs fail.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Folic acid 5 mg, maternal vitamin K from 36 weeks, neonatal IM vitamin K.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Limited human pregnancy data; signal for low-birth-weight and preterm birth in some registries. Acceptable for severe pain / epilepsy when alternatives unsuitable. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Limited pregnancy data; small signals for low birth weight and preterm birth in some cohorts (confounded by indication). No clear teratogenicity signal. Used for refractory neuropathic pain in pregnancy when paracetamol / amitriptyline inadequate.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: For epilepsy, lamotrigine / levetiracetam preferred.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; modest milk transfer.

oneLiner: Limited pregnancy data with possible signal for major congenital malformations — avoid if alternative available. Limited lactation data — gabapentin preferred if needed.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Nordic registry (2016, JAMA) and EUROmediCAT signal for cardiac defects and oral cleft — best avoided if alternative exists. Used for anxiety, neuropathic pain, refractory epilepsy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Switch preconception where possible. If essential, fetal cardiac echo at 20 weeks.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited data; gabapentin (more data) preferred if needed.

references.label: Winterfeld U et al. Pregabalin in pregnancy. Neurology 2016.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy — orofacial cleft risk (3-5×), small-for-gestational-age. Less common: hypospadias. Limited lactation data.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Orofacial cleft risk 3-5× background. Small-for-gestational-age. Maternal weight loss / metabolic acidosis. Switch preconception.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: For migraine: amitriptyline or propranolol preferred. For epilepsy: lamotrigine / levetiracetam.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited lactation data; infant exposure measurable.

references.label: FDA Drug Safety Communication: Topiramate and oral cleft. 2011.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy with some teratogenicity signal less than carbamazepine but more than lamotrigine. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Major congenital malformation rate ~ 3%. Better tolerated than carbamazepine but still less safe than lamotrigine / levetiracetam.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Maternal hyponatraemia.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; low milk transfer.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy. In lactation — sertraline preferred (long half-life of fluoxetine + norfluoxetine accumulates in infants).
