pregnancy.riskSummary: SSRI. Extensive pregnancy data; no consistent teratogenicity. Neonatal adaptation syndrome / small PPHN signal as class.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: For new starts in pregnant patient prefer sertraline. Continue if already established and effective.

lactation.riskSummary: Highest milk transfer of the SSRIs; long-half-life active metabolite (norfluoxetine) accumulates in nursing infants — case reports of colic, irritability, poor feeding. If starting an SSRI in a nursing mother, prefer sertraline.

oneLiner: AVOID initiation in 1st trimester — small increased risk of cardiac defects. Continue if essential. Low milk transfer in lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: SSRI with a small but reproducible increased risk of cardiac septal defects when used in 1st trimester (OR ~ 1.5). For new starts in pregnancy, prefer sertraline.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: If already established before pregnancy and effective, balance switch / continuation risk with psychiatrist.

lactation.riskSummary: Low milk transfer; well tolerated.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: SSRI. No consistent teratogenicity signal. Maternal QT prolongation at higher doses — review with ECG.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Class neonatal adaptation syndrome / small PPHN signal.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; low milk transfer.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Active S-enantiomer of citalopram; similar safety profile.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Class effect monitoring.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy. Compatible with lactation but more sedation reports than SSRIs.

pregnancy.riskSummary: SNRI. No consistent teratogenicity. Class neonatal adaptation syndrome; possible small increased PPHN risk.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Severe maternal hypertension at high doses — BP monitoring.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; modest milk transfer; case reports of infant sedation.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy (limited but reassuring data). Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Tetracyclic antidepressant. Limited but reassuring pregnancy data. Useful when sedation / appetite stimulation desirable.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Maternal weight gain.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; modest milk transfer.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy (long safety record); preferred TCA for neuropathic pain / depression when SSRI unsuitable. Compatible with lactation at low doses.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Tricyclic antidepressant. Long pregnancy safety record. Used for depression, migraine prophylaxis, neuropathic pain (10-75 mg ON).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Anticholinergic side-effects.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible at typical doses (10-75 mg). Higher doses: monitor infant sedation.

oneLiner: Use with caution in pregnancy — small absolute risk of Ebstein anomaly (RR ~ 2× but absolute risk small). AVOID in lactation in most cases (infant level can rise with dehydration / illness).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Crosses placenta. Ebstein anomaly historically overestimated (absolute risk ~ 1-2/1000 vs 1/20,000 background). Continue under specialist if benefit outweighs risk. Fetal echo at 20 weeks. Increased dose requirement through pregnancy; reduce 24-48 h before delivery to preconception dose to avoid maternal toxicity once volume contracts. Neonatal floppy baby / thyroid / nephrogenic DI possible.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Maternal renal function and serum level monitoring; avoid NSAIDs / dehydration (lithium toxicity).

lactation.riskSummary: AVOID in most cases — infant lithium levels can rise with intercurrent illness / dehydration; reports of cyanosis, ECG changes, hypothermia. If essential, monitor infant lithium, TSH, creatinine.

references.label: Patorno E et al. Lithium use in pregnancy and the risk of cardiac malformations. NEJM 2017;376:2245-54.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation when an antipsychotic is needed. Maternal metabolic / weight monitoring; gestational diabetes screening.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Atypical antipsychotic. No consistent teratogenicity signal. Maternal metabolic side-effects (weight gain, GDM) — screen with OGTT. Neonatal extrapyramidal / withdrawal symptoms after late-pregnancy exposure.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Continue established treatment; relapse in pregnancy is harmful to mother and fetus.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; one of the best-studied antipsychotics in lactation.

references.label: NICE CG192 — Antenatal and Postnatal Mental Health.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation. Lower placental transfer than olanzapine.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Atypical antipsychotic. Reassuring pregnancy data. Lowest placental transfer of common atypicals.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Metabolic monitoring.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; low milk transfer.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation. Hyperprolactinaemia common — may affect breast milk supply / fertility.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Atypical antipsychotic. Hyperprolactinaemia (can suppress fertility and lactation). No consistent teratogenicity.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Hyperprolactinaemia screening.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; low milk transfer.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy (typical antipsychotic with long safety record). Compatible with lactation in low doses.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Typical antipsychotic. Long safety record. Useful for acute agitation, delirium, hyperemesis gravidarum (low-dose).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: EPS, QT monitoring.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible at typical low doses.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy. Compatible with lactation but may suppress prolactin / milk supply.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Atypical antipsychotic / partial D2 agonist. Reassuring pregnancy data.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Lower prolactin; may reduce milk supply.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; may suppress milk supply (D2 agonism reduces prolactin).

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy only under specialist care (treatment-resistant schizophrenia) — agranulocytosis monitoring continues. AVOID in lactation (infant agranulocytosis risk).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia. Continue if benefit outweighs risk. Maternal and neonatal agranulocytosis monitoring. Neonatal floppy-baby / extrapyramidal symptoms possible.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist (perinatal psychiatry) prescribing.

lactation.riskSummary: AVOID — risk of infant agranulocytosis, sedation, seizures; high milk transfer.
lactation.data: RID 0.5-5%; not orally bioavailable below adult dose but agranulocytosis risk.

oneLiner: Use with caution — short-term use acceptable (status epilepticus, acute severe anxiety, eclampsia adjunct). Chronic / late-pregnancy use causes neonatal withdrawal / floppy baby. Acceptable lactation in single doses.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Benzodiazepine. Crosses placenta. Late-pregnancy chronic use causes neonatal sedation, floppy baby, withdrawal. 1st-trimester signal for oral cleft is weak. Single doses for status epilepticus / severe acute anxiety are acceptable.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: For status: IV lorazepam 4 mg, repeat once. For eclampsia: magnesium sulfate first-line.

lactation.riskSummary: Single doses acceptable; chronic use causes infant sedation / poor feeding.

oneLiner: Avoid prolonged use in pregnancy (neonatal withdrawal, floppy baby). Single therapeutic doses (status epilepticus, alcohol withdrawal) acceptable. Caution in lactation (long half-life, infant accumulation).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Same class effects as lorazepam. Longer half-life makes neonatal washout slower.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Prefer lorazepam for repeated dosing in pregnancy.

lactation.riskSummary: Avoid repeated dosing; single doses acceptable. Long half-life means accumulation.

oneLiner: Acceptable for single-dose procedural sedation / induction / status epilepticus in pregnancy. Caution late pregnancy (neonatal sedation). Compatible with lactation as single doses.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Short-acting benzodiazepine. Single doses for procedural sedation, induction, or out-of-hospital status (buccal / IM) are acceptable. Chronic use causes neonatal effects as a class.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Buccal midazolam is community first-line for seizure cluster.

lactation.riskSummary: Single doses compatible; short half-life.

oneLiner: Avoid in pregnancy where possible — limited data; sedative-hypnotic class effects. Acceptable single occasional doses in lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Z-drug. Limited pregnancy data. Avoid in 1st trimester if alternative; sleep hygiene + CBT-I preferred. Short courses occasionally acceptable.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Tolerance / dependence with prolonged use.

lactation.riskSummary: Single occasional doses acceptable; chronic use causes infant sedation.

oneLiner: Avoid in pregnancy where possible; some signal for preterm birth and low birth weight. Acceptable single doses in lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Z-drug. Some cohort signals for preterm birth, low birth weight, SGA (confounded by indication). Use sleep hygiene + CBT-I first line.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Short courses if essential.

lactation.riskSummary: Single occasional doses acceptable; chronic infant sedation reported.

oneLiner: PREFERRED treatment for diabetes (T1DM, T2DM, GDM) requiring pharmacotherapy in pregnancy. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Does not cross placenta. Standard of care for diabetes in pregnancy. Rapid-acting (aspart, lispro) and intermediate (NPH) have most pregnancy data; long-acting analogues (glargine, detemir, degludec) reassuring in registries. Insulin requirements rise through pregnancy (1.5-2× by 3rd trimester) then fall abruptly postpartum.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: For T1DM: continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion (pump) or multiple daily injections. Target HbA1c < 6.5% preconception; fasting glucose < 5.3 mmol/L, postprandial < 7.8 mmol/L in pregnancy.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; not orally absorbed by infant.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy if alternative available — placental transfer; risk of neonatal hypoglycaemia and possible higher macrosomia vs insulin. Use insulin or metformin instead. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Sulfonylurea. Crosses placenta. Higher neonatal hypoglycaemia and macrosomia vs insulin in MFMU randomised trial. NICE and ACOG do not recommend as first-line for GDM.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Use insulin (preferred) or metformin.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; not detected in milk.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy — switch to insulin (preferred) or metformin. Limited lactation data.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Sulfonylurea. Less pregnancy data than glibenclamide; risk of neonatal hypoglycaemia. Switch preconception.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Use insulin or metformin.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited data; insulin/metformin preferred.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy — limited data; animal nephrotoxicity. Switch to insulin / metformin preconception. Limited lactation data — avoid.

pregnancy.riskSummary: SGLT2 inhibitor. Limited human data; renal maturation toxicity in animal studies. Switch preconception. Same approach for HFrEF/CKD indications.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Switch to insulin / metformin for glycaemic control.

lactation.riskSummary: AVOID — limited data; theoretical concern for infant renal effects.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy and lactation — same class concerns as empagliflozin.

pregnancy.riskSummary: SGLT2 inhibitor — class effect avoidance.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Switch preconception.

lactation.riskSummary: AVOID.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy — limited data; switch to insulin / metformin. Limited lactation data.

pregnancy.riskSummary: DPP-4 inhibitor. Limited human pregnancy data; no robust teratogenicity signal but insufficient reassurance.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Switch preconception.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited data; insulin preferred.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy — limited data; animal embryofetal toxicity. Stop preconception (clearance varies; semaglutide longer washout). Limited lactation data.

pregnancy.riskSummary: GLP-1 receptor agonist. Animal embryofetal toxicity. Switch preconception. Semaglutide / dulaglutide require longer washout (≥ 1-2 months before conception, per manufacturer).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Switch to insulin (T2DM) or stop (obesity indication, lifestyle / pre-conception care).

lactation.riskSummary: AVOID — limited data.

oneLiner: PREFERRED — required throughout pregnancy and lactation for maternal hypothyroidism. Increase dose by ~ 25-50% in early pregnancy.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Endogenous hormone. Replacement is mandatory in hypothyroidism. Inadequate replacement causes pregnancy loss, preterm birth, neurodevelopmental impairment. Increase dose by ~ 25-50% in early pregnancy; check TSH every 4-6 weeks. Target TSH < 2.5 mU/L 1st trimester; < 3.0 mU/L 2nd/3rd.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Postpartum return to preconception dose.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible — physiological hormone; very small amounts in milk.

references.label: ATA Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Thyroid Disease During Pregnancy and the Postpartum. 2017.

oneLiner: PREFERRED antithyroid drug in 1st trimester (carbimazole/methimazole embryopathy). Switch to carbimazole 2nd trimester (PTU hepatotoxicity). Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Used for Graves' disease / hyperthyroidism in pregnancy. PTU preferred in 1st trimester to avoid the carbimazole / methimazole embryopathy (aplasia cutis, choanal / oesophageal atresia, omphalocele). PTU has its own concern of severe hepatotoxicity — switch to carbimazole from 16 weeks. Lowest effective dose to keep maternal free T4 at upper limit of reference range.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Coordinate with endocrine specialist; monitor fetal thyroid (goitre, growth) with ultrasound.

trimesterNotes.note: PTU preferred.
Switch to carbimazole.
Carbimazole.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible — low milk transfer; preferred antithyroid in lactation.

oneLiner: AVOID in 1st trimester (embryopathy syndrome). PREFERRED 2nd / 3rd trimester (PTU hepatotoxicity). Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Carbimazole and its active metabolite methimazole cause an embryopathy (aplasia cutis, choanal atresia, oesophageal atresia, omphalocele, dysmorphism) in ~ 2-4% of 1st-trimester exposures. Switch to PTU for the 1st trimester; switch back to carbimazole from 16 weeks (PTU hepatotoxicity).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Lowest effective dose.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible at typical doses (≤ 20 mg/day carbimazole).

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation for maternal autoimmune / inflammatory disease. Maternal GDM, hypertension, infection monitoring. Lowest effective dose.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Crosses placenta but largely inactivated by placental 11β-HSD2 — fetal exposure low. Small signal for oral cleft with 1st-trimester high-dose exposure (absolute risk ~ 3-5/1000). Maternal risks: GDM, hypertension, infection. Long-term high-dose: adrenal suppression risk for neonate — stress-dose steroid cover at delivery if maternal prednisolone > 7.5 mg/day for > 3 weeks.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Use lowest dose. Screen for GDM (75 g OGTT).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible at ≤ 20 mg/day; very low milk transfer. At higher doses (> 40 mg) some advise timing feeds 4 h post-dose.

references.label: EULAR points to consider for use of antirheumatic drugs in pregnancy. 2016.

oneLiner: Used for fetal lung maturation (24-34 wk threatened preterm birth) and maternal indications. Crosses placenta — for non-obstetric maternal disease prefer prednisolone where possible.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Long-acting potent corticosteroid. NOT inactivated by placental 11β-HSD2 — high fetal exposure. STANDARD of care: single course (12 mg IM × 2 doses, 24 h apart) for women at risk of preterm birth between 24+0 and 33+6 weeks (ACOG; NICE NG25). For maternal autoimmune disease prefer prednisolone (placentally inactivated). Repeated courses or high-dose chronic use may impact fetal growth and neurodevelopment.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Antenatal corticosteroids reduce neonatal RDS, IVH, NEC, mortality.

lactation.riskSummary: Acceptable; for single antenatal courses compatible with subsequent breastfeeding.

references.label: NICE NG25 — Preterm Labour and Birth.

oneLiner: PREFERRED antenatal corticosteroid for fetal lung maturation 24-34 weeks. Compatible with breastfeeding after antenatal courses.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Antenatal corticosteroid of choice in many centres — 12 mg IM × 2 doses 24 h apart at 24+0 to 33+6 weeks for women at risk of preterm birth in next 7 days. Reduces neonatal RDS, IVH, NEC, mortality.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: ACOG/NICE: consider for late preterm (34+0-36+6) in selected cases. Avoid more than 2 rescue courses.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation for adrenal insufficiency replacement. Stress doses at delivery.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Mineralocorticoid replacement for Addison's / CAH. Required dose unchanged in pregnancy generally; monitor BP / electrolytes.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Stress-dose hydrocortisone IV at labour.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; very low milk levels.

references.label: Endocrine Society. Adrenal Insufficiency in Pregnancy.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation as glucocorticoid replacement (adrenal insufficiency) and for stress-dose cover at delivery.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Largely inactivated by placental 11β-HSD2. Standard glucocorticoid replacement in Addison's / hypopituitarism. Stress-dose at delivery: IV 100 mg at onset of labour, 200 mg/24 h infusion until delivery.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Continue maintenance through pregnancy.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable preconception for prolactinoma fertility restoration; usually stopped once pregnancy confirmed unless tumour expansion. AVOID in lactation (suppresses lactation).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Dopamine agonist. Used to restore ovulation in hyperprolactinaemia. Once pregnancy confirmed, typically stop (microadenomas) — monitor for tumour expansion symptoms. Continue if macroadenoma.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Cabergoline (longer half-life) often preferred preconception.

lactation.riskSummary: Suppresses lactation — not used in breastfeeding mothers. Once used postpartum to suppress lactation, now generally avoided (cardiovascular adverse events).

oneLiner: Acceptable preconception for prolactinoma; stop on pregnancy confirmation unless macroadenoma. Suppresses lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Dopamine agonist. Longer half-life and better tolerated than bromocriptine. Same pregnancy management.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Cabergoline for postpartum lactation suppression is licensed but should be used cautiously (hypertension, stroke reports).

lactation.riskSummary: Suppresses lactation.

oneLiner: CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy (no indication). Combined oral contraceptive use BEFORE conception not teratogenic. Avoid combined hormonal contraception in lactation < 6 weeks postpartum (VTE; lactation suppression).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Inadvertent COCP exposure in early pregnancy does NOT increase malformation rates — reassure patients. Combined hormonal contraception itself has no indication during pregnancy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: For HRT — generally stopped on pregnancy confirmation (no indication).

lactation.riskSummary: Combined hormonal contraception is AVOIDED in the first 6 weeks postpartum (VTE risk) and may suppress lactation if started before milk supply established. Progestogen-only methods preferred during breastfeeding.

references.label: FSRH UK Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy — used for luteal phase support in ART, prevention of preterm birth in selected women. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Used for luteal phase support in IVF and to prevent recurrent preterm birth (vaginal progesterone in women with short cervix / prior preterm). No teratogenicity at therapeutic doses.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: OPPTIMUM (vaginal) and PROLONG (IM 17-hydroxyprogesterone caproate) trials. 17-OHPC withdrawn from market in 2023 after failed confirmatory trial.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy (teratogen — craniofacial, genitourinary). AVOID in lactation. Effective contraception during and 2 months after treatment.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Selective estrogen receptor modulator. Teratogenic in animals; case reports of human malformations (Goldenhar, craniofacial). For early breast cancer in young women: balance interruption / fertility / cancer outcome with oncology (POSITIVE trial shows 2-year interruption acceptable for ER+ early disease).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Effective contraception during AND ≥ 2 months after stopping.

lactation.riskSummary: AVOID — suppresses lactation; theoretical antiestrogenic effect on infant.

reproductive.contraception: Effective non-hormonal or progestogen-only contraception during treatment and for 2 months after stopping. Combined hormonal contraception contraindicated (cancer-driver concerns).

references.label: Partridge AH et al. POSITIVE trial. NEJM 2023.

oneLiner: PREFERRED in pregnancy and lactation — short-acting beta-2 agonist for asthma. Maternal uncontrolled asthma is itself dangerous.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Inhaled SABA. Low systemic exposure. Maternal poorly-controlled asthma causes hypoxia → fetal hypoxia, growth restriction, prematurity. Treat as in non-pregnant adult. Continue regular controllers; do not down-titrate based on pregnancy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: For acute severe asthma in pregnancy: same management as non-pregnant — high-flow O2, nebulised salbutamol, oral / IV steroid, magnesium IV as needed.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; minimal milk transfer at inhaled doses.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation — combined with inhaled corticosteroid for moderate-severe asthma.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Inhaled LABA. Used in combination with inhaled corticosteroid (ICS/LABA — never LABA monotherapy). Reassuring pregnancy registry data.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Continue established treatment; uncontrolled asthma is more dangerous than therapy.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible — minimal milk transfer.

oneLiner: PREFERRED inhaled corticosteroid in pregnancy and lactation alongside budesonide. Maintain controller therapy.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Inhaled corticosteroid. Largest pregnancy safety dataset alongside budesonide. Continue at lowest effective dose.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Do not down-titrate ICS in pregnancy.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible — minimal systemic absorption.

oneLiner: PREFERRED ICS in pregnancy and lactation (extensive registry data).

pregnancy.riskSummary: ICS. Most reassuring pregnancy registry data (SMART registry). Used for asthma, EGPA, and oral / enteric formulations for IBD.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Continue at lowest effective dose.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation; budesonide has more data but fluticasone reassuring.

pregnancy.riskSummary: ICS. Reassuring registry data.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Continue.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation — short-acting anticholinergic for asthma exacerbation, COPD.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Inhaled anticholinergic. Minimal systemic absorption. Used adjunctively in acute severe asthma and COPD.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: No specific pregnancy concerns at inhaled doses.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Limited pregnancy data; acceptable if essential for asthma / COPD when alternatives inadequate. Limited lactation data.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Inhaled long-acting anticholinergic. Limited pregnancy data; no signal in available reports. Used for severe asthma and COPD.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Continue if essential.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited data; minimal systemic absorption expected.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation; FDA black-box for neuropsychiatric effects (mother), but no consistent teratogenicity signal.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Leukotriene receptor antagonist. No teratogenicity in registry data. Continue if established and effective.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: FDA black-box for neuropsychiatric AEs (2020) — review benefit/risk; counsel mood/behaviour.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; low milk transfer.

references.label: FDA Drug Safety Communication: Montelukast neuropsychiatric. March 2020.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation for GORD when antacids / lifestyle inadequate.

pregnancy.riskSummary: PPI. Reassuring pregnancy safety data (large cohort studies — no malformation signal). First-line for GORD in pregnancy not responding to lifestyle / alginates / H2RA.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Step-up algorithm: lifestyle → antacid/alginate → ranitidine/famotidine → omeprazole.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; low milk transfer.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation — same PPI class.

pregnancy.riskSummary: PPI class effect — reassuring data.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: As omeprazole.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Historically used; WITHDRAWN globally 2020 due to NDMA contamination. Use famotidine instead.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Withdrawn from market (FDA, MHRA, EMA 2020) due to N-nitrosodimethylamine (NDMA) probable-carcinogen contamination. Historic pregnancy use was extensive without safety concerns; use famotidine.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Replace with famotidine 20-40 mg BD.

lactation.riskSummary: Withdrawn — use famotidine.

references.label: FDA market withdrawal of ranitidine. April 2020.

oneLiner: PREFERRED H2 antagonist in pregnancy and lactation since ranitidine withdrawal.

pregnancy.riskSummary: H2 antagonist. Reassuring pregnancy data. Step-up for GORD before PPI.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: 20-40 mg BD.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; low milk transfer.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy for moderate-severe N+V/hyperemesis when first-line antiemetics fail; small absolute increase in oral cleft from 1st-trimester exposure remains debated. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: 5-HT3 antagonist. Some studies (Danish registry; large US Medicaid cohort) show small absolute increase in oral cleft (~ 3/10,000 additional cases) with 1st-trimester use; other studies find no signal. Maternal QT prolongation; avoid in maternal long-QT. For hyperemesis: doxylamine-pyridoxine, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, cyclizine are first-line; ondansetron when these fail.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: 4-8 mg PO/IV BD-QDS PRN.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; low milk transfer.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 69 — Nausea and Vomiting in Pregnancy.
Huybrechts KF et al. JAMA 2018 ondansetron in pregnancy.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy as antiemetic. Compatible with lactation but may suppress prolactin / supply at high doses — short courses preferred.

pregnancy.riskSummary: D2 antagonist + prokinetic. No teratogenicity. Used for hyperemesis gravidarum, postoperative N+V. Extrapyramidal AE — limit to ≤ 5 days as licensed.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: 10 mg TDS PO/IV/IM.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; historically used as galactagogue (limited evidence), short courses acceptable.

oneLiner: Acceptable for hyperemesis gravidarum and vertigo. Compatible with lactation as short course.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Phenothiazine. Long pregnancy experience as antiemetic. Extrapyramidal AE.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: 5-10 mg PO/IM TDS.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy as first-line antiemetic for nausea/vomiting in pregnancy. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Antihistamine antiemetic. Long pregnancy experience. First-line in UK practice (alongside doxylamine-pyridoxine, promethazine).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: 50 mg PO/IM TDS.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; low milk transfer.

oneLiner: PREFERRED first-line for nausea / vomiting of pregnancy (ACOG, FIGO).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Doxylamine (antihistamine) + pyridoxine (B6). Strongest evidence base for nausea/vomiting of pregnancy; FDA-approved combination (Diclegis). First-line per ACOG.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: 10/10 mg up to QDS. May add metoclopramide / cyclizine / ondansetron if inadequate.

lactation.riskSummary: Acceptable; possible mild infant drowsiness with doxylamine.

references.label: ACOG Practice Bulletin 189 — Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy.

oneLiner: Compatible in pregnancy and lactation — non-absorbed osmotic laxative.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Non-absorbed disaccharide. First-line for constipation in pregnancy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: 15-30 mL BD-TDS.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation for short courses. Bulk laxatives / lactulose preferred long-term.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Stimulant laxative. Acceptable short-term; chronic use can cause hypokalaemia and dependence. Lactulose / fibre / macrogol first-line.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; possible loose stools in infant.

oneLiner: Limited pregnancy data — use for short courses for symptomatic diarrhoea after exclusion of infection. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Mu-opioid receptor agonist (gut). Limited human data; one cohort suggested small increase in major malformations (not replicated). Use short-term for symptomatic diarrhoea after exclusion of bacterial / inflammatory cause.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: AVOID in bloody diarrhoea / suspected colitis.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; very low milk transfer.

oneLiner: PREFERRED for IBD / rheumatoid disease in pregnancy and lactation. Co-prescribe folic acid 5 mg.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Compatible with pregnancy throughout. Folate antagonist — co-prescribe folic acid 5 mg/day periconception and through pregnancy. Used for IBD and rheumatoid arthritis.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Reversible reduction in sperm count in men — relevant if male partner taking it and conception attempted.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; rare reports of infant bloody diarrhoea — monitor.

oneLiner: PREFERRED in pregnancy and lactation for SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome, rheumatoid disease. Reduces flare and improves outcomes.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Compatible throughout pregnancy. Reduces SLE flares, improves pregnancy outcomes in SLE / APS. Continue through pregnancy. No teratogenicity in extensive registries. Continue at 400 mg/day usual dose.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Annual ophthalmology screening (retinopathy).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; low milk transfer.

oneLiner: PREFERRED immunosuppressant in pregnancy and lactation for IBD, transplant, autoimmune disease.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Compatible. Fetal liver lacks the enzyme to convert azathioprine to its active 6-thioguanine metabolite, theoretically protecting the fetus. Long pregnancy experience in IBD, transplant, lupus nephritis. Maintain therapeutic dose; do not lower for pregnancy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: TPMT status should be confirmed. Monitor LFTs and FBC.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible at typical doses; small amounts in milk; long-term cohorts of breastfed infants show normal growth and development.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation — particularly for transplant maintenance, severe IBD, refractory autoimmune disease. Monitor maternal levels, BP, renal function.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Calcineurin inhibitor. Extensive transplant pregnancy experience. No specific malformation pattern. Maternal hypertension, renal impairment, GDM monitoring.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Therapeutic level monitoring; clearance may change.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; infant exposure low; long-term cohorts reassuring.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation — preferred over ciclosporin in many transplant programmes.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Calcineurin inhibitor. Reassuring transplant pregnancy data. Similar monitoring to ciclosporin. Hyperglycaemia / GDM risk.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Level monitoring; clearance often increased in pregnancy — dose adjustment common.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; infant exposure low.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy through ~ 16-20 weeks; placental transfer increases 3rd trimester — interrupt in late 2nd / 3rd trimester if disease quiescent; avoid live vaccines in infant 6 months. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Anti-TNF (IgG1). Active placental transfer in 2nd / 3rd trimesters via FcRn — detectable in infant for up to 6-12 months. Continue through pregnancy in active disease; consider last dose ~ 20 weeks if quiescent (specialist decision). Live vaccines (e.g. BCG, rotavirus) AVOIDED in infants exposed in utero until antibody clears (typically 6 months; check level if BCG considered).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Inactivated vaccines proceed normally.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible — large protein, negligible oral bioavailability.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy with same 2nd/3rd-trimester placental-transfer considerations as infliximab. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Anti-TNF IgG1. Same placental transfer dynamics as infliximab.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Live vaccines in exposed infants per specialist.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy through 1st-2nd trimester; lower placental transfer than infliximab/adalimumab. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Anti-TNF (Fc-fusion). Lower placental transfer than IgG monoclonals.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Live vaccine consideration as with anti-TNF class.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: PREFERRED anti-TNF in pregnancy — pegylated Fab fragment with NEGLIGIBLE placental transfer. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Pegylated Fab fragment — no Fc → no FcRn-mediated placental transfer. CRIB study showed negligible transfer to fetus. Preferred anti-TNF in women of childbearing potential and through pregnancy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Live vaccines in infant proceed normally (no fetal antibody exposure).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; minimal milk transfer.

references.label: Mariette X et al. CRIB study. Ann Rheum Dis 2018.

oneLiner: Avoid in 2nd / 3rd trimester (B-cell depletion in fetus). 1st-trimester exposure acceptable when essential (severe lymphoma, autoimmune disease). Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Anti-CD20 monoclonal (IgG1). Placental transfer in 2nd/3rd trimesters → fetal/neonatal B-cell depletion. 1st-trimester exposure has no clear teratogenicity. For B-cell lymphoma in pregnancy, treat as indicated. Live vaccines avoided in exposed infant until B-cell recovery.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist-led; ideally dose at conception postponed to 2nd / 3rd trimester.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible — large protein, low oral bioavailability.

oneLiner: CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy — teratogenic; long half-life requires cholestyramine washout before conception. AVOID in lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Pyrimidine synthesis inhibitor. Teratogenic in animals. Active metabolite has very long half-life (months). Before conception (or with inadvertent exposure): cholestyramine 8 g TDS × 11 days washout, then confirm plasma level < 0.02 mg/L on two tests 2 weeks apart.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Effective contraception during AND for ≥ 2 years after stopping (unless washout).

lactation.riskSummary: AVOID.

reproductive.contraception: Effective contraception during and ≥ 2 years after stopping (or until cholestyramine washout confirms low plasma level).
reproductive.pregnancyTesting: Before initiation and periodically during treatment.

oneLiner: CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy — teratogenic (microtia, orofacial cleft, cardiac defects). Effective contraception during and 6 weeks after stopping. AVOID in lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Teratogenic — microtia / external auditory canal atresia, cleft lip/palate, cardiac, renal, ophthalmic anomalies. Switch to azathioprine preconception (for transplant, lupus nephritis).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: REMS / MHRA Pregnancy Prevention Programme. Sperm DNA effect concern in males — counsel.

lactation.riskSummary: AVOID — limited data; theoretical concern.

reproductive.contraception: Two complementary methods during treatment AND for 6 weeks after stopping (women); 90 days (men) per MHRA.

oneLiner: Standard for labour induction / augmentation and active management of 3rd stage. Compatible with lactation; in fact promotes letdown.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Endogenous hormone. Used IV for induction / augmentation of labour and IM/IV in active management of 3rd stage to reduce PPH.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Water-intoxication risk with prolonged high-dose IV infusion. Tachysystole monitoring.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible — supports lactation (letdown reflex).

oneLiner: Acceptable alternative to oxytocin for PPH prevention after Caesarean / vaginal delivery. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Long-acting oxytocin analogue. Single IM/IV dose after delivery for PPH prophylaxis (CHAMPION trial). Heat-stable formulation supports use in resource-limited settings.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Single 100 microg IV/IM dose.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

references.label: Widmer M et al. CHAMPION trial. NEJM 2018.

oneLiner: Used for medical management of miscarriage, medical abortion, labour induction, and PPH treatment / prevention. CONTRAINDICATED if continuing pregnancy desired (teratogen — Möbius sequence with 1st-trimester failed abortion).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Prostaglandin E1 analogue. Multiple obstetric indications (MIFI, miscarriage management, labour induction, PPH treatment per WHO). Teratogenic — Möbius sequence and limb defects in continuing pregnancies after failed 1st-trimester termination. Use only when ending or completing pregnancy is the goal, or postpartum.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Different doses for different indications — confirm protocol.

trimesterNotes.note: Used for medical abortion / missed miscarriage (with mifepristone). Contraindicated if continuing pregnancy desired.
Used for labour induction (PGE1 protocol) and postpartum for PPH.

lactation.riskSummary: Acceptable in single therapeutic postpartum dose; not used chronically.

references.label: WHO recommendations for the prevention and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage. 2012/2018.

oneLiner: Used with misoprostol for medical abortion / management of miscarriage; not for continuing pregnancy.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Antiprogesterone. Used for medical abortion (with misoprostol) and management of missed miscarriage. Not used in continuing pregnancy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Per NICE NG140 / WHO; 200 mg PO then misoprostol 24-48 h later.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited lactation data; single therapeutic dose acceptable.

references.label: WHO. Safe abortion: technical and policy guidance.

oneLiner: Used for PPH (3rd-line / second-line) after delivery. CONTRAINDICATED in maternal hypertension / pre-eclampsia. Compatible with single doses in lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Ergot alkaloid; sustained uterine contraction. CONTRAINDICATED antepartum — for postpartum PPH only. AVOID in maternal hypertension, pre-eclampsia, ischaemic heart disease (severe vasoconstriction risk).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: 500 microg IM (or 250 microg slow IV). Often combined with oxytocin as Syntometrine.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible in single therapeutic dose; chronic use can suppress prolactin.

oneLiner: PREFERRED for eclampsia treatment and severe pre-eclampsia seizure prophylaxis. Also for fetal neuroprotection at extreme preterm delivery. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Established for: (1) eclampsia seizure treatment and prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia (Magpie, Collaborative Eclampsia Trial); (2) fetal neuroprotection before anticipated preterm delivery < 30 (-34) weeks (reduces cerebral palsy). NOT recommended for tocolysis (no benefit; cumulative high-dose maternal harm).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Loading 4 g IV over 5-10 min, maintenance 1 g/h IV for 24 h. Monitor reflexes, RR, urine output, levels (target 2-3.5 mmol/L). Calcium gluconate antidote available.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; transient milk magnesium rise without infant consequences.

references.label: Altman D et al. Magpie trial. Lancet 2002.

oneLiner: PREFERRED — recommended in every pregnancy in any trimester. Protects mother (high-risk for severe influenza) and infant in first 6 months.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Inactivated influenza vaccine recommended in EVERY pregnancy regardless of trimester per CDC, RCOG, ACOG, WHO, JCVI. Pregnant women are at high risk of severe influenza (hospitalisation, ICU, death — see 2009 H1N1 pandemic data). Vaccination also protects infant via transplacental antibody and via lactation in the first 6 months.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Live attenuated nasal influenza vaccine (LAIV) is NOT used in pregnancy — give inactivated injection.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible — encouraged.

references.label: CDC ACIP. Influenza Vaccination of Pregnant Women.
RCOG Patient Information: Influenza in Pregnancy.

oneLiner: PREFERRED — recommended in every pregnancy 16-32 weeks for neonatal pertussis prevention.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Recommended in EVERY pregnancy (16-32 weeks, ideally before 32 wk for optimal antibody transfer) per JCVI / ACIP. Transplacental pertussis antibody protects neonate before primary vaccination — programme reduces infant pertussis death.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Boostrix-IPV in UK; Tdap in US.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: PREFERRED — recommended in pregnancy and lactation; benefit substantial.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Recommended in pregnancy per RCOG, ACOG, CDC, WHO. Pregnant women have higher COVID-19 severe disease risk. Vaccination is non-replicating mRNA — no in-vivo replication. Extensive registry data show no excess miscarriage / preterm / SGA. Transplacental antibody and milk antibody confer infant protection.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Boosters per current programme.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: LIVE attenuated — CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy. Avoid pregnancy for 1 month after. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Live attenuated. Theoretical fetal varicella syndrome risk — registries show no actual case but contraindication maintained on precautionary basis. Inadvertent administration is NOT itself an indication for termination — counsel and follow up. Avoid pregnancy for 1 month after vaccination.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Screen susceptible women postpartum and immunise before next pregnancy.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: LIVE — CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy; avoid conception for 1 month after. Compatible with lactation; postpartum is the right time for susceptible women.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Live attenuated. Theoretical (not observed) fetal risk. Avoid pregnancy for 1 month after. Inadvertent vaccination is not itself an indication for termination. Screen rubella immunity preconception / in early pregnancy; vaccinate susceptible women immediately postpartum.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Common postpartum opportunity.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible — recommended postpartum.

oneLiner: Infant vaccine — not given to mother. For infants exposed in utero to TNF / B-cell immunosuppressants, defer until antibody clears (per specialist).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Live attenuated infant vaccine. Maternal anti-TNF / rituximab placental transfer can cause infant immunosuppression in first 6 months — defer rotavirus (and BCG in some settings) until antibody clears.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist (rheumatology / gastroenterology / neonatology) review of in-utero biologic exposure.

lactation.riskSummary: Maternal vaccine context not applicable; infant vaccine compatible during maternal breastfeeding.

oneLiner: LIVE — CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy (maternal). Infant BCG: defer if in-utero exposure to biologics until antibody clears.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Live attenuated. Not given to pregnant mothers. Neonatal BCG — defer in infants exposed to maternal anti-TNF or rituximab in utero until antibody clears (typically 6 months).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Standard neonatal BCG schedule in non-exposed infants per programme.

lactation.riskSummary: N/A maternal vaccine; infant vaccine compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy — inactivated; recommended for at-risk women. Neonatal birth-dose recommended for all infants of HBsAg+ mothers.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Inactivated. Safe in pregnancy. Recommend in at-risk women (healthcare workers, multiple partners, IDU, household contact of HBV carrier). Universal neonatal birth-dose for infants of HBsAg+ mothers (+ HBIG) per WHO/UK schedule.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Maternal antiviral (tenofovir) from 28-30 weeks if maternal HBV DNA > 200,000 IU/mL.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

references.label: WHO Hepatitis B vaccine position paper.

oneLiner: Not routinely given in pregnancy (defer until postpartum). Inadvertent exposure: no signal of harm. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Inactivated VLP. Not routinely recommended in pregnancy (insufficient direct safety data, no clear harm signal in registries). Defer until postpartum. Inadvertent vaccination not an indication for termination.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Catch-up postpartum if eligible.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: LIVE — avoid in pregnancy where possible; if travel to endemic area unavoidable, vaccinate (benefit > risk).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Live attenuated. Avoid in pregnancy where possible; when travel to endemic area is unavoidable, vaccinate after specialist advice — risk of severe disease outweighs theoretical vaccine risk. Limited but reassuring registry data.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Defer breastfeeding for 2-4 weeks if infant < 6 months (neonatal YEL-AVD case reports).

lactation.riskSummary: Defer breastfeeding for 2-4 weeks after vaccination if infant < 6 months.

references.label: WHO Yellow Fever Vaccine Position Paper.

oneLiner: PREFERRED — 400 microg/day for all women planning pregnancy; 5 mg/day if higher-risk for NTD (prior affected pregnancy, AED therapy, diabetes, BMI ≥ 30, sickle cell, coeliac, malabsorption).

pregnancy.riskSummary: PRIMARY PREVENTION of NTDs. 400 microg/day for all women trying to conceive AND until 12 weeks. 5 mg/day for higher-risk: prior NTD pregnancy, AED use, diabetes, BMI ≥ 30, sickle cell, coeliac, malabsorption, family history of NTD. Folic acid 5 mg also indicated with sulfasalazine, methotrexate (preconception washout), trimethoprim use.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Continue folic acid 5 mg/day throughout pregnancy if high-risk.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: PREFERRED — first-line for iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Standard treatment for iron deficiency anaemia. Routine antenatal supplementation per WHO; UK targets treatment of demonstrated deficiency. Side-effects (GI) may limit adherence — alternate-day dosing or alternate salt may help.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Ferrous sulfate 200 mg OD-TDS (65 mg elemental); fumarate 210 mg OD-TDS (68 mg elemental).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

references.label: BSH Guideline on the Management of Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy.
WHO Daily Iron and Folic Acid Supplementation.

oneLiner: Acceptable in 2nd / 3rd trimester for iron deficiency anaemia intolerant of oral. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Used from 2nd trimester for iron deficiency anaemia not responding to / intolerant of oral iron, or rapid correction needed (e.g. severe anaemia in late pregnancy). Reassuring registry data. Reactions / hypophosphataemia (FCM) monitoring.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Hb < 105 g/L + ferritin < 30 microg/L = iron deficiency anaemia per BSH.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy; recommended in populations with low dietary calcium for pre-eclampsia prophylaxis (WHO 1.5-2 g/day from 20 wk).

pregnancy.riskSummary: WHO recommends calcium supplementation 1.5-2 g/day from 20 weeks in populations with low dietary calcium intake for pre-eclampsia prevention. Safe; avoid co-administration with iron (chelation).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Antacid use is acceptable.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: PREFERRED — supplementation 400-1000 IU/day recommended in pregnancy and lactation in deficiency / at-risk groups.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Recommended in pregnancy at 400-1000 IU/day (NICE PH56). Higher-risk groups (dark skin, limited sun, BMI ≥ 30) may need higher (treat deficiency to 25-OH-D > 50 nmol/L).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Treat deficiency: 50,000 IU/week × 6-8 weeks then maintenance.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Compatible in pregnancy and lactation. Treat deficiency (vegan diet, pernicious anaemia, post-bariatric).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Essential nutrient. Treat deficiency through pregnancy (oral or IM hydroxocobalamin). Untreated deficiency causes maternal anaemia and infant neurodevelopmental risk.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Vegan / vegetarian / post-bariatric women particularly.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: AVOID high-dose supplementation in pregnancy (> 10,000 IU/day) — teratogen. Diet and routine prenatal vitamins (≤ 5000 IU) are safe.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Teratogen at high doses (> 10,000 IU/day retinol — craniofacial, cardiac, CNS, thymus defects). Avoid liver / liver pâté in pregnancy. Routine prenatal multivitamins (≤ 5000 IU) are safe. Beta-carotene is non-teratogenic.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: In vitamin A deficiency (Global South contexts) WHO recommends carefully dosed postpartum supplementation.

lactation.riskSummary: Acceptable at physiological doses; high-dose supplementation should be avoided.

references.label: WHO Vitamin A supplementation in pregnancy.

oneLiner: ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy — severe teratogen (retinoid embryopathy). Mandatory Pregnancy Prevention Programme. AVOID in lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Powerful teratogen — retinoid embryopathy (craniofacial, CNS, cardiovascular, thymus defects); 30% major malformation rate in 1st-trimester exposure. Mandatory MHRA Pregnancy Prevention Programme: dual contraception 1 month before, during, and 1 month after; monthly pregnancy testing; signed risk acknowledgement.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Inadvertent exposure: urgent referral; counsel on dose, timing, parental wishes.

lactation.riskSummary: AVOID — limited data; theoretical infant CNS / cardiac risk.

reproductive.contraception: Two complementary methods 1 month before, throughout, and 1 month after treatment.
reproductive.pregnancyTesting: Monthly during treatment; before each prescription.

references.label: MHRA Pregnancy Prevention Programme for oral retinoids.

oneLiner: ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy — historic teratogen (phocomelia, multiple organ defects). Mandatory Pregnancy Prevention Programme. AVOID in lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Among the most teratogenic drugs known (1957-61 disaster, > 10,000 affected infants). Phocomelia, amelia, multiple organ defects. Reintroduced for myeloma, ENL leprosy under STRICT pregnancy prevention. Same applies to lenalidomide and pomalidomide.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Sperm: counsel male patients on barrier contraception.

lactation.riskSummary: AVOID.

reproductive.contraception: Two complementary methods throughout treatment AND for ≥ 4 weeks after stopping (women); barrier method for men.
reproductive.pregnancyTesting: Mandatory before initiation and during treatment per programme.

references.label: MHRA Thalidomide / lenalidomide / pomalidomide Pregnancy Prevention Programme.

oneLiner: AVOID from 20 weeks gestation — same NSAID class warning as ibuprofen. Limited lactation data.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Selective COX-2 inhibitor; same FDA 20-week class warning. Avoid in pregnancy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Use paracetamol; ibuprofen postpartum.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited lactation data; ibuprofen preferred.

oneLiner: AVOID throughout pregnancy (NSAID, antepartum) — but useful postpartum analgesic (compatible with lactation).

pregnancy.riskSummary: NSAID. Avoid antepartum (class warning). Used postpartum as part of multimodal analgesia (ERAS for Caesarean) — single doses compatible with breastfeeding.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: 15-30 mg IV/IM, max 5 days.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible postpartum — single doses; low milk transfer.

references.label: ACOG Committee Opinion 742 — Postpartum Pain Management.

oneLiner: Compatible in pregnancy and lactation for local / regional anaesthesia and antiarrhythmic.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Widely used local anaesthetic (incl. epidural, spinal) and antiarrhythmic. Crosses placenta but no teratogenicity. Safe in dental / minor procedures with or without adrenaline.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Avoid intravascular injection (toxicity).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

references.label: ACOG Committee Opinion on Non-Obstetric Surgery in Pregnancy.

oneLiner: Compatible in pregnancy and lactation — standard for epidural / spinal labour anaesthesia.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Long-acting amide local anaesthetic. Standard for epidural labour analgesia and spinal Caesarean. No teratogenicity.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Avoid intravascular injection — cardiotoxicity.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable for labour analgesia. Compatible with breastfeeding immediately after use.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Inhaled labour analgesia (Entonox = 50:50 N2O:O2). Rapid onset / offset. No teratogenicity in short labour use. Chronic occupational exposure: theoretical fertility / pregnancy loss (operating theatre staff).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible — rapid washout.

oneLiner: PREFERRED in pregnancy and lactation — first-line for syphilis (only effective treatment in pregnancy), GBS prophylaxis, listeria (with gentamicin).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Penicillin class. First-line for syphilis in pregnancy (long-acting benzathine penicillin G IM — desensitise if allergic, do NOT substitute, alternatives are not adequate to prevent congenital syphilis). Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis: 3 g IV initial then 1.5 g every 4 h until delivery (UK). Listeria.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: For severe penicillin allergy, formal desensitisation before benzathine penicillin in syphilis-pregnant patients.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

references.label: BASHH UK National Guideline on Syphilis.

oneLiner: PREFERRED in pregnancy and lactation for staph SSTI, cellulitis, mastitis.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Anti-staphylococcal penicillin. Long pregnancy safety record. First-line for cellulitis, mastitis (with amoxicillin/clindamycin for breast abscess).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: 500 mg-1 g QDS.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation — broader spectrum. AVOID in preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM) — associated with neonatal necrotising enterocolitis (ORACLE I trial).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Generally acceptable in pregnancy. EXCEPTION: AVOID in PPROM — ORACLE I showed increased necrotising enterocolitis in infants of mothers given co-amoxiclav for PPROM. For PPROM use erythromycin instead (per RCOG).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Standard 625 mg TDS or 1 g BD.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

references.label: Kenyon S et al. ORACLE I. Lancet 2001.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation. Used for moderate infection, surgical prophylaxis at Caesarean.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Second-generation cephalosporin. Used at Caesarean for surgical prophylaxis (alongside amoxicillin / co-amoxiclav). No teratogenicity.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Single 1.5 g IV at Caesarean.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation for severe sepsis / chorioamnionitis / pyelonephritis.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Broad-spectrum beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor. Used for severe maternal sepsis, chorioamnionitis, complicated UTI.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: 4.5 g IV every 6-8 h.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible — large molecule, low milk transfer.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation for severe sepsis / resistant organisms.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Carbapenem. Reserved for severe sepsis / multidrug-resistant organisms. No teratogenicity in case series.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: 1 g IV every 8 h (2 g for meningitis).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Compatible in pregnancy and lactation for BV (vaginal gel/cream) and acne (topical).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Topical/vaginal preparations have low systemic absorption. Vaginal clindamycin 2% × 7 nights is an alternative to metronidazole for BV.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Vaginal cream can weaken latex condoms.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Avoid in pregnancy (defer treatment to postpartum); fungal nail infection is not urgent. Limited lactation data — avoid systemic; topical compatible.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Limited human data; defer onychomycosis treatment to postpartum — there is no urgency.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Topical preparations have negligible absorption.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited data; defer if possible.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy for severe invasive fungal infection. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Used for cryptococcal meningitis, invasive aspergillosis, severe candidaemia in pregnancy. No teratogenicity in case series.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Liposomal preparations preferred (lower nephrotoxicity).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible — large molecule, low milk transfer.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy for acute SVT termination. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: First-line for SVT termination in pregnancy. Half-life seconds. No fetal harm reported.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: 6 mg rapid IV, then 12 mg, then 12 mg PRN.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy for maternal SVT, fetal SVT (transplacental therapy). Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Class Ic antiarrhythmic. Used maternally for SVT and transplacentally for fetal SVT / hydrops. Avoid in structural heart disease, ischaemic heart disease.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist cardiology / fetal medicine.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy for maternal arrhythmia and fetal SVT. Compatible with lactation but infant monitoring (bradycardia).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Class III antiarrhythmic + beta-blocker. Used for maternal/fetal arrhythmia. QT prolongation — review ECG.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist cardiology.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible with monitoring (higher milk transfer than other beta-blockers).

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation for opioid / alcohol use disorder — emerging reassuring data.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Opioid antagonist. Used for opioid and alcohol use disorder. Emerging registry data are reassuring. Naloxone challenge required before initiation to avoid precipitated withdrawal.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist (addiction medicine).

lactation.riskSummary: Limited but emerging reassuring data; low milk transfer.

references.label: ACOG Committee Opinion 711 — Opioid Use Disorder in Pregnancy.

oneLiner: Compatible in pregnancy and lactation for emergency opioid overdose reversal — life-saving.

pregnancy.riskSummary: For acute opioid overdose in pregnancy — give. Precipitated withdrawal in opioid-dependent mother is a known risk but maternal hypoxia / death is worse for fetus. Same approach if maternal overdose.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: IM/IV titrate to respiratory adequacy.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Limited pregnancy data — switch to behavioural / psychosocial support; avoid if possible. Limited lactation data.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Limited human pregnancy data. Stop alcohol use is the highest priority; specialist (addiction) prescribing if continued.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Counselling, CBT, naltrexone alternatives.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited lactation data.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy — limited data; risk of ethanol-disulfiram reaction with inadvertent ethanol exposure. Avoid in lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibitor. Limited pregnancy data; reports of fetal malformations confounded by alcohol exposure. Use psychosocial / behavioural support / naltrexone / acamprosate.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Stop preconception.

lactation.riskSummary: AVOID.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy — does not cross placenta well; fetus depends on maternal T4. Use levothyroxine (T4).

pregnancy.riskSummary: T3 does not cross placenta well. Fetus depends on maternal T4. Switch combination T3/T4 therapy to T4 alone preconception.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist endocrine input.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited lactation data; switch to levothyroxine.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation for hypocalcaemia / hypoparathyroidism / CKD.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Used for hypoparathyroidism, CKD-related bone disease, severe vitamin D deficiency. Monitor calcium closely (hypercalcaemia risk).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist supervision.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; small amounts in milk.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation — sedating antihistamine; long safety record.

pregnancy.riskSummary: First-generation antihistamine. Long pregnancy safety record. Used for allergic symptoms.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Sedation.

lactation.riskSummary: Single doses acceptable; chronic use may suppress milk supply / cause infant sedation.

oneLiner: PREFERRED non-sedating antihistamine in pregnancy and lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Second-generation antihistamine. Extensive pregnancy safety record. No sedation.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: 10 mg OD.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible — minimal milk transfer.

oneLiner: PREFERRED non-sedating antihistamine alongside loratadine in pregnancy and lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Second-generation antihistamine. Reassuring pregnancy data.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: 10 mg OD.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Compatible in pregnancy and lactation — mild/moderate potency for limited areas. Avoid potent steroids on large areas in 1st trimester.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Mild/moderate potency for small areas — compatible throughout pregnancy. Very potent (clobetasol) on large areas / prolonged use: small signal for low birth weight — use lowest potency.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Avoid application to nipple immediately before feed (wipe off).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; if applied to nipple, wipe before feeding.

oneLiner: First-line tocolytic agent — 48 h delay for antenatal steroids / in-utero transfer. Same active as for HTN; this slug is the obstetric indication.

pregnancy.riskSummary: NICE first-line tocolytic for threatened preterm birth 24-33+6 weeks. Aim: 48 h to deliver antenatal corticosteroids and arrange in-utero transfer. Not for prolonged tocolysis.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: 20 mg PO then 10-20 mg every 6 h, max 48 h.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

references.label: NICE NG25 — Preterm Labour and Birth.

oneLiner: Acceptable tocolytic — oxytocin antagonist; alternative to nifedipine for threatened preterm labour.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Oxytocin/vasopressin receptor antagonist tocolytic. Fewer maternal cardiovascular side-effects than nifedipine but more expensive. Same 48 h indication.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: IV infusion.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible — short half-life.

oneLiner: Used for tocolysis < 32 weeks; AVOID after 32 weeks (ductus arteriosus closure, oligohydramnios). Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: NSAID tocolytic. Reserved for tocolysis < 32 weeks (avoid after 32 — same ductal closure / oligohydramnios as other NSAIDs). Short courses 48 h.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Avoid prolonged courses.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible postpartum.

oneLiner: PREFERRED in pregnancy for Rh D-negative women — routine antenatal prophylaxis (28 weeks ± 34 weeks) and after sensitising events. Compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Standard care for Rh D-negative non-sensitised women: routine prophylaxis at 28 weeks (single 1500 IU per NICE) ± 34 weeks (two-dose regimen), and after potentially sensitising events (miscarriage > 12 wk, ectopic, APH, ECV, abdominal trauma, amniocentesis). Postnatal dose within 72 h if baby Rh D-positive.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Cell-free fetal DNA testing now allows targeted antenatal prophylaxis to Rh D-positive fetuses only.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

references.label: NICE TA156 — Routine Antenatal Anti-D Prophylaxis.
BSH guidelines on the use of anti-D.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy where possible — anti-VEGF systemic absorption with theoretical impact on placental development. Use only if vision-threatening AMD/DR without alternative.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Intravitreal anti-VEGF. Systemic absorption is small but VEGF is critical to placentation. Defer treatment where possible. If essential (rapid sight loss), specialist input.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Consider laser / corticosteroid alternatives where possible.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited data; minimal systemic absorption.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy — systemic anti-VEGF; placental development concerns. Effective contraception required.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Systemic anti-VEGF monoclonal. Affects vasculogenesis. Used in oncology. Effective contraception during AND for 6 months after stopping.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Same considerations apply to aflibercept (systemic).

lactation.riskSummary: AVOID.

reproductive.contraception: Effective contraception during and ≥ 6 months after stopping.

oneLiner: Compatible in pregnancy and lactation — negligible systemic absorption.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Topical for HSV labialis. Negligible absorption.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: For genital HSV use oral aciclovir.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Compatible in pregnancy and lactation. Given to neonates of HBsAg+ mothers within 12 h of birth alongside HBV vaccine.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Passive immunisation. No teratogenicity. Standard for neonates of HBsAg+ mothers (within 12 h) and post-exposure prophylaxis.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Standard schedule.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Compatible in pregnancy and lactation — given to seronegative pregnant women after significant VZV exposure (within 10 days).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Passive immunisation. Indication: VZV-seronegative pregnant woman with significant chickenpox/shingles exposure, ideally within 10 days. Reduces (does not eliminate) maternal varicella and possibly congenital varicella syndrome.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Aciclovir from day 7 post-exposure also given as PEP in some protocols (RCOG 2015).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy — Td/Tdap recommended schedule.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Inactivated. Safe in pregnancy. WHO maternal/neonatal tetanus elimination programme.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Often given as Tdap (includes pertussis component).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy — inactivated; for women with specific risk factors.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Inactivated. Recommended in pregnancy for women with asplenia, CKD, immunocompromise, chronic respiratory disease where clinically appropriate.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Routine pregnancy schedule per programme.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: PREFERRED at 28-36 weeks in autumn/winter for infant RSV protection (FDA-approved 2023; UK and US programmes 2024).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Recombinant prefusion F protein vaccine (Abrysvo). Given 28-36 wk gestation; transplacental antibody protects infant from severe RSV in first 6 months. Reduced severe lower respiratory tract illness in MATISSE trial.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Alternative: infant monoclonal (nirsevimab) at birth in season.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

references.label: Kampmann B et al. MATISSE trial. NEJM 2023;388:1451-64.

oneLiner: See individual drug records for sertraline, fluoxetine, paroxetine, citalopram, escitalopram. Sertraline preferred in lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Class-level summary. Sertraline is preferred SSRI in pregnancy and lactation. Paroxetine avoided in 1st trimester. Class effects: neonatal adaptation, small PPHN signal. Untreated maternal depression is harmful — continuity of effective treatment is the priority.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Refer to specific records for individual SSRIs.

lactation.riskSummary: Class summary; sertraline preferred.

oneLiner: PREFERRED over continued smoking in pregnancy and lactation. Intermittent forms (gum, lozenge) preferred over patch.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Smoking in pregnancy causes growth restriction, prematurity, stillbirth, SUDI. NRT is much safer than continued smoking. UK guidance: support smoking cessation in pregnancy with behavioural intervention + NRT if needed. Intermittent forms (gum, lozenge) preferred over continuous patch.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Varenicline and bupropion are NOT recommended in pregnancy (limited safety data).

lactation.riskSummary: Preferred over continued smoking. Time feed before next dose / remove patch before sleep if breastfeeding.

references.label: NICE PH26 — Quitting smoking in pregnancy.

oneLiner: Limited pregnancy data; defer treatment to postpartum; use NRT in pregnancy if pharmacotherapy needed. Limited lactation data.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Limited pregnancy safety data. NRT preferred. Continue treating smoking actively, with behavioural and NRT support.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Postpartum varenicline acceptable if not breastfeeding.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited lactation data.

oneLiner: Limited pregnancy data; NRT preferred for smoking cessation in pregnancy. Acceptable in lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Limited pregnancy data — some signal for cardiac malformations (inconsistent). NRT preferred for smoking cessation. As antidepressant in pregnancy: SSRIs preferred.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Lowers seizure threshold.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; low milk transfer.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation as antiemetic / sedating antihistamine.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Phenothiazine antihistamine. Long pregnancy experience for nausea/vomiting of pregnancy and motion sickness.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: 25 mg PO/IM TDS-QDS.

lactation.riskSummary: Acceptable; possible infant sedation.

oneLiner: Used in intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy for maternal symptom relief; PITCHES trial showed no improvement in perinatal outcomes but UDCA still used for pruritus.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Used in intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP). PITCHES trial (Lancet 2019) — no improvement in stillbirth, preterm birth, or NICU admission. RCOG GTG-43 now downgrades recommendation but UDCA may still be used for maternal pruritus.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor bile acids; consider early delivery based on bile acid level (RCOG GTG-43 thresholds).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

references.label: Chappell LC et al. PITCHES trial. Lancet 2019.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation for IBD maintenance.

pregnancy.riskSummary: 5-aminosalicylate. Standard IBD maintenance. Active disease in pregnancy is a greater risk than treatment. Continue through pregnancy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Avoid phthalate-containing extended-release preparations where possible (animal data only).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; rare reports of infant diarrhoea.

oneLiner: Limited pregnancy data; defer treatment of OAB to postpartum where possible. Limited lactation data — small case series.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Anticholinergic. Limited pregnancy data; behavioural / bladder training first-line for OAB.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Defer if possible.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited data.

oneLiner: Compatible in pregnancy and lactation for leg cramps / constipation / magnesium deficiency.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Oral magnesium supplementation for leg cramps in pregnancy — modest evidence. Constipation.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Magnesium oxide or hydroxide preparations.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy for nausea (evidence for symptom reduction at 1 g/day).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Multiple RCTs support ginger 250 mg QDS (or up to 1 g/day) for nausea of pregnancy. Reasonable first-line non-pharmacological. No teratogenicity in cohorts.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Confirm dose / preparation.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Compatible in pregnancy and lactation at recommended doses; high-dose supplementation not advised.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Routine prenatal vitamin contains zinc. Avoid mega-doses.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Standard dietary intake.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Compatible in pregnancy and lactation; supplementation recommended in iodine-deficient regions (150 microg/day antenatal).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Iodine is essential for fetal thyroid / neurodevelopment. UK / WHO recommend 150 microg/day in pregnancy and lactation. Severe deficiency causes cretinism. EXCESS (e.g. iodine-containing antiseptics on large areas, amiodarone) causes fetal goitre / hypothyroidism.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Use povidone-iodine sparingly in pregnancy.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible at recommended doses.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy for acute migraine when paracetamol inadequate — sumatriptan has most data. Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: 5-HT1B/1D agonist. Most pregnancy data for sumatriptan — no consistent teratogenicity signal across registries. Use when paracetamol (± antiemetic) inadequate; avoid ergotamine alkaloids.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Class — preference for sumatriptan based on volume of safety data.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; low milk transfer.

references.label: Marchenko A et al. Triptans in pregnancy systematic review. Headache 2015.

oneLiner: CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy (uteroplacental vasoconstriction; oxytocic at high doses). AVOID in lactation (infant ergotism reports).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Vasoconstrictor / oxytocic. Contraindicated in pregnancy for migraine — uteroplacental ischaemia.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Use paracetamol / triptans instead.

lactation.riskSummary: AVOID — case reports of infant ergotism (vomiting, diarrhoea, seizures).

oneLiner: Use with caution in pregnancy; systemic absorption from eye drops can cause neonatal beta-blocker effects. Compatible with lactation but monitor infant.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Systemic absorption from eye drops sufficient to cause maternal / fetal beta-blockade. Punctal occlusion after dosing reduces absorption. Specialist co-management with ophthalmology.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist supervision.

lactation.riskSummary: Monitor infant for bradycardia / hypoglycaemia.

oneLiner: Limited pregnancy data — uveoscleral PGF analogue; theoretical oxytocic concern. Acceptable in lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Prostaglandin F analogue. Theoretical concern for uterine contraction (though doses are local). Specialist co-management.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Defer initiation to postpartum if possible.

lactation.riskSummary: Acceptable.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation per WHO for schistosomiasis and other helminths.

pregnancy.riskSummary: WHO removed pregnancy contraindication (2003); treat schistosomiasis in pregnancy. No teratogenicity in case series.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Single-dose or short-course.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; short course; brief interruption of breastfeeding (24 h) no longer required per WHO.

oneLiner: Acceptable in 2nd / 3rd trimester for soil-transmitted helminth treatment (WHO programmatic deworming). AVOID 1st trimester.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Avoid 1st trimester (animal teratogenicity at high doses; limited human data). From 2nd trimester, WHO recommends single-dose deworming in endemic areas as part of antenatal care.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Single 400 mg dose.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Avoid in pregnancy if elective (e.g. scabies — use permethrin); WHO accepts in mass drug administration programmes from 2nd trimester. Acceptable in lactation as single dose.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Limited human pregnancy data; WHO permits in MDA programmes (onchocerciasis, lymphatic filariasis) from 2nd trimester. For scabies, topical permethrin preferred.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist tropical medicine advice.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible; single dose.

oneLiner: PREFERRED in pregnancy and lactation for scabies / lice — negligible systemic absorption.

pregnancy.riskSummary: First-line topical for scabies in pregnancy. Negligible systemic absorption.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: 5% cream overnight, repeat 7-14 days.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: PREFERRED in pregnancy and lactation when oral route not tolerated. Same safety profile as oral.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Same drug as oral paracetamol; PK studied in pregnancy. Used postoperatively (post-Caesarean) and when N+V limit oral route.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: 1 g IV every 6 h; max 4 g/day (lower in low body weight).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: PREFERRED for PPH treatment within 3 h of birth (WOMAN trial). Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: WOMAN trial (2017): 1 g IV tranexamic acid within 3 h of birth reduces death from postpartum haemorrhage (1.5% vs 1.9%, RR 0.81). WHO recommends as part of PPH management. Also used in heavy menstrual bleeding (postpartum not directly relevant).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: 1 g IV slow, can repeat once after 30 min if bleeding continues.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

references.label: WHO Recommendation on Tranexamic Acid for PPH. 2017.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and lactation for diabetes insipidus, mild VWD prophylaxis at delivery.
