pregnancy.riskSummary: Synthetic vasopressin analogue. Long pregnancy experience for cranial DI (dose may need adjustment in pregnancy due to placental vasopressinase). Used at delivery for von Willebrand disease (type 1, responder).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor maternal sodium (hyponatraemia risk).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: PREFERRED postpartum dose within 72 h for Rh D-negative mothers with Rh D-positive infant.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Cross-reference with anti-D prophylaxis: routine postnatal 500 IU IM within 72 h if neonate Rh D-positive. Kleihauer testing if large fetomaternal haemorrhage suspected.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Standard postnatal protocol.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Avoid in pregnancy if alternative — limited human data. Used in selected ITP with severe thrombocytopenia under haematology.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Thrombopoietin receptor agonist for refractory ITP. Limited pregnancy data; specialist haematology decisions. For ITP in pregnancy, first-line steroids / IVIG.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist haematology.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited data.

oneLiner: Compatible in pregnancy and lactation for ITP, autoimmune disease, immunodeficiency replacement.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Pooled human IgG. Standard treatment for severe ITP in pregnancy, alloimmune diseases (e.g. HDFN, NAIT), CIDP, primary immunodeficiency replacement. No teratogenicity.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Dose 1-2 g/kg over 2-5 days for autoimmune indications.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Class-level: AVOID 1st trimester (teratogenic). Many regimens can be given in 2nd / 3rd trimester for breast cancer, lymphoma, leukaemia under specialist oncology guidance. AVOID in lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Class summary. 1st-trimester chemotherapy causes major malformations and miscarriage. 2nd / 3rd-trimester chemotherapy for breast cancer, Hodgkin lymphoma, AML, others can be given with acceptable fetal outcomes in registry follow-up (INCIP, ESGO). Multidisciplinary care.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Refer to oncology / MFM / pharmacology for individual regimen safety. Delivery timed ≥ 3 weeks after last cytotoxic to allow maternal/neonatal marrow recovery.

lactation.riskSummary: AVOID — most cytotoxics excreted in milk; infant marrow suppression.

references.label: Amant F et al. Pediatric outcome after in utero chemotherapy exposure. NEJM 2015.
ESGO/ESMO guidelines on cancer in pregnancy.

oneLiner: CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy. Letrozole IS used preconception for ovulation induction (rapid clearance). Contraindicated in lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Used in breast cancer treatment — contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic in animals; case reports in humans). Letrozole is also used SHORT-COURSE for ovulation induction in PCOS (rapidly cleared before implantation); this distinct use is supported by NICE / international guidance.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Effective contraception with breast cancer use.

lactation.riskSummary: AVOID.

reproductive.contraception: Effective non-hormonal contraception during breast cancer treatment.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy if needed for severe asthma; ICS/LABA preferred. Compatible with lactation but infant irritability with high maternal levels.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Long pregnancy experience; clearance may change. Reserved for severe asthma not controlled on ICS/LABA. Therapeutic level monitoring.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Aim 5-15 mg/L.

lactation.riskSummary: Infant irritability / tachycardia with high maternal levels.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy for severe asthma (EXPECT registry). Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Anti-IgE monoclonal. EXPECT registry data reassuring for severe asthma in pregnancy. Continue if disease severity warrants.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist (severe asthma).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible — large protein, low oral bioavailability.

references.label: Namazy J et al. EXPECT registry. JACI 2020.

oneLiner: Limited pregnancy data; avoid if alternative; specialist cardiology decision in refractory angina. Limited lactation data.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Limited human data; animal embryotoxicity at high doses. Specialist co-management.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Defer initiation; continue if essential.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited data.

oneLiner: Acceptable for maternal angina, severe hypertension in pre-eclampsia (IV GTN). Compatible with lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Vasodilator. Used IV/IM/SL for hypertensive crisis in pre-eclampsia (when labetalol / hydralazine inadequate) and for maternal angina.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Headache, hypotension. IV GTN useful for uterine relaxation (e.g. retained placenta, internal podalic version, breech extraction).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible.

oneLiner: Aminopenicillin considered safe across all trimesters and compatible with breastfeeding. Widely used in pregnancy (intrapartum GBS prophylaxis, UTI).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Penicillins, including ampicillin, are among the most extensively used antibiotics in pregnancy with a long record of safety and no evidence of teratogenicity. Used in all trimesters for maternal infection and intrapartum group B streptococcus (GBS) prophylaxis.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Renal clearance increases in pregnancy and may lower serum levels; standard or higher dosing is generally appropriate. First-line penicillin choice for many obstetric indications.
pregnancy.data: Large observational datasets and decades of clinical use show no increase in congenital malformations.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Excreted into milk in small amounts; not expected to cause adverse effects beyond rare modification of infant bowel flora, candidiasis, or sensitisation.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for diarrhoea or thrush. No interruption of breastfeeding required.
lactation.data: Low relative infant dose; long-established compatibility per LactMed.

oneLiner: Penicillin/beta-lactamase inhibitor considered safe in pregnancy and compatible with breastfeeding. Avoid in threatened very preterm labour (NEC signal from ORACLE).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Amoxicillin and clavulanate have not been associated with an increased risk of malformations and are widely used in pregnancy. The main caveat is the ORACLE trial signal of increased neonatal necrotising enterocolitis when co-amoxiclav was given for preterm prelabour rupture of membranes / spontaneous preterm labour with intact membranes; co-amoxiclav is therefore avoided in that specific setting.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Acceptable for maternal infections in pregnancy. Avoid routine use for threatened preterm labour with intact membranes (use erythromycin for PPROM per local guidance).
pregnancy.data: ORACLE I/II trials informed the NEC caution; otherwise extensive reassuring exposure data.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Both components transfer into milk in small amounts; possible infant effects are altered bowel flora, diarrhoea, thrush, or rarely rash.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for GI upset or candidiasis. No need to interrupt breastfeeding.
lactation.data: Low relative infant dose per LactMed.

references.label: Kenyon S et al. ORACLE trials. Lancet 2001.

oneLiner: Narrow-spectrum penicillin considered safe in all trimesters and compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Oral penicillin with a long record of safe use in pregnancy and no evidence of teratogenicity. Used for streptococcal infection and rheumatic-fever/asplenia prophylaxis.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Standard dosing. A penicillin of choice where its spectrum is adequate.
pregnancy.data: Decades of use; no malformation signal.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Small amounts in milk; potential for infant bowel-flora change, thrush, or sensitisation only.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for diarrhoea/thrush. Breastfeeding may continue.
lactation.data: Low relative infant dose per LactMed.

oneLiner: Treatment of choice for maternal syphilis in all trimesters — preferred for preventing congenital syphilis. Compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Long-acting penicillin and the recommended treatment for maternal syphilis in pregnancy; it is the only regimen reliably shown to treat and prevent congenital syphilis. No teratogenicity. Penicillin allergy should prompt desensitisation rather than substitution, because alternatives do not reliably treat the fetus.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction can occur after the first dose, occasionally precipitating uterine contractions/fetal monitoring changes — administer with appropriate monitoring in later pregnancy. Stage-appropriate dosing per WHO/CDC.
pregnancy.data: WHO and CDC guidance designate benzathine penicillin as treatment of choice for syphilis in pregnancy.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Penicillins transfer into milk in small amounts; only minor effects (bowel flora, thrush, sensitisation) are expected.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Breastfeeding may continue.

references.label: WHO guidelines for the treatment of Treponema pallidum (syphilis). 2016.
CDC STI Treatment Guidelines: Syphilis during pregnancy.

oneLiner: Penicillin considered safe in pregnancy and compatible with breastfeeding; used for syphilis and other infections where indicated.

pregnancy.riskSummary: An intramuscular penicillin; the penicillin class is among the safest antibiotic groups in pregnancy with no teratogenic signal. Used as an alternative penicillin regimen for syphilis and other susceptible infections.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction possible when treating syphilis. Standard dosing.
pregnancy.data: Penicillin class safety established over decades.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Small amounts in milk; minor infant effects only (flora change, thrush, sensitisation).
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Breastfeeding may continue.

oneLiner: First-generation cephalosporin considered safe in pregnancy; standard surgical prophylaxis for Caesarean section. Compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Cephalosporins as a class have a strong safety record in pregnancy with no consistent evidence of teratogenicity. Cefazolin is the recommended prophylactic antibiotic for Caesarean delivery.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Give within 60 minutes before skin incision for Caesarean prophylaxis. Increased volume of distribution/clearance in pregnancy may warrant higher prophylactic doses by weight.
pregnancy.data: Widely used; reassuring observational data.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Very low transfer into milk; possible minor effects on infant bowel flora.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Breastfeeding may continue.
lactation.data: Low relative infant dose per LactMed.

references.label: ACOG. Use of Prophylactic Antibiotics in Labor and Delivery.

oneLiner: Third-generation cephalosporin considered safe in pregnancy and compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Cephalosporins are considered safe in pregnancy; no teratogenic signal. Used for serious maternal infection where broad gram-negative cover is needed.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Pharmacokinetic changes in pregnancy increase clearance; ensure adequate dosing for serious infection.
pregnancy.data: Class safety established; specific reassuring data for third-generation agents.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Low milk transfer; possible alteration of infant bowel flora or thrush.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for diarrhoea/thrush. Breastfeeding may continue.
lactation.data: Low relative infant dose per LactMed.

oneLiner: Antipseudomonal third-generation cephalosporin considered safe in pregnancy and compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Cephalosporin with no evidence of teratogenicity; the class is regarded as safe in pregnancy. Reserved for serious infections requiring antipseudomonal cover.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Adjust dosing for increased renal clearance in pregnancy where treating serious infection.
pregnancy.data: Class safety established.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Low milk transfer; minor infant effects (bowel flora, thrush) only.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for GI upset. Breastfeeding may continue.
lactation.data: Low relative infant dose per LactMed.

oneLiner: Oral third-generation cephalosporin considered safe in pregnancy and compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Cephalosporin class considered safe in pregnancy with no teratogenic signal. Used orally for susceptible infections including UTI and gonorrhoea where appropriate.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Standard dosing. For gonorrhoea, follow current resistance-aware guidance (ceftriaxone IM is generally preferred first line).
pregnancy.data: Class safety established.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Limited data but consistent with the cephalosporin class; minor infant effects only.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for diarrhoea/thrush. Breastfeeding may continue.

oneLiner: Fourth-generation cephalosporin considered safe in pregnancy and compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Cephalosporin with no evidence of teratogenicity; the class is considered safe in pregnancy. Used for serious infections requiring broad gram-negative and antipseudomonal cover.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Account for increased renal clearance in pregnancy when dosing for serious infection.
pregnancy.data: Class safety established.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Low milk transfer; minor infant effects (flora change, thrush) only.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for GI upset. Breastfeeding may continue.
lactation.data: Low relative infant dose per LactMed.

oneLiner: Carbapenem with limited but reassuring pregnancy data; compatible with breastfeeding. Reserve for resistant/serious infection.

pregnancy.riskSummary: No evidence of teratogenicity in available data; beta-lactams as a group are considered safe in pregnancy. Human pregnancy data are limited, so reserve for serious or resistant infections where benefit is clear.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Increased renal clearance in pregnancy may reduce exposure; ensure adequate dosing.
pregnancy.data: Limited human data; animal studies do not show teratogenicity.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Very low milk levels and poor oral absorption by the infant make adverse effects unlikely beyond minor flora change.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for diarrhoea/thrush. Breastfeeding may continue.
lactation.data: Low relative infant dose per LactMed.

oneLiner: Limited human pregnancy data without a clear malformation signal; minimal milk transfer and poor oral absorption make it compatible with breastfeeding. Reserve for resistant gram-positive infection.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Human pregnancy data are limited. Available reports and registries have not identified a clear teratogenic signal, but experience is insufficient to designate it preferred. Use when needed for serious resistant gram-positive infection and alternatives are unsuitable.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor creatine kinase as usual. Specialist infectious-disease input recommended.
pregnancy.data: Limited human data; animal studies do not show teratogenicity.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Excreted into milk in very low concentrations and poorly absorbed orally by the infant, so adverse effects are unlikely.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for GI upset. Breastfeeding may continue.
lactation.data: A reported case showed milk levels far below the infant therapeutic threshold per LactMed.

oneLiner: Generally avoided in pregnancy (use only when no safer alternative); fluoroquinolone-class arthropathy concern. Acceptable as short course during breastfeeding with infant monitoring.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Fluoroquinolones are generally avoided in pregnancy because of animal cartilage/arthropathy findings, although large human cohorts have not confirmed an increased malformation or arthropathy risk. Use only when the infection is serious, the organism is susceptible, and no safer alternative (e.g. beta-lactam) exists.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Prefer penicillins/cephalosporins for routine infections. Reserve fluoroquinolones for specific indications (e.g. resistant TB, certain serious gram-negative infections) under specialist guidance.
pregnancy.data: Human cohort/meta-analysis data are largely reassuring but the class remains second-line in pregnancy by convention.

lactation.riskSummary: Excreted into milk; theoretical concerns about infant arthropathy and effects on bowel flora. Short courses are generally considered acceptable with monitoring; some sources prefer alternatives for prolonged therapy.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for diarrhoea, thrush, and (theoretical) joint symptoms. Consider alternatives for long courses.
lactation.data: Quinolones appear in milk in low to moderate amounts per LactMed.

references.label: UKTIS: Use of fluoroquinolones in pregnancy. https://uktis.org

oneLiner: Generally avoided in pregnancy (fluoroquinolone class; limited data). Acceptable as short course during breastfeeding with infant monitoring.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Fluoroquinolone generally avoided in pregnancy because of class arthropathy concerns and more limited human data than older quinolones. Reserve for serious infection (e.g. drug-resistant TB) where benefit clearly outweighs risk and alternatives are unsuitable.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Prefer beta-lactams for routine infections. Specialist guidance for TB or resistant organisms.
pregnancy.data: Limited human pregnancy data for moxifloxacin specifically; class generally second-line.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited data; class effects suggest low to moderate milk transfer. Short courses generally acceptable with infant monitoring; alternatives preferred for long courses.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for diarrhoea, thrush, joint symptoms. Consider alternatives for prolonged therapy.
lactation.data: Quinolone class appears in milk in low to moderate amounts per LactMed.

oneLiner: AVOID from the second trimester onward (tetracycline class — fetal tooth discolouration and bone effects). Short courses acceptable in breastfeeding; avoid prolonged use.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Tetracyclines, including minocycline, are avoided from about 15 weeks (second and third trimesters) because they bind to developing teeth and bone, causing permanent dental discolouration and reversible inhibition of bone growth. High intravenous doses have also been linked to maternal hepatotoxicity. First-trimester inadvertent exposure has not been clearly teratogenic, but the drug should be stopped and an alternative used.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Use alternative antibiotics (e.g. erythromycin) for indications such as acne or chlamydia in pregnancy.
pregnancy.data: Class effect on fetal teeth/bone is well established.

trimesterNotes.note: Avoid; switch to an alternative. Inadvertent early exposure not clearly teratogenic.
Avoid — tooth discolouration and bone effects.
Avoid — tooth discolouration and bone effects.

lactation.riskSummary: Short maternal courses are acceptable; the calcium in milk binds tetracyclines and limits infant absorption. Prolonged or repeated courses are not recommended because of theoretical effects on infant teeth and bone.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Avoid prolonged maternal therapy while breastfeeding; prefer a non-tetracycline alternative for long courses.
lactation.data: Limited absorption due to milk calcium chelation per LactMed.

oneLiner: Oral fosfomycin is a recommended single-dose UTI option in pregnancy; the IV form has more limited pregnancy data but no clear teratogenic signal. Compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Fosfomycin has not shown teratogenicity; oral single-dose fosfomycin is a recommended option for uncomplicated UTI/asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy. Intravenous fosfomycin is used for serious resistant infections and has more limited but non-alarming pregnancy data.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Reserve IV form for serious/resistant infection with specialist input. Confirm local susceptibility for UTI use.
pregnancy.data: Reassuring data for oral use in pregnancy; limited but non-concerning data for IV.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Excreted into milk in small amounts; adverse effects in breastfed infants are unlikely.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for diarrhoea. Breastfeeding may continue.
lactation.data: Low relative infant dose per LactMed.

oneLiner: Considered safe in pregnancy for serious/disseminated HSV or VZV infection; compatible with breastfeeding. The drug of choice for severe maternal herpesvirus disease.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Aciclovir has a large body of reassuring pregnancy data (including a manufacturer pregnancy registry) with no increase in birth defects. Intravenous aciclovir is the treatment of choice for severe or disseminated maternal HSV and varicella infection, including varicella pneumonia, in any trimester.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Maintain hydration to reduce risk of crystalluria/nephrotoxicity. Used for severe disease; oral valaciclovir/aciclovir used for suppression near term.
pregnancy.data: Aciclovir pregnancy registry and large cohorts show no teratogenic signal.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Although aciclovir concentrates in milk, the infant dose is small and well below paediatric therapeutic doses; no adverse effects reported.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Breastfeeding may continue. The drug is itself used to treat neonates.
lactation.data: Relative infant dose low; infant exposure far below treatment dose per LactMed.

references.label: UKTIS: Use of aciclovir in pregnancy. https://uktis.org

oneLiner: Inhaled neuraminidase inhibitor with minimal systemic absorption; acceptable in pregnancy for influenza and compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Inhaled zanamivir produces low systemic exposure, limiting fetal exposure. It is an option for influenza in pregnancy; however oseltamivir is often preferred for treating serious illness because of more systemic data and reliable absorption. Pregnancy is a risk group for severe influenza.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Avoid in women with underlying airways disease (bronchospasm risk). Oseltamivir preferred for severe or lower-respiratory disease.
pregnancy.data: Limited but reassuring pregnancy data; low systemic absorption.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Minimal systemic absorption and low milk transfer make infant exposure negligible.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Breastfeeding may continue.
lactation.data: Low systemic absorption; expected low milk levels per LactMed.

references.label: CDC. Influenza antiviral medications: recommendations for pregnant women.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy where possible — animal teratogen/embryotoxic; reserve for sight- or life-threatening CMV. Breastfeeding generally not recommended on this therapy (data lacking).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Valganciclovir (prodrug of ganciclovir) is teratogenic and embryotoxic in animals and ganciclovir is mutagenic/affects spermatogenesis; human data are very limited. Avoid in pregnancy unless treating a sight- or life-threatening CMV infection (e.g. CMV retinitis/disease in immunocompromised mothers) where benefit outweighs risk.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist (infectious disease/ophthalmology) input required. Effective contraception advised during therapy.
pregnancy.data: Animal teratogenicity; minimal human pregnancy data.

lactation.riskSummary: Breastfeeding is generally not recommended during therapy. There are no data on ganciclovir/valganciclovir in human milk, and given its toxicity profile most sources advise against breastfeeding while taking it.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Consider the maternal indication and discuss feeding alternatives with specialists.
lactation.data: No published milk data; toxicity concern drives the recommendation per LactMed.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy where possible — animal teratogen/embryotoxic; reserve for sight- or life-threatening CMV. Breastfeeding generally not recommended on this therapy (data lacking).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Ganciclovir is teratogenic and embryotoxic in animals, mutagenic, and impairs spermatogenesis; human pregnancy data are minimal. Avoid unless treating sight- or life-threatening CMV disease where the maternal benefit outweighs fetal risk.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist input required; effective contraception during and after therapy per labelling.
pregnancy.data: Animal teratogenicity; minimal human data.

lactation.riskSummary: Breastfeeding generally not recommended during therapy; no human milk data and significant toxicity potential.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Discuss feeding alternatives with specialists.
lactation.data: No published milk data per LactMed; toxicity drives recommendation.

oneLiner: PREFERRED antiretroviral in pregnancy (PMTCT of HIV) and the agent of choice for hepatitis B in pregnancy. Compatible with breastfeeding; infant exposure via milk is trivial.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Tenofovir disoproxil is a backbone antiretroviral recommended throughout pregnancy for HIV treatment and prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT), with extensive reassuring safety data. It is also the treatment of choice for chronic hepatitis B in pregnancy, given in the third trimester (and continued as indicated) to reduce perinatal HBV transmission alongside neonatal immunoprophylaxis.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor maternal renal function. Do not stop HIV/HBV therapy in pregnancy without specialist advice. Tenofovir is part of WHO-preferred regimens (e.g. with lamivudine/emtricitabine and dolutegravir).
pregnancy.data: Large PMTCT and hepatitis B cohorts demonstrate efficacy and safety.

lactation.riskSummary: Infant exposure through breast milk is trivial, and no adverse effects have been reported up to 2 years of age in breastfed infants of mothers on tenofovir; infant plasma tenofovir is typically undetectable. Note: in HIV, the decision to breastfeed depends on maternal viral suppression and local/national guidance, not on tenofovir toxicity.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: For HBV-positive (HIV-negative) mothers, breastfeeding on tenofovir is considered compatible. For HIV, follow PMTCT breastfeeding guidance.
lactation.data: Breast milk and infant plasma studies show minimal exposure per LactMed.

references.label: WHO. Consolidated guidelines on HIV (PMTCT) and on hepatitis B.

oneLiner: Acceptable antiretroviral/anti-HBV agent in pregnancy with accumulating reassuring data; compatible with breastfeeding (very low infant exposure).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Tenofovir alafenamide is increasingly used in pregnancy for HIV and hepatitis B, with growing reassuring efficacy and safety data; it achieves adequate exposure in pregnancy and is included in current guideline-preferred regimens. Tenofovir disoproxil has the larger pregnancy evidence base, but TAF is considered acceptable.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist HIV/hepatology management; do not interrupt therapy without advice.
pregnancy.data: Pregnancy pharmacokinetic and outcome studies are reassuring; evidence base smaller than TDF.

lactation.riskSummary: Very low infant exposure via milk; no adverse effects reported. As with all HIV therapy, breastfeeding decisions follow PMTCT guidance and maternal viral suppression.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Follow local HIV/HBV breastfeeding guidance.

oneLiner: PREFERRED NRTI backbone in pregnancy for HIV treatment/PMTCT; compatible with breastfeeding (low infant exposure).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Emtricitabine (commonly co-formulated with tenofovir) is a recommended NRTI backbone throughout pregnancy with extensive reassuring data and no teratogenic signal. It is part of guideline-preferred PMTCT regimens.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Do not interrupt antiretroviral therapy in pregnancy without specialist advice.
pregnancy.data: Large PMTCT cohorts; reassuring.

lactation.riskSummary: Low infant exposure via milk. As with all HIV therapy, breastfeeding decisions follow PMTCT guidance and maternal viral suppression rather than drug toxicity.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Follow local HIV breastfeeding guidance.

oneLiner: WHO-preferred first-line HIV regimen including in pregnancy; earlier neural-tube-defect signal not confirmed in updated Tsepamo data. Compatible with breastfeeding per PMTCT guidance.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Dolutegravir-based regimens are WHO-preferred first-line HIV therapy for all populations including pregnant women and those of childbearing potential. An early neural-tube-defect (NTD) signal from the Tsepamo surveillance study (Botswana) was not confirmed with longer follow-up: NTD rates with periconceptional dolutegravir (about 0.1%) were similar to other antiretrovirals, prompting WHO to strengthen its recommendation. High-dose folic acid and adequate periconceptional folate remain prudent.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Dolutegravir achieves rapid viral suppression, valuable late in pregnancy. Lamivudine is a well-established, safe NRTI. Do not interrupt therapy without specialist advice.
pregnancy.data: Tsepamo updated analyses; WHO antiretroviral guidance.

lactation.riskSummary: Both components transfer into milk in low amounts and are considered compatible; breastfeeding decisions in HIV depend on maternal viral suppression and local PMTCT policy rather than drug toxicity.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Follow local HIV breastfeeding guidance; monitor infant per program.
lactation.data: Low milk transfer of dolutegravir and lamivudine per LactMed.

references.label: Zash R et al. Tsepamo study updates on dolutegravir and neural tube defects.
WHO. Updated recommendations on dolutegravir (preferred first-line ART).

oneLiner: Used in pregnancy/PMTCT with long experience; risk of maternal hepatotoxicity/rash, especially when starting at higher CD4. Low infant exposure in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Nevirapine has extensive use in HIV treatment and PMTCT and no teratogenic signal. The principal concern is maternal toxicity (severe rash/Stevens-Johnson, hepatotoxicity) — risk is higher when initiating at higher CD4 counts, so initiation is approached cautiously. Newer regimens (dolutegravir-based) are now generally preferred, but nevirapine remains in use in some programs.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor liver enzymes and for rash, particularly in the first weeks of therapy. Use lead-in dosing as per labelling.
pregnancy.data: Large PMTCT experience; maternal toxicity well characterised.

lactation.riskSummary: Transfers into milk; in breastfed infants of treated mothers, moderate rash has been reported in a small percentage but serious infant hepatotoxicity has not. As with all HIV therapy, breastfeeding follows PMTCT guidance.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for rash. Follow local HIV breastfeeding guidance.
lactation.data: Comparative infant safety data summarised in LactMed.

oneLiner: Acceptable boosted protease inhibitor in pregnancy (PMTCT) with substantial experience; compatible with breastfeeding (low infant exposure).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Lopinavir/ritonavir has been widely used in pregnancy for HIV treatment and PMTCT without a clear increase in birth defects. Drug levels fall in the third trimester, so dose adjustment may be considered to maintain virological control. Now often superseded by dolutegravir-based regimens but remains an option.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Consider therapeutic concerns about reduced third-trimester exposure. Do not interrupt therapy without specialist advice.
pregnancy.data: Large PMTCT experience.

lactation.riskSummary: Both components transfer into milk in low amounts and are considered compatible; breastfeeding in HIV depends on maternal suppression and local PMTCT policy.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Follow local HIV breastfeeding guidance.

oneLiner: Acceptable as a low-dose pharmacokinetic booster in pregnancy with extensive HIV/PMTCT experience; compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Low-dose ritonavir is used as a booster for protease inhibitors in HIV regimens used in pregnancy, with substantial experience and no clear teratogenic signal. (Note: ritonavir is also the booster in nirmatrelvir/ritonavir for COVID-19.)
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Used as part of a boosted regimen; manage as for the partner protease inhibitor. Do not interrupt HIV therapy without advice.
pregnancy.data: Large PMTCT experience as a booster.

lactation.riskSummary: Transfers into milk in low amounts and is considered compatible; breastfeeding in HIV follows PMTCT guidance.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Follow local HIV breastfeeding guidance.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy where possible — tenofovir is the preferred anti-HBV agent in pregnancy. Limited milk data; an alternative is usually preferred while breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Entecavir is generally not recommended in pregnancy; tenofovir disoproxil (or tenofovir alafenamide) is the preferred antiviral for chronic hepatitis B in pregnancy because of its larger safety dataset and PMTCT evidence. Women on entecavir who become pregnant are usually switched to tenofovir.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Switch to tenofovir preconception or in early pregnancy under hepatology guidance. Do not abruptly stop HBV therapy without advice (flare risk).
pregnancy.data: Limited human pregnancy data; preference for tenofovir is guideline-based.

lactation.riskSummary: There is little information on entecavir in human milk, and an alternative (tenofovir) may be preferred, especially while nursing a newborn or preterm infant.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Prefer tenofovir-based therapy if treatment needed while breastfeeding.
lactation.data: No adequate milk data per LactMed.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy where possible — animal teratogen and post-marketing malformation reports; reserve for serious systemic mycosis. Breastfeeding generally avoided (limited data, toxicity concern).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Itraconazole is teratogenic in animals (skeletal and other defects) and post-marketing reports describe congenital abnormalities, although causality is unproven. Avoid in pregnancy; reserve for serious or life-threatening systemic fungal infection where benefit clearly outweighs risk. Do not use for superficial infections (e.g. onychomycosis) in pregnancy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Effective contraception advised during therapy and for a period afterward per labelling. Specialist input for systemic mycoses.
pregnancy.data: Animal teratogenicity; limited human data.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited data indicate maternal itraconazole produces milk levels below infant treatment doses, but IDSA and other sources advise avoiding itraconazole during breastfeeding owing to lack of safety data and toxicity concerns.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Prefer a better-studied antifungal (e.g. fluconazole for candidiasis) while breastfeeding where appropriate.
lactation.data: Sparse milk data per LactMed; avoidance is precautionary.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy — teratogenic/embryotoxic in animals; reserve for life-threatening invasive mycosis. Avoid breastfeeding (no milk data, toxicity concern).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Voriconazole is teratogenic and embryotoxic in animal studies; human pregnancy data are very limited. Avoid in pregnancy unless treating a life-threatening invasive fungal infection (e.g. invasive aspergillosis) where no safer alternative exists and benefit outweighs risk.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Effective contraception advised during therapy. Specialist (infectious disease) management essential.
pregnancy.data: Animal teratogenicity; minimal human data.

lactation.riskSummary: There are no data on voriconazole in human milk; given its toxicity, it should be avoided during breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Discuss feeding alternatives with specialists if treatment is essential.
lactation.data: No milk data per LactMed; avoidance precautionary.

references.label: Pilmis B et al. Antifungal drugs during pregnancy. J Antimicrob Chemother 2015.

oneLiner: AVOID systemic ketoconazole in pregnancy (teratogenic in animals, antiandrogen, maternal hepatotoxicity). Topical forms have negligible absorption. Limited milk data for oral use.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Systemic (oral) ketoconazole is teratogenic in animals, has antiandrogenic effects, and carries a risk of maternal hepatotoxicity; oral use is now restricted generally and should be avoided in pregnancy. Topical ketoconazole has negligible systemic absorption and is considered low risk.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Avoid oral ketoconazole; use safer systemic antifungals where indicated. Topical use is acceptable for localised dermatophyte/seborrhoeic conditions.
pregnancy.data: Animal teratogenicity; antiandrogen activity; hepatotoxicity restricts oral use.

lactation.riskSummary: Topical ketoconazole is considered compatible (negligible absorption). For oral ketoconazole there are limited milk data; given hepatotoxicity concern an alternative is generally preferred while breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Avoid applying topical product to the breast where the infant could ingest it. Prefer fluconazole for systemic candidiasis if needed.
lactation.data: Sparse oral milk data; topical negligible per LactMed.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy (animal teratogen/embryotoxic). Limited milk data; alternatives preferred while breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Griseofulvin is embryotoxic and teratogenic in animals; the manufacturer advises against use in pregnancy. As it treats non-urgent superficial fungal infections, it should be avoided in pregnancy and treatment deferred or a safer agent used.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Defer treatment of dermatophyte infection until after pregnancy where possible, or use topical therapy. Effective contraception advised during and after therapy per labelling.
pregnancy.data: Animal teratogenicity; precautionary avoidance.

lactation.riskSummary: There is little information on griseofulvin in human milk; because it treats non-urgent conditions and has limited safety data, an alternative is generally preferred while breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Use topical antifungals where feasible.

oneLiner: PREFERRED treatment for vaginal/skin candidiasis in pregnancy — negligible systemic absorption. Compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Topical and intravaginal clotrimazole has negligible systemic absorption and a long record of safe use in pregnancy. It is a first-line treatment for vulvovaginal candidiasis in pregnancy (a 7-day course is often recommended in pregnancy).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Avoid using an applicator for vaginal therapy if there is concern (e.g. cervical) — manual insertion may be advised in late pregnancy per local practice.
pregnancy.data: Extensive reassuring use; minimal absorption.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Negligible maternal systemic absorption means infant exposure via milk is essentially nil.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: If applied to the nipple/breast for candidiasis, wipe off before feeds where practical.

oneLiner: Acceptable for oral/topical candidiasis in pregnancy and breastfeeding — low systemic absorption. Watch for warfarin interaction.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Topical and oral-gel miconazole have limited systemic absorption and are widely used for cutaneous and oropharyngeal candidiasis with a reassuring record. The intravaginal azoles (clotrimazole/miconazole) are preferred over oral fluconazole for vaginal candidiasis in pregnancy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Miconazole (even topical/gel) can potentiate warfarin — monitor INR if co-administered. Use the gel with care in infants because of a choking concern with large amounts.
pregnancy.data: Low systemic absorption; reassuring use.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Minimal maternal absorption; miconazole gel is itself used to treat oral thrush in infants, so milk exposure is not a concern.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Apply nipple preparations after feeds and wipe off before feeding where practical.

oneLiner: CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy (2nd/3rd-trimester fetotoxicity; avoid 1st trimester too). PREFERRED ACE inhibitor during breastfeeding if an ACEi is needed.

pregnancy.riskSummary: ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy. Second- and third-trimester exposure causes a fetopathy — oligohydramnios, fetal renal failure, hypotension, skull hypoplasia, limb contractures and death. First-trimester exposure is best avoided; switch women of childbearing potential to a pregnancy-appropriate agent preconception or at the first positive test.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Switch to labetalol, nifedipine MR or methyldopa for blood-pressure control. Counsel on contraception while on an ACEi if pregnancy is not desired.
pregnancy.data: Regulatory advice (Medsafe/MHRA) and cohort data confirm fetotoxicity, particularly second/third trimester.

trimesterNotes.note: Avoid; switch preconception. No convincing first-trimester malformation signal but stop and substitute.
Contraindicated — fetal renal/oligohydramnios effects.
Contraindicated — fetal renal failure, hypotension, skull hypoplasia, death.

lactation.riskSummary: Enalapril (with captopril) is the ACE inhibitor of choice in breastfeeding — very low milk transfer and a reassuring record. Considered acceptable, with caution in premature or very-low-birth-weight infants.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for hypotension/poor feeding in preterm or low-birth-weight babies.

reproductive.contraception: Effective contraception while on an ACE inhibitor if pregnancy is not desired.

references.label: Medsafe. ACE inhibitors and ARBs contraindicated in pregnancy. 2024.

oneLiner: CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy (ACEi fetotoxicity). During breastfeeding use with caution — enalapril/captopril preferred owing to more data.

pregnancy.riskSummary: ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy. Second/third-trimester exposure causes fetal renal failure, oligohydramnios, hypotension, skull hypoplasia and death; avoid first-trimester use as well. Switch preconception or at first positive pregnancy test.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Substitute labetalol, nifedipine MR or methyldopa.
pregnancy.data: Class fetotoxicity established.

trimesterNotes.note: Avoid; switch preconception.
Contraindicated — fetal renal/oligohydramnios effects.
Contraindicated — fetal renal failure, hypotension, death.

lactation.riskSummary: Ramipril can be used with caution during breastfeeding, but enalapril or captopril are preferred because they have more published lactation data.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: If an ACE inhibitor is required while breastfeeding, prefer enalapril or captopril. Caution in preterm/low-birth-weight infants.
lactation.data: Limited ramipril milk data per LactMed.

references.label: SPS (NHS). Using ACE inhibitors during breastfeeding.

oneLiner: CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy (ARB fetotoxicity, similar to ACE inhibitors). Avoid in breastfeeding where possible — minimal data; better-studied alternatives preferred.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Angiotensin receptor blockers are contraindicated in pregnancy and share the ACE-inhibitor fetopathy — second/third-trimester exposure causes oligohydramnios, fetal renal failure, hypotension, skull hypoplasia and death. No convincing first-trimester malformation signal, but avoid and switch preconception.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Substitute labetalol, nifedipine MR or methyldopa. Counsel on contraception if on an ARB and not planning pregnancy.
pregnancy.data: UKTIS/regulatory advice; fetotoxicity established.

trimesterNotes.note: Avoid; switch preconception.
Contraindicated — fetal renal/oligohydramnios effects.
Contraindicated — fetal renal failure, hypotension, death.

lactation.riskSummary: There is almost no published evidence on ARBs in breastfeeding, so they are not favoured in national guidelines while breastfeeding; use with caution and prefer a better-studied antihypertensive.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Prefer enalapril/captopril or labetalol/nifedipine postpartum if treatment needed while breastfeeding.
lactation.data: Minimal ARB milk data per LactMed/UKTIS.

reproductive.contraception: Effective contraception while on an ARB if pregnancy is not desired.

references.label: UKTIS. Use of angiotensin II receptor antagonists in pregnancy. https://uktis.org

oneLiner: CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy (ARB fetotoxicity). Avoid in breastfeeding where possible — minimal data; better-studied alternatives preferred.

pregnancy.riskSummary: ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy with the same fetopathy as ACE inhibitors (oligohydramnios, fetal renal failure, hypotension, skull hypoplasia, death) in the second and third trimesters. Avoid and switch preconception.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Substitute a pregnancy-appropriate agent (labetalol, nifedipine MR, methyldopa).
pregnancy.data: UKTIS/regulatory advice.

lactation.riskSummary: Very limited lactation data for ARBs; not favoured during breastfeeding in national guidelines. Use with caution and prefer a better-studied agent.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Prefer enalapril/labetalol/nifedipine postpartum if treatment needed.
lactation.data: Minimal ARB milk data per LactMed/UKTIS.

references.label: UKTIS. Use of angiotensin II receptor antagonists in pregnancy. https://uktis.org

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy (used for arrhythmia/SVT and rate control); compatible with breastfeeding (low milk transfer).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Calcium-channel blocker with substantial use in pregnancy for maternal supraventricular tachycardia and rate control; no clear teratogenic signal. Intravenous use near delivery can cause maternal hypotension and reduce uteroplacental perfusion, so it is used with care.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor maternal blood pressure, particularly with IV use. Adenosine is generally preferred for acute SVT termination in pregnancy.
pregnancy.data: Reassuring observational use.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Excreted into milk in small amounts (low relative infant dose); no adverse effects reported.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: No specific monitoring required.

oneLiner: Use with caution in pregnancy (some animal teratogenicity; prefer better-studied agents). Compatible with breastfeeding (low milk transfer).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Calcium-channel blocker with some animal teratogenicity and more limited human pregnancy data than nifedipine; use with caution and prefer better-characterised agents (nifedipine, labetalol, verapamil) where suitable. May be used when specifically indicated.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Prefer nifedipine for hypertension/tocolysis and labetalol/methyldopa for chronic hypertension in pregnancy.
pregnancy.data: Animal teratogenicity; limited human data.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Low milk transfer; no adverse effects reported. Acceptable when a calcium-channel blocker is needed during breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: No specific monitoring required.

oneLiner: May be used in pregnancy for hypertension when first-line agents are insufficient; caution near term (neonatal effects). Caution in breastfeeding (theoretical effect on milk and infant).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Centrally acting antihypertensive used in pregnancy when standard agents (labetalol, nifedipine, methyldopa) are insufficient; no clear teratogenic signal. Use with caution near delivery because of possible neonatal effects and rebound hypertension if abruptly stopped.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Generally a later-line antihypertensive in pregnancy. Avoid abrupt discontinuation (rebound hypertension).
pregnancy.data: Limited but non-alarming human data.

lactation.riskSummary: Use with caution. Clonidine passes into milk and could theoretically cause sedation/hypotension in the infant; it may also reduce prolactin and milk supply. Prefer alternatives during breastfeeding where possible.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for sedation/poor feeding and watch maternal milk supply.
lactation.data: Detectable in milk; potential prolactin suppression per LactMed.

oneLiner: Avoid initiating diuretics for hypertension in pregnancy (volume depletion, electrolyte effects); prefer labetalol/nifedipine/methyldopa. Limited milk data — caution in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Thiazide-type diuretics are generally avoided as antihypertensives in pregnancy because they can reduce maternal plasma volume (theoretically impairing placental perfusion) and cause electrolyte disturbance and neonatal effects (thrombocytopenia, hyponatraemia). Not teratogenic per se, but not a preferred pregnancy antihypertensive.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Switch to labetalol, nifedipine MR or methyldopa for blood-pressure control in pregnancy.
pregnancy.data: Class effects on volume/electrolytes drive avoidance.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited specific data; thiazide-type diuretics may suppress milk production (especially at higher doses) and reduce supply. Use with caution; prefer alternatives during breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Watch maternal milk supply; monitor infant.
lactation.data: Possible lactation suppression per LactMed (thiazide class).

oneLiner: Used in pregnancy mainly for phaeochromocytoma and resistant hypertension; limited general data — caution. Limited milk data — caution in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Alpha-blocker with limited pregnancy data; principal obstetric use is alpha-blockade in phaeochromocytoma and as add-on therapy for resistant hypertension. No clear teratogenic signal, but data are limited so use with caution and a clear indication.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Used under specialist guidance (e.g. phaeochromocytoma). Prefer established first-line agents for routine hypertension.
pregnancy.data: Limited human pregnancy data.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited lactation data; use with caution and monitor the infant for hypotension/sedation. Prefer better-studied agents where possible.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for poor feeding/hypotension.

oneLiner: Diuretics generally avoided as antihypertensives in pregnancy; limited amiloride data. Limited milk data — caution in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Potassium-sparing diuretic with limited pregnancy data. Diuretics are generally avoided for new antihypertensive treatment in pregnancy; amiloride may be continued in specific conditions (e.g. Liddle/Gitelman, certain endocrine disorders) under specialist guidance. No strong teratogenic signal but data are sparse.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist input for the underlying indication. Prefer pregnancy-established antihypertensives for blood-pressure control.
pregnancy.data: Limited human pregnancy data.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited lactation data; use with caution and prefer better-studied agents. Diuretics may theoretically affect milk supply.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant and maternal milk supply.

oneLiner: PREFERRED treatment for diabetes in pregnancy — does not cross the placenta in clinically significant amounts. Fully compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Insulin is the treatment of choice for type 1, type 2 and gestational diabetes requiring pharmacotherapy in pregnancy. Human insulin does not cross the placenta in significant amounts, and tight glycaemic control reduces fetal/maternal complications. Insulin requirements typically rise as pregnancy progresses.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Doses usually increase through pregnancy then fall sharply postpartum — anticipate dose reduction after delivery to avoid hypoglycaemia, especially with breastfeeding.
pregnancy.data: Standard of care; extensive experience.

lactation.riskSummary: Fully compatible. Insulin is a large protein that is digested in the infant gut and not absorbed; any amount in milk is harmless. Breastfeeding itself lowers maternal insulin requirements.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Reduce dose and watch for maternal hypoglycaemia while breastfeeding.
lactation.data: Not orally bioavailable to the infant per LactMed.

oneLiner: PREFERRED basal insulin in pregnancy — long experience, does not cross the placenta. Fully compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Isophane (NPH) insulin is a long-established basal insulin in pregnancy and a recommended option for diabetes in pregnancy. Insulin does not cross the placenta in significant amounts; good glycaemic control improves outcomes.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Anticipate rising requirements through pregnancy and a marked fall postpartum (hypoglycaemia risk with breastfeeding).
pregnancy.data: Standard of care; extensive experience.

lactation.riskSummary: Fully compatible. Not orally bioavailable to the infant; breastfeeding lowers maternal insulin needs.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Reduce dose and watch for maternal hypoglycaemia while breastfeeding.
lactation.data: Not absorbed by infant per LactMed.

oneLiner: Acceptable basal insulin analogue in pregnancy with accumulating reassuring data; compatible with breastfeeding (not absorbed by infant).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Insulin glargine has accumulating reassuring data in pregnancy and is used as a basal insulin; observational studies have not shown increased adverse outcomes compared with NPH. Insulin does not cross the placenta in significant amounts; tight control improves outcomes. Some guidelines still default to NPH/isophane given longest experience.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Anticipate rising requirements through pregnancy and postpartum fall. Either glargine or NPH is acceptable per current obstetric diabetes guidance.
pregnancy.data: Cohort data reassuring; smaller evidence base than NPH.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Insulin is digested in the infant gut and not absorbed; harmless in milk.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Reduce dose and watch for maternal hypoglycaemia while breastfeeding.
lactation.data: Not orally bioavailable to infant per LactMed.

oneLiner: PREFERRED rapid-acting insulin analogue in pregnancy — well studied, does not cross the placenta meaningfully. Compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Insulin aspart is a rapid-acting analogue with randomised-trial and cohort data supporting safety and efficacy in pregnancy; it is a recommended prandial insulin in pregnancy. Insulin does not cross the placenta in significant amounts.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Anticipate rising requirements through pregnancy and postpartum fall.
pregnancy.data: RCT/cohort data in pregnancy.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Not orally absorbed by the infant; breastfeeding lowers maternal insulin needs.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Reduce dose and watch for maternal hypoglycaemia while breastfeeding.
lactation.data: Not absorbed by infant per LactMed.

oneLiner: Avoid in pregnancy — insulin is preferred; limited data and animal growth/loss effects. No milk data — avoid in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Thiazolidinedione with limited human pregnancy data; insulin (and, where appropriate, metformin) is preferred for diabetes in pregnancy. Animal studies show growth restriction and fetal loss at high exposure. Avoid in pregnancy; switch to insulin.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Switch to insulin (and/or metformin) preconception or on confirming pregnancy.
pregnancy.data: Limited human data; insulin preferred.

lactation.riskSummary: No data on pioglitazone in human milk; given the lack of safety data and availability of preferred agents, avoid during breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Use insulin or metformin while breastfeeding instead.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy — animal reproductive toxicity, limited human data; stop before a planned pregnancy (long half-life). No milk data — avoid in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: GLP-1 receptor agonist with limited human pregnancy data and adverse reproductive findings in animals (embryofetal toxicity/malformations, growth effects). Because of its long half-life, stop semaglutide at least about 2 months before a planned pregnancy and switch diabetes therapy to insulin (and/or metformin). Avoid in pregnancy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Discontinue before planned conception given the prolonged half-life; substitute insulin. Not for weight management in pregnancy.
pregnancy.data: Animal reproductive toxicity; minimal human data.

lactation.riskSummary: No information on semaglutide in human milk. As a large peptide it is likely poorly absorbed orally by the infant, but absence of data and availability of preferred agents mean it should generally be avoided during breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Use insulin/metformin for diabetes while breastfeeding.

oneLiner: Avoid where possible in pregnancy (teratogenic potential and adverse neurodevelopment); if used, give vitamin K and monitor neonate. Caution in breastfeeding — infant sedation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Phenobarbital is associated with an increased risk of major congenital malformations (including cardiac and oro-facial defects) and with adverse neurodevelopment in exposed children; it should be avoided in pregnancy where a safer antiseizure medication (e.g. lamotrigine, levetiracetam) can control seizures. If continued for refractory epilepsy, do not stop abruptly (status risk); give high-dose folic acid periconceptionally and neonatal vitamin K, and monitor the neonate for sedation and withdrawal.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Prefer lower-risk agents preconception. Neonatal withdrawal and sedation can occur; vitamin K to mother/neonate to reduce haemorrhagic disease risk.
pregnancy.data: Registry and cohort data show malformation and neurodevelopmental signals.

lactation.riskSummary: Use with caution. Phenobarbital passes into milk (relative infant dose around 3-4% but accumulation possible due to long half-life) and can cause infant sedation, poor feeding and (on abrupt weaning) withdrawal. Monitor the infant; consider infant levels if symptomatic.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor for drowsiness, poor weight gain and developmental milestones; do not wean the infant off milk abruptly if the mother stops.

references.label: Tomson T et al. Antiepileptic drugs in pregnancy and breastfeeding. PMC9185784.

oneLiner: Limited human pregnancy data — use only if clearly needed; no clear malformation signal so far. Limited milk data — caution in breastfeeding with infant monitoring.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Newer antiseizure medication with limited human pregnancy data; available reports have not shown a clear teratogenic signal but numbers are small. Use in pregnancy only when needed for seizure control; better-established agents (lamotrigine, levetiracetam) are generally preferred. Do not stop abruptly. High-dose folic acid advised periconceptionally.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Maintain seizure control; specialist neurology input. Levels may change in pregnancy.
pregnancy.data: Limited registry data.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited information on lacosamide in milk; use with caution and monitor the infant for drowsiness and poor feeding. Where possible prefer an antiseizure medication with more lactation data.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant clinically; check level if symptomatic.

oneLiner: PREFERRED inhaled corticosteroid in pregnancy — best-studied ICS; keeping asthma controlled protects mother and fetus. Compatible with breastfeeding (negligible infant exposure).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Inhaled budesonide is the most extensively studied inhaled corticosteroid in pregnancy with reassuring data and no clear increase in malformations. Maintaining good asthma control is important: poorly controlled asthma is associated with preterm birth, low birth weight and pre-eclampsia. ICS therapy should be continued in pregnancy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Do not stop preventer therapy in pregnancy. Budesonide is often the ICS of choice but any needed ICS is preferable to uncontrolled asthma.
pregnancy.data: Large pregnancy cohorts; reassuring.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. The amount of inhaled budesonide entering milk is minute and infant exposure is negligible (low oral bioavailability).
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Continue as needed for asthma control while breastfeeding.

oneLiner: PREFERRED/acceptable inhaled corticosteroid in pregnancy — continue for asthma control. Compatible with breastfeeding (negligible infant exposure).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Inhaled beclometasone is considered safe and is recommended for maintaining asthma control in pregnancy. Good asthma control reduces the risk of preterm birth, low birth weight and pre-eclampsia. Continue preventer therapy throughout pregnancy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Do not stop preventer therapy. Budesonide has the largest pregnancy dataset, but beclometasone is an acceptable continuation if already controlling the patient.
pregnancy.data: Reassuring class data.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Inhaled corticosteroids produce negligible milk levels and infant exposure; expert opinion considers them acceptable in breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Continue as needed for asthma control while breastfeeding.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy for significant reflux/peptic disease when antacids/lifestyle insufficient; compatible with breastfeeding (low milk transfer).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Proton pump inhibitors, including esomeprazole (the S-isomer of omeprazole), have substantial reassuring human pregnancy data without a clear increase in major malformations. Acceptable for moderate-to-severe gastro-oesophageal reflux or peptic disease in pregnancy when lifestyle measures and antacids are inadequate. Omeprazole has the largest dataset of the class.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Step up from antacids/alginates as needed. Use the lowest effective dose.
pregnancy.data: Large cohort data for the PPI class.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. PPIs are acid-labile and largely degraded in the infant's stomach; milk levels are low. No adverse effects reported.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: No specific monitoring required.
lactation.data: Low relative infant dose per LactMed.

oneLiner: PREFERRED for reflux/peptic symptoms in pregnancy — minimal systemic absorption. Compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Sucralfate is a non-systemic mucosal protectant that is minimally absorbed; it is considered a good first-line option for reflux/peptic symptoms in pregnancy. No teratogenic signal.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Aluminium content is the main consideration with prolonged use/renal impairment, but systemic absorption is minimal. Separate from other oral drugs (reduces their absorption).
pregnancy.data: Minimal absorption; reassuring use.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Negligible systemic absorption means essentially no transfer into milk.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: No specific monitoring required.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy for reflux/peptic disease; other H2 blockers or PPIs often preferred (cimetidine has antiandrogenic/enzyme-inhibition properties). Compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: H2-receptor antagonists, including cimetidine, have reassuring pregnancy data and no clear teratogenic signal. Cimetidine has weak antiandrogenic activity and inhibits hepatic enzymes (drug interactions); other H2 antagonists (e.g. famotidine) or PPIs are often preferred, but cimetidine is acceptable when needed.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Check for interacting medications (CYP inhibition). Use lowest effective dose.
pregnancy.data: Reassuring H2-blocker class data.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Cimetidine is concentrated somewhat in milk, but no adverse effects have been reported; other H2 antagonists with lower milk levels (e.g. famotidine) may be preferred.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant; prefer famotidine if minimising milk levels is desired.
lactation.data: Concentrates in milk but no reported harm per LactMed.

oneLiner: Limited pregnancy data — use only if clearly needed (maternal QT caution). Compatible with breastfeeding and used off-label as a galactagogue, but screen for QT-prolongation risk.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Human pregnancy data for domperidone are limited; it does not cross the blood-brain barrier well but information is insufficient to call it preferred. Use only when clearly needed for refractory nausea/gastroparesis, weighing maternal QT-prolongation risk.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Avoid in women with cardiac conduction abnormalities or on other QT-prolonging drugs. Prefer better-studied antiemetics in pregnancy where possible.
pregnancy.data: Limited human pregnancy data.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Domperidone passes into milk in very small amounts (well under 0.01% of the maternal weight-adjusted dose) and is used off-label as a galactagogue. The principal safety concern is maternal QT prolongation, not infant exposure.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Before galactagogue use consider maternal cardiac risk (personal/family history of arrhythmia, QT-prolonging drugs); some clinicians check an ECG. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time.
lactation.data: Very low relative infant dose per LactMed; AAP lists it compatible.

references.label: ABM Clinical Protocol #9: Use of galactogogues.

oneLiner: Acceptable for refractory nausea/vomiting in pregnancy (early data reassuring); limited milk data — caution in breastfeeding with infant monitoring.

pregnancy.riskSummary: A 5-HT3 antagonist used for chemotherapy/refractory nausea. Available early-pregnancy exposure data did not show an increased risk of major or minor fetal anomalies. Reserve for nausea/vomiting not controlled by first-line antiemetics (e.g. doxylamine-pyridoxine, antihistamines, metoclopramide).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Used when first-line antiemetics fail. Ondansetron has the largest 5-HT3 dataset in pregnancy.
pregnancy.data: Reassuring early-exposure study; smaller dataset than ondansetron.

lactation.riskSummary: No information on granisetron in human milk; use with caution and monitor the infant. An alternative with more data may be preferred for routine use.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for constipation/irritability; prefer better-studied agents if possible.

references.label: Pasternak B et al. Safety of granisetron exposure in early pregnancy. 2019.

oneLiner: Acceptable for short-term antispasmodic use in pregnancy (poorly absorbed quaternary amine); compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Hyoscine butylbromide is a quaternary ammonium antispasmodic that is poorly absorbed orally and does not cross the blood-brain barrier; it has no clear teratogenic signal and is used for visceral/smooth-muscle spasm in pregnancy. It is sometimes used in labour to aid cervical dilatation.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Standard antimuscarinic cautions (tachycardia, dry mouth). Short-term use as needed.
pregnancy.data: Poor absorption; reassuring use.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Poor oral absorption and quaternary structure mean negligible milk transfer and minimal infant exposure.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: No specific monitoring required for occasional use.
lactation.data: Negligible expected milk transfer per LactMed.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy (first-generation antihistamine with long use); use occasionally in breastfeeding — sedation/irritability and possible milk-supply effects with regular use.

pregnancy.riskSummary: A first-generation H1 antihistamine with a long record of use in pregnancy and no clear teratogenic signal; used for allergy, pruritus and as an adjunct for nausea. First-generation antihistamines are generally considered acceptable in pregnancy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Sedating; counsel on drowsiness. Near term, large/regular doses theoretically could contribute to neonatal effects.
pregnancy.data: Long clinical experience; reassuring.

lactation.riskSummary: Occasional use is acceptable, but regular use of sedating antihistamines can cause infant drowsiness/irritability and (theoretically, especially with combined products) reduce milk supply. Non-sedating antihistamines (e.g. loratadine, cetirizine) are preferred for regular use while breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Prefer non-sedating antihistamines for regular use; monitor infant for sedation/poor feeding.

oneLiner: Avoid in the third trimester / near delivery (neonatal CNS effects/withdrawal reported with high doses). Acceptable earlier when needed. Use cautiously in breastfeeding (limited data, sedation).

pregnancy.riskSummary: A first-generation antihistamine used for anxiety, pruritus and as an antiemetic. No clear major teratogenic signal at usual doses, but the manufacturer advises against use near delivery because high maternal doses have been associated with neonatal CNS depression, irritability and withdrawal-type effects. Use with caution; avoid late third trimester / peripartum.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Avoid near delivery; prefer better-studied agents in late pregnancy. Sedating.
pregnancy.data: Limited human data; neonatal effects with high peripartum doses.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited lactation data; as a sedating antihistamine it may cause infant drowsiness. Use cautiously and prefer non-sedating antihistamines for regular use.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for sedation/poor feeding.
lactation.data: Sparse milk data; sedation concern per LactMed.

oneLiner: PREFERRED for treating/preventing iron-deficiency anaemia in pregnancy. Compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Oral iron is the standard treatment and prophylaxis for iron-deficiency anaemia in pregnancy, which is common and associated with adverse maternal and fetal outcomes when untreated. Iron supplementation in pregnancy is recommended by WHO. No teratogenicity at therapeutic doses (overdose is, however, toxic).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: GI side-effects (constipation, nausea) are common; take with vitamin C / away from tea/calcium to aid absorption. Keep iron tablets away from children (acute overdose risk).
pregnancy.data: WHO/NICE antenatal anaemia guidance.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Iron is a normal milk constituent; maternal supplementation does not adversely affect the infant and helps correct maternal anaemia.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: No specific monitoring of the infant required.

references.label: WHO. Daily iron and folic acid supplementation in pregnancy.

oneLiner: PREFERRED — recommended supplement in pregnancy and lactation at standard doses. Compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Vitamin D supplementation is recommended in pregnancy (commonly 400 IU/day, higher for deficiency) and is safe at recommended doses. Adequate maternal vitamin D supports maternal and neonatal bone health. Avoid excessive megadoses (hypercalcaemia risk).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Standard supplementation (e.g. 400 IU/day) or treatment doses for documented deficiency. Avoid toxic megadoses.
pregnancy.data: Antenatal supplementation guidance (NICE/WHO).

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Maternal supplementation at recommended doses is safe; higher maternal doses can raise milk vitamin D content but breastfed infants are usually given their own supplement per local guidance.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Breastfed infants commonly receive a vitamin D supplement regardless of maternal intake.
lactation.data: Safe at recommended doses per LactMed.

references.label: NICE. Maternal and child nutrition guidance.

oneLiner: PREFERRED first-line for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy (alone or with doxylamine). Compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Pyridoxine is a recommended first-line treatment for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy, used alone or combined with doxylamine, with a strong safety record. It is also an essential vitamin in pregnancy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: First-line antiemetic in pregnancy per ACOG. Very high chronic doses can cause peripheral neuropathy (not at antiemetic doses).
pregnancy.data: ACOG nausea/vomiting of pregnancy guidance; long safety record.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible at normal/therapeutic doses. Very high maternal doses have historically been associated with lactation suppression, so avoid excessive doses; ordinary supplementation/antiemetic use is fine.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Avoid very high chronic doses while breastfeeding; standard doses are safe.
lactation.data: Safe at usual doses per LactMed.

references.label: ACOG Practice Bulletin 189. Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy.

oneLiner: Avoid in the first trimester; acceptable from the second trimester for soil-transmitted helminths (WHO public-health deworming). Compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Mebendazole is poorly absorbed orally. WHO recommends single-dose mebendazole (or albendazole) for deworming pregnant women only after the first trimester as a public-health intervention in endemic areas; systematic reviews have not found a significant increase in adverse birth outcomes with exposure. Avoid in the first trimester where the organogenesis period and limited data warrant caution; defer treatment if not urgent.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Defer non-urgent treatment past the first trimester. Pinworm in pregnancy is often managed with hygiene measures first.
pregnancy.data: WHO deworming-in-pregnancy guidance; reassuring systematic-review data after first trimester.

trimesterNotes.note: Avoid; defer non-urgent treatment.
Acceptable (WHO public-health deworming).
Acceptable.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Minimal oral absorption and minimal milk excretion; WHO classifies it as compatible with breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: No special precautions required.

oneLiner: PREFERRED treatment for scabies and head lice in pregnancy and breastfeeding — minimal systemic absorption.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Topical permethrin is the first-line treatment for scabies and head lice in pregnancy. Systemic absorption through skin is minimal and there is no teratogenic signal; it is considered the safest scabicide/pediculicide in pregnancy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Treat close contacts and decontaminate bedding/clothing per scabies protocol. Oral ivermectin is reserved for cases where topical therapy is unsuitable.
pregnancy.data: Minimal absorption; reassuring use.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Negligible systemic absorption; preferred treatment for scabies/lice while breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: If treating the breast/nipple area for scabies, cleanse before feeds where practical.

references.label: CDC. Scabies treatment in pregnant/lactating women.

oneLiner: PREFERRED in pregnancy for eclampsia/severe pre-eclampsia seizure prophylaxis and fetal neuroprotection. Compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Magnesium sulphate is the agent of choice for prevention and treatment of eclamptic seizures in severe pre-eclampsia/eclampsia and for fetal neuroprotection before anticipated very preterm birth (reduces cerebral palsy). It is given for short, defined periods peripartum. The 'D' legacy category reflects concern about prolonged use (>5-7 days) causing fetal/neonatal hypocalcaemia and bone demineralisation; short obstetric courses are standard of care.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor for magnesium toxicity (loss of reflexes, respiratory depression); have calcium gluconate available as antidote. Avoid prolonged tocolytic use (>5-7 days) due to fetal bone effects.
pregnancy.data: MAGPIE trial (eclampsia prophylaxis); Cochrane reviews of fetal neuroprotection.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Maternal magnesium minimally raises milk magnesium and infant oral absorption is poor; normal levels are reached quickly. No adverse effects expected.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Peripartum use does not preclude breastfeeding once the mother is stable.

references.label: Altman D et al. MAGPIE trial. Lancet 2002.

oneLiner: Used postpartum for refractory postpartum haemorrhage (uterotonic) — not for use in ongoing pregnancy. Limited milk data; brief postpartum use compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Carboprost is a prostaglandin uterotonic used to treat refractory postpartum haemorrhage and (separately) for second-trimester termination. It causes strong uterine contraction and is contraindicated for use in an ongoing/desired pregnancy. Avoid in women with significant asthma (bronchospasm).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Second- or third-line uterotonic for PPH after oxytocin and ergometrine. Avoid in active asthma. Not a maintenance medication.
pregnancy.data: Established PPH management agent.

lactation.riskSummary: Brief postpartum administration is compatible with breastfeeding; the short half-life means little persists. Limited specific milk data.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Breastfeeding can proceed once the mother is stable after PPH management.
lactation.data: Short-acting; limited milk data per LactMed.

references.label: WHO recommendations for the prevention and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage.

oneLiner: Generally avoided for malaria prophylaxis in pregnancy (limited data); may be used for treatment when benefit outweighs risk. Limited milk data; not recommended when nursing infants under 5 kg.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Atovaquone-proguanil has not been adequately studied in pregnancy and is generally avoided for prophylaxis, though limited data suggest adverse-event rates are not increased. It may be used for malaria treatment in pregnancy when the benefit outweighs the uncertainty and preferred agents are unsuitable. Folate-dependent organisms: proguanil is a folate antagonist, so adequate folate is advised.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: For malaria prophylaxis in pregnancy, alternatives (e.g. mefloquine) are often preferred. For treatment, follow regional/specialist guidance.
pregnancy.data: Limited but non-alarming pregnancy data.

lactation.riskSummary: Little information on use during breastfeeding. CDC does not recommend it for malaria prevention while nursing an infant weighing under 5 kg, but it can be used for treatment of breastfeeding women of infants of any weight when benefit outweighs risk.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Avoid for prophylaxis if nursing an infant under 5 kg; treatment use is acceptable when indicated.

references.label: CDC. Malaria prophylaxis in pregnant/breastfeeding women.
