oneLiner: Artemisinin-based combination therapy: avoided in the first trimester historically, but WHO now considers ACTs acceptable in all trimesters for uncomplicated malaria; acceptable in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) are first-line for uncomplicated falciparum malaria. Historically artemisinins were avoided in the first trimester because of embryotoxicity in animals, but accumulating human data are reassuring and WHO now considers ACTs (including artemether-lumefantrine and dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine) acceptable in all trimesters for uncomplicated malaria when the alternative (quinine plus clindamycin) is less effective or unavailable. Untreated malaria in pregnancy carries major maternal/fetal risk.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Piperaquine prolongs QT — caution with other QT-prolonging drugs/cardiac risk. Follow current national malaria guidance for trimester-specific choice.
pregnancy.data: WHO malaria treatment guidelines; reassuring human pregnancy data for ACTs.

lactation.riskSummary: Acceptable. Limited data but the small amounts in milk are not expected to harm the infant; treatment of maternal malaria should not be withheld during breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Treat maternal malaria as indicated; monitor infant.
lactation.data: Limited milk data per LactMed; treatment not withheld.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for malaria (treatment in pregnancy).

oneLiner: Avoid in the first trimester (manufacturer advice); acceptable later for indicated anaerobic/protozoal infection. Withhold breastfeeding during and for 3 days after a dose (manufacturer/LactMed advice).

pregnancy.riskSummary: A nitroimidazole related to metronidazole. The manufacturer advises against first-trimester use; human data are more limited than for metronidazole. After the first trimester it may be used for indicated protozoal/anaerobic infections (e.g. trichomoniasis, giardiasis, amoebiasis) when benefit outweighs risk. No clear teratogenic signal in available data but caution is advised.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Metronidazole has the larger pregnancy dataset and is often preferred. Avoid alcohol (disulfiram-like reaction).
pregnancy.data: Limited human data; class similar to metronidazole.

lactation.riskSummary: Tinidazole passes into milk; the manufacturer and LactMed advise withholding breastfeeding during therapy and for about 72 hours after the last dose (express and discard milk). For single-dose therapy this interruption is short.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Interrupt breastfeeding for ~3 days after the dose; or prefer metronidazole which allows continued breastfeeding in many regimens.
lactation.data: Milk transfer documented; temporary interruption advised per LactMed.

oneLiner: Limited human pregnancy data — use only if clearly needed. Limited milk data — caution in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Antiprotozoal/anthelmintic with limited human pregnancy data; animal studies have not shown teratogenicity. Use only when clearly needed (e.g. symptomatic cryptosporidiosis/giardiasis) and benefit outweighs the uncertainty.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Many parasitic indications can be deferred or managed supportively in pregnancy; reserve for clear need.
pregnancy.data: Limited human data; no animal teratogenicity.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited information on nitazoxanide in milk; use with caution and monitor the infant. Where possible defer or use a better-studied agent.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for GI upset.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy for clear indications (leprosy, dermatitis herpetiformis, PCP prophylaxis); watch maternal/fetal/neonatal haemolysis, especially with G6PD deficiency. Caution in breastfeeding (infant haemolysis risk).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Dapsone has a long record of use in pregnancy for leprosy, dermatitis herpetiformis and as an alternative for Pneumocystis prophylaxis, without a clear teratogenic signal. The main risk is dose-related haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia in the mother and fetus/neonate, particularly with G6PD deficiency; folic acid supplementation is advised.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Screen/consider G6PD status. Co-prescribe folic acid. Monitor maternal haemoglobin.
pregnancy.data: Long clinical experience; haemolysis is the key concern.

lactation.riskSummary: Use with caution. Dapsone is excreted into milk in appreciable amounts and has caused haemolytic anaemia in a breastfed infant; risk is higher in G6PD-deficient infants. Monitor the infant for haemolysis; some sources advise avoiding in the newborn/preterm period.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor breastfed infant for haemolysis/jaundice; consider infant G6PD status.
lactation.data: Appreciable milk transfer; reported infant haemolysis per LactMed.

oneLiner: CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy — risk of hypospadias/ambiguous genitalia in a male fetus. Pregnant women should not handle crushed/broken tablets. Not relevant to maternal use in lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Finasteride inhibits conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT), which is essential for normal development of male external genitalia. It is teratogenic to a male fetus (risk of hypospadias and abnormal genital development) and is contraindicated in pregnancy. It is used in men (BPH, androgenetic alopecia); the principal pregnancy concern is fetal exposure. Pregnant women or those who may become pregnant should not handle crushed or broken tablets (intact coated tablets prevent contact during normal handling).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Not for use in women who are or may become pregnant. Counsel about tablet handling. Semen exposure delivers only trace amounts and is generally not considered a meaningful fetal risk.
pregnancy.data: Animal data show dose-dependent hypospadias in male offspring; mechanism well understood.

lactation.riskSummary: Finasteride is not indicated in women; there are no data on use during breastfeeding and it should be avoided. The relevant safety message concerns fetal exposure, not breastfed-infant exposure.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Not used by breastfeeding women.
lactation.data: No lactation data; not used in women.

references.label: FDA label: Finasteride (Propecia). Contraindication in pregnancy; tablet-handling warning.

oneLiner: CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy — risk of male-fetus genital abnormalities (long half-life). Pregnant women should not handle capsules. Not relevant to maternal use in lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Dutasteride, like finasteride, inhibits DHT formation and risks abnormal development of male external genitalia (e.g. hypospadias); it is contraindicated in pregnancy. It has a long half-life and persists for an extended period after stopping. Used in men (BPH); the principal concern is fetal exposure.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Not for use in women of childbearing potential who may become pregnant. Pregnant women should not handle leaking capsules. Men donating blood should wait per labelling because of the long half-life.
pregnancy.data: Class mechanism predicts male-fetus genital effects; long half-life.

lactation.riskSummary: Not indicated in women; no lactation data; avoid. The relevant safety concern is fetal, not breastfed-infant, exposure.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Not used by breastfeeding women.
lactation.data: No lactation data; not used in women.

references.label: FDA label: Dutasteride (Avodart). Contraindication in pregnancy; capsule-handling warning.

oneLiner: Use with caution in pregnancy — first-trimester Ebstein's anomaly/cardiac risk (small absolute increase); needs specialist management and level monitoring. AVOID/caution in breastfeeding (infant toxicity reported).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Lithium in the first trimester is associated with a small increased risk of cardiac malformations, notably Ebstein's anomaly; the absolute risk is lower than once feared but real. Discontinuing lithium risks serious relapse of bipolar disorder, so decisions are individualised with specialist input. If continued, monitor levels closely (clearance rises in pregnancy then falls abruptly at delivery — toxicity risk peripartum), arrange fetal cardiac assessment, and adjust dosing around delivery.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist perinatal-psychiatry management. Fetal echocardiography. Frequent level monitoring; reduce dose/hold around delivery to avoid maternal/neonatal toxicity. Neonatal effects ('floppy baby', thyroid/renal) can occur.
pregnancy.data: Cohort data (e.g. NEJM 2017) quantify the cardiac-malformation risk.

lactation.riskSummary: Lithium passes into milk and infant serum levels can be appreciable; reversible neonatal toxicity (hypotonia, thyroid and renal changes) has been reported. Many authorities advise against breastfeeding on lithium, or to do so only with close infant monitoring of lithium levels, thyroid and renal function under specialist guidance.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: If breastfeeding is undertaken, monitor infant lithium level, TSH, renal function and hydration; avoid in dehydration/intercurrent illness.
lactation.data: Appreciable milk transfer; infant toxicity reported per LactMed.

references.label: Patorno E et al. Lithium use in pregnancy and risk of cardiac malformations. NEJM 2017.

oneLiner: Limited human pregnancy data — use only if clearly needed. No milk data — caution in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Anxiolytic with limited human pregnancy data; animal studies have not shown teratogenicity. Use only when clearly needed and after considering better-studied options (e.g. SSRIs where appropriate). No clear teratogenic signal but data are sparse.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Weigh against better-characterised anxiolytic/antidepressant options in pregnancy.
pregnancy.data: Limited human data; no animal teratogenicity.

lactation.riskSummary: No information on buspirone in human milk; use with caution and monitor the infant for sedation/poor feeding. Prefer agents with lactation data where possible.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for sedation.

oneLiner: Acceptable for induction/maintenance of anaesthesia in pregnancy (including Caesarean) and in breastfeeding — rapidly cleared, very low milk transfer.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Propofol is widely used for induction and maintenance of general anaesthesia in pregnant women, including at Caesarean section, with a reassuring record. Like all general anaesthetics it crosses the placenta and can cause transient neonatal depression when used at delivery, managed by the anaesthetic/neonatal team. No established teratogenicity.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Standard obstetric anaesthetic practice. Neonatal team aware if used at delivery.
pregnancy.data: Extensive anaesthetic use; reassuring.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Propofol is rapidly cleared and milk levels are very low; breastfeeding can resume as soon as the mother is awake and alert after anaesthesia.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Resume breastfeeding once recovered from anaesthesia; no need to discard milk.
lactation.data: Very low milk transfer per LactMed.

oneLiner: Acceptable inhalational anaesthetic in pregnancy (including Caesarean); compatible with breastfeeding — rapidly eliminated.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Volatile anaesthetic widely used in pregnancy and at Caesarean delivery with a reassuring record. It crosses the placenta (transient neonatal depression possible at delivery) and relaxes the uterus (relevant to obstetric haemorrhage at high concentrations). No established teratogenicity at clinical exposures.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Standard obstetric anaesthesia. Uterine relaxation at high MAC may increase bleeding — managed by the anaesthetic team.
pregnancy.data: Extensive anaesthetic use.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Rapidly eliminated by exhalation with minimal milk transfer; breastfeeding can resume once the mother is awake and alert.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Resume breastfeeding after recovery; no need to discard milk.
lactation.data: Rapid elimination; minimal milk levels per LactMed.

oneLiner: Used in pregnancy for anaesthesia/analgesia when indicated (caution near delivery — neonatal effects, increased uterine tone); compatible with breastfeeding after recovery.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Ketamine is used in pregnancy for induction/anaesthesia (e.g. in haemodynamic instability) and procedural analgesia. It crosses the placenta; high doses can increase uterine tone and cause neonatal depression at delivery, so dosing is controlled. No established teratogenicity at clinical anaesthetic exposures; (separate concerns exist for repeated high-dose/recreational use).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Used under anaesthetic/critical-care supervision. Avoid high doses near delivery (uterine tone, neonatal depression). Not first-line for chronic pain in pregnancy.
pregnancy.data: Anaesthetic use documented; controlled dosing.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible after recovery. Short single anaesthetic/analgesic exposures produce low milk levels and are rapidly cleared; resume breastfeeding once the mother is alert and oriented.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Resume breastfeeding after recovery from sedation; repeated/prolonged use needs individual assessment.
lactation.data: Rapid clearance; limited but reassuring milk data per LactMed.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy for emergency/anaesthetic indications (bradycardia, premedication, organophosphate poisoning). Brief use compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Atropine crosses the placenta but has been used in pregnancy for emergency and anaesthetic indications (symptomatic bradycardia, antimuscarinic premedication, and as an antidote in organophosphate/anticholinesterase poisoning) without an established teratogenic signal. In life-threatening situations (e.g. poisoning) it should not be withheld.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Use for clear indications; in poisoning, treat the mother as the priority. Crosses placenta and can affect fetal heart rate.
pregnancy.data: Emergency/anaesthetic use; no teratogenic signal at usual exposures.

lactation.riskSummary: Brief use is compatible. Small amounts may pass into milk; occasional/single doses are unlikely to harm the infant, though antimuscarinics could theoretically reduce milk supply with repeated use.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant after repeated use; single emergency/anaesthetic doses are not a concern.
lactation.data: Limited milk data; brief use compatible per LactMed.

oneLiner: PREFERRED — the life-saving drug of choice for maternal anaphylaxis and cardiac arrest in pregnancy; do not withhold. Compatible with breastfeeding (negligible oral bioavailability).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Adrenaline is the first-line, life-saving treatment for anaphylaxis and is used in maternal cardiac arrest/resuscitation in pregnancy. Although it reduces uteroplacental blood flow transiently, treating maternal anaphylaxis/arrest is the priority — untreated maternal collapse is far more dangerous to the fetus. Do not withhold in an emergency.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Give IM adrenaline promptly for anaphylaxis exactly as in non-pregnant patients. Follow maternal resuscitation algorithms (including perimortem Caesarean considerations).
pregnancy.data: Standard emergency care; benefit clearly outweighs theoretical risk.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Adrenaline has a very short half-life and is not orally bioavailable, so any trace in milk would not affect the infant. Emergency use does not preclude breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: No interruption of breastfeeding required.
lactation.data: Short half-life; not orally bioavailable per LactMed.

references.label: Resuscitation Council/ACOG. Maternal resuscitation and anaphylaxis management.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy for acute indications (hypertensive emergencies, uterine relaxation for retained placenta/breech, acute coronary/heart-failure care); monitor maternal blood pressure. Limited milk data; brief use acceptable.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Glyceryl trinitrate is used in pregnancy for acute indications including hypertensive emergencies, acute pulmonary oedema, and as a short-acting uterine relaxant (e.g. for uterine inversion, retained placenta, intrapartum fetal distress, breech/second-twin manipulation). No established teratogenicity; the main effect is maternal (and potentially fetal) hypotension.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor maternal blood pressure closely; transient hypotension can reduce uteroplacental perfusion. Short-acting and titratable.
pregnancy.data: Established acute obstetric/cardiac use.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited specific milk data; brief or acute use is considered acceptable given the short half-life. Monitor the infant if used repeatedly.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Brief/acute use compatible; monitor infant if prolonged.
lactation.data: Short half-life; limited milk data per LactMed.

oneLiner: PREFERRED — the antidote of choice for paracetamol overdose in pregnancy; do not withhold (protects mother and fetus). Compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: N-acetylcysteine is the antidote of choice for paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning in pregnancy and should be given according to standard protocols when indicated; it crosses the placenta and helps protect the fetus from paracetamol hepatotoxicity. Untreated maternal paracetamol overdose threatens both mother and fetus, so treatment must not be delayed.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Treat per standard paracetamol-overdose nomogram/protocol; do not lower the threshold to treat in pregnancy. Used at term/labour as needed.
pregnancy.data: Standard toxicology practice; placental transfer is protective.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Short therapeutic courses (e.g. for overdose) are not expected to harm a breastfed infant; NAC is also used directly in infants.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: No interruption of breastfeeding required for antidotal use.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy for indicated acute poisoning — not absorbed systemically. Compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Activated charcoal is not absorbed from the GI tract and has no direct fetal exposure; it is used in pregnancy for gut decontamination after suitable ingestions within the appropriate time window, with airway-protection precautions. Treating maternal poisoning benefits the fetus.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Standard indications/timing and aspiration precautions apply (airway protection if reduced consciousness). No dose change for pregnancy.
pregnancy.data: Not systemically absorbed; standard toxicology use.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Not absorbed and therefore not present in milk; no infant exposure.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: No interruption of breastfeeding required.

oneLiner: Acceptable for bacterial conjunctivitis in pregnancy and breastfeeding — minimal systemic absorption from topical ocular use.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Topical ocular chloramphenicol produces minimal systemic absorption, so the theoretical concerns associated with systemic chloramphenicol (grey baby syndrome near term, bone marrow effects) are not expected from eye drops/ointment. It is commonly used for bacterial conjunctivitis in pregnancy. Systemic chloramphenicol, by contrast, is avoided especially near term.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Use the ophthalmic form for eye infection; avoid systemic chloramphenicol near term. Punctal occlusion can further reduce systemic absorption.
pregnancy.data: Minimal systemic absorption from ocular use.

lactation.riskSummary: Acceptable. Systemic absorption from eye drops is minimal and milk levels would be negligible; theoretical infant marrow concerns relate to systemic dosing, not topical ocular use.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant only if used extensively; ocular use is low risk.

oneLiner: PREFERRED topical antibiotic in pregnancy and breastfeeding (impetigo, nasal MRSA decolonisation) — negligible systemic absorption.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Topical mupirocin has negligible systemic absorption through intact or broken skin and no teratogenic signal; it is a preferred topical antibiotic for impetigo, infected dermatoses and nasal Staphylococcus/MRSA decolonisation in pregnancy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: For localised skin/nasal infection. Polyethylene glycol vehicle: caution with large areas/broken skin in renal impairment, but systemic exposure is minimal.
pregnancy.data: Negligible absorption; reassuring use.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Minimal absorption and negligible milk transfer. If applied to the nipple/areola, wash/wipe before feeds to avoid the infant ingesting ointment.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Wipe off nipple applications before feeding.

oneLiner: Acceptable topical antibiotic in pregnancy and breastfeeding (skin/eye infection) — low systemic absorption.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Topical fusidic acid (skin and ophthalmic) has low systemic absorption and no teratogenic signal; it is used for localised staphylococcal skin infections and bacterial conjunctivitis in pregnancy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: For localised infection. Mupirocin is an alternative topical antistaphylococcal agent.
pregnancy.data: Low systemic absorption; reassuring use.

lactation.riskSummary: Acceptable. Low systemic absorption and negligible milk transfer. If applied to the nipple area, wipe off before feeds.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Wipe off nipple applications before feeding.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and breastfeeding for inflammatory skin disease — prefer mild/moderate potency and limit area/duration of potent steroids (potent/large-area use linked to fetal growth restriction).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Topical corticosteroids are used in pregnancy for eczema/psoriasis and other inflammatory dermatoses. Mild-to-moderate-potency steroids are considered low risk. Large cumulative amounts of POTENT/very-potent topical steroids (e.g. >300 g over pregnancy) have been associated with low birth weight/fetal growth restriction, so use the lowest effective potency over the smallest area for the shortest time. (Note: this entry is topical betamethasone; antenatal systemic betamethasone for fetal lung maturation is a separate, recommended use.)
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Prefer mild/moderate potency; limit potent-steroid quantity and duration. Monitor fetal growth if large amounts of potent steroid are required.
pregnancy.data: Cohort data link high cumulative potent topical steroid use to low birth weight.

lactation.riskSummary: Acceptable. Minimal systemic absorption from appropriate topical use; negligible milk transfer. Avoid applying potent steroid to the nipple/areola where the infant feeds, or wipe off before feeds.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Do not apply to the nipple immediately before feeding; wipe off if used there.

references.label: Chi CC et al. Topical corticosteroids in pregnancy. Cochrane review.

oneLiner: PREFERRED skin/cord antiseptic in pregnancy and breastfeeding — minimal systemic absorption; used for neonatal cord care in many settings.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Topical chlorhexidine antiseptic is poorly absorbed through skin/mucosa and is widely used in pregnancy for skin preparation, hand hygiene and (in some settings) vaginal/perineal cleansing. WHO recommends chlorhexidine for neonatal umbilical cord care in high-mortality settings. No teratogenic concern from topical use.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Avoid getting solution in the eyes/middle ear. For skin antisepsis and (where used) intrapartum/cord care.
pregnancy.data: Minimal absorption; WHO cord-care guidance.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Negligible systemic absorption; if used on the breast/nipple as an antiseptic, rinse before feeds to avoid the infant ingesting it.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Rinse nipple area before feeding if used there.

references.label: WHO recommendations on newborn cord care (chlorhexidine).

oneLiner: Avoid in pregnancy where possible (limited data; some malformation reports) — defer gout urate-lowering until after pregnancy. Compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Human pregnancy data for allopurinol are limited and there are case reports of a possible pattern of malformations with first-trimester exposure (resembling features of mycophenolate embryopathy in a few reports), though causality is unproven. Because urate-lowering therapy for gout is not urgent, it is generally avoided/deferred in pregnancy; if a specific non-deferrable indication exists, weigh carefully with specialist input.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Stop/defer urate-lowering therapy in pregnancy where possible. Manage acute gout flares with pregnancy-appropriate agents.
pregnancy.data: Limited human data; some malformation case reports.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Allopurinol and its active metabolite pass into milk but no adverse effects have been reported in breastfed infants; considered acceptable during breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant; generally well tolerated.
lactation.data: Detectable in milk without reported harm per LactMed.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy for established indications (notably familial Mediterranean fever, where it should be continued); compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Despite theoretical concerns (colchicine arrests cell division), large experience in women with familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) shows no clear increase in malformations, and continuing colchicine in FMF during pregnancy improves outcomes (reduces flares and amyloid risk). It is also used for pericarditis and gout flares. Considered acceptable when indicated.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Continue colchicine in FMF through pregnancy. Avoid toxic doses; reduce in renal impairment and with interacting drugs (e.g. strong CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors).
pregnancy.data: Large FMF pregnancy cohorts are reassuring.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Colchicine passes into milk in small amounts; long experience in FMF mothers shows no adverse effects in breastfed infants. Taking the dose after a feed can further reduce exposure.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for GI upset; timing the dose after feeds can minimise exposure.
lactation.data: Low milk levels; reassuring FMF data per LactMed.

oneLiner: Limited human pregnancy data — use only when preferred regimens are unsuitable; no clear teratogen signal. Breastfeeding follows HIV/PMTCT guidance.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Doravirine is a newer NNRTI with limited human pregnancy data; animal studies do not show teratogenicity. It is not among the most-studied first-line agents in pregnancy (dolutegravir-based regimens are preferred), so use with caution and specialist input where preferred options are unsuitable.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist HIV management; do not interrupt therapy without advice. Pharmacokinetics in pregnancy less characterised.
pregnancy.data: Limited human pregnancy data.

lactation.riskSummary: Little information in human milk; breastfeeding decisions in HIV depend on maternal viral suppression and local PMTCT policy. Use with caution.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Follow local HIV breastfeeding guidance.

oneLiner: Acceptable boosted protease inhibitor in pregnancy (PMTCT) with substantial experience; watch maternal hyperbilirubinaemia. Breastfeeding follows HIV/PMTCT guidance.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Boosted atazanavir has substantial pregnancy experience and no clear teratogenic signal; it is an acceptable PMTCT regimen component. Atazanavir raises unconjugated bilirubin (maternal jaundice); theoretical neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia has not emerged as a significant clinical problem but is monitored. Third-trimester levels may fall (booster dosing considerations).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor maternal bilirubin. Acid-reducing agents reduce atazanavir absorption — manage co-medications. Do not interrupt therapy without advice.
pregnancy.data: Substantial PMTCT experience.

lactation.riskSummary: Low milk transfer; breastfeeding in HIV depends on maternal suppression and local PMTCT policy rather than drug toxicity.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Follow local HIV breastfeeding guidance.

oneLiner: AVOID the cobicistat-boosted form in pregnancy — inadequate exposure with cobicistat boosting in 2nd/3rd trimester (risk of virological failure); use ritonavir-boosted darunavir or a preferred regimen instead.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Darunavir is not teratogenic, but COBICISTAT-boosted regimens (including darunavir/cobicistat and elvitegravir/cobicistat) achieve substantially reduced drug exposures in the second and third trimesters, risking loss of virological control and increased mother-to-child transmission. Guidelines therefore advise AVOIDING cobicistat-boosted regimens in pregnancy; if darunavir is needed, use the ritonavir-boosted twice-daily form, or switch to a preferred regimen (e.g. dolutegravir-based).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Switch off cobicistat boosting in pregnancy. Specialist HIV management; do not interrupt therapy without advice.
pregnancy.data: Pharmacokinetic studies show reduced cobicistat-boosted exposures in late pregnancy.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited milk data; breastfeeding in HIV depends on maternal suppression and PMTCT policy. Use with caution.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Follow local HIV breastfeeding guidance.

references.label: DHHS/WHO perinatal HIV guidelines: cobicistat-boosted regimens not recommended in pregnancy.

oneLiner: CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy — potent teratogen/embryocide (FDA category X); also contraindicated in male partners of pregnant women. Avoid conception for 6 months after either partner's therapy. No milk data — avoid in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Ribavirin is a powerful teratogen and embryocide demonstrated in all animal species tested (skull, palate, eye, jaw, limb, skeletal and gastrointestinal malformations). It is contraindicated in pregnant women AND in the male partners of pregnant women. Extreme care must be taken to avoid pregnancy during therapy and for 6 months after completing treatment in both female patients and female partners of treated male patients (two reliable forms of contraception are advised).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Mandatory contraception (both partners) during and for 6 months after therapy; pregnancy testing before, during and after. Pregnancy registry reporting recommended.
pregnancy.data: Animal teratogenicity across all species; FDA category X; ribavirin pregnancy registry.

lactation.riskSummary: No information on ribavirin in human milk; given the severe toxicity profile it should be avoided during breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Avoid breastfeeding on ribavirin; use alternative HCV regimens (DAAs) where possible.
lactation.data: No milk data per LactMed; avoidance based on toxicity.

reproductive.pregnancyTesting: Negative test required before therapy; monthly during and for 6 months after.
reproductive.contraception: Two reliable contraceptive methods during and for 6 months after therapy — for female patients and for female partners of male patients.

references.label: FDA label: Ribavirin (Copegus/Rebetol). Category X; contraindicated in pregnancy and male partners.

oneLiner: Limited human pregnancy data (no DAA regimen is formally approved in pregnancy) but animal studies and early human experience are reassuring; use is individualised. Emerging milk data show very low infant exposure.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Direct-acting antivirals for hepatitis C are not formally established as safe in pregnancy, but sofosbuvir/velpatasvir lacks animal teratogenicity and early pharmacokinetic/clinical studies in the second and third trimesters report it to be safe and well tolerated. (This regimen does NOT contain ribavirin, which is the teratogenic component to avoid.) Decisions about treating HCV during pregnancy are individualised; many clinicians defer treatment until postpartum unless there is a clear benefit to earlier therapy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Avoid any ribavirin-containing regimen in pregnancy. Consider deferring DAA treatment to postpartum, or treating in pregnancy on a case-by-case basis with specialist input.
pregnancy.data: No animal teratogenicity; reassuring early human PK/safety studies.

lactation.riskSummary: Not formally studied in nursing mothers, but a small study found infant exposure via milk to be under ~0.7% of the weight-adjusted dose, suggesting low risk. Use with caution pending more data.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Discuss timing of therapy relative to breastfeeding with the specialist.
lactation.data: Very low milk transfer in a small series per LactMed.

references.label: Pharmacokinetics of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir in pregnancy. PMC12561008.

oneLiner: May be used in pregnancy for severe COVID-19 — pregnant women are a risk group; compassionate-use and observational data are reassuring. Limited milk data — caution in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Pregnant women are at increased risk of severe COVID-19. Remdesivir was used in pregnancy under compassionate use during the pandemic and observational data (including in hospitalised pregnant women) have been reassuring without a clear safety signal; pregnancy should not be a reason to withhold remdesivir when indicated for severe COVID-19.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Use for the same indications as non-pregnant patients (severe/hospitalised COVID-19). Monitor liver enzymes/renal function per protocol.
pregnancy.data: Compassionate-use and observational pregnancy data are reassuring.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited information in human milk; the large molecule and intravenous administration suggest low oral infant exposure, but data are sparse, so use with caution and monitor the infant.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Short therapeutic course; monitor infant. Treat severe maternal disease as indicated.

oneLiner: May be considered in pregnancy for COVID-19 at high risk of progression — limited but reassuring data; pregnancy is a risk group. Watch extensive drug interactions (ritonavir). Brief course generally compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Pregnant women are at higher risk of severe COVID-19. Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir has limited but accumulating reassuring pregnancy data; ritonavir has extensive safe use in pregnancy (HIV). It may be considered for pregnant women with COVID-19 at high risk of progression, weighing the major drug-interaction profile of ritonavir.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Screen carefully for drug interactions (ritonavir is a potent CYP3A inhibitor). Start within 5 days of symptom onset. Individualise with maternal-medicine input.
pregnancy.data: Limited but reassuring pregnancy data; ritonavir component well characterised.

lactation.riskSummary: A brief (5-day) course is generally considered compatible; ritonavir transfers into milk in low amounts and nirmatrelvir exposure is expected to be low. Monitor the infant.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Short course; monitor infant for GI upset.
lactation.data: Low milk transfer expected per LactMed.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy — fetal ototoxicity risk (aminoglycoside class); use only when no safer alternative for serious infection. Compatible with breastfeeding (poor oral infant absorption).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Aminoglycosides cross the placenta and carry a risk of fetal ototoxicity (irreversible congenital deafness has been reported, most clearly with streptomycin) and potential nephrotoxicity. Avoid in pregnancy; reserve for serious/life-threatening infection (e.g. resistant gram-negative sepsis, MDR-TB) where no safer alternative exists and benefit outweighs risk, with close monitoring.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Use only when essential; monitor levels, renal function and consider neonatal hearing assessment after in-utero exposure. Prefer beta-lactams where possible.
pregnancy.data: Documented fetal ototoxicity for the class; UKTIS guidance.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Aminoglycosides are poorly absorbed from the infant gut; milk levels are low and systemic infant exposure is minimal. Monitor infant for diarrhoea/thrush.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: No interruption of breastfeeding required; monitor infant GI flora.
lactation.data: Poor oral bioavailability; low milk levels per LactMed.

references.label: UKTIS. Use of aminoglycoside antibiotics in pregnancy. https://uktis.org/monographs/use-of-aminoglycoside-antibiotics-in-pregnancy/

oneLiner: CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy — clearest aminoglycoside link to congenital deafness; avoid (use alternative TB/infection regimens). Compatible with breastfeeding (poor oral infant absorption).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Streptomycin has the clearest documented association among aminoglycosides with fetal ototoxicity — reports of total, irreversible, bilateral congenital deafness in children exposed in utero. It is therefore contraindicated/avoided in pregnancy; alternative regimens (e.g. for TB) should be used. Reserve only for situations with no alternative and overriding maternal benefit.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Use a streptomycin-sparing TB regimen in pregnancy. If unavoidable, counsel about deafness risk and arrange neonatal hearing assessment.
pregnancy.data: Well-documented congenital deafness reports.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Poorly absorbed from the infant gut; low milk levels and minimal systemic infant exposure. Monitor infant for GI effects.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: No interruption of breastfeeding required.

oneLiner: May be used in pregnancy for drug-resistant TB — WHO found no major safety concern and treats pregnant women as other adults; accumulating reassuring data. Limited milk data — caution in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Bedaquiline is a key drug for multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB). WHO concluded there are no major safety concerns with use in pregnancy and recommends treating pregnant women with TB as other adults; case series and cohort data report favourable maternal and infant outcomes. Untreated MDR-TB is dangerous to mother and fetus, so effective treatment should not be withheld. Long half-life means prolonged tissue retention.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist TB management; monitor QT interval (bedaquiline prolongs QT). Treat MDR-TB rather than withholding therapy in pregnancy.
pregnancy.data: WHO 2020 update; pregnancy/breastfeeding cohort (PMC9296589).

lactation.riskSummary: Bedaquiline passes into milk and infant exposure can be appreciable (it is lipophilic with a long half-life); data are limited. Use with caution and monitor the infant; the benefit of treating maternal MDR-TB and the protective effect of breastfeeding are weighed against infant exposure per specialist guidance.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant; individualised feeding decision with TB specialists.
lactation.data: Appreciable milk transfer; limited data per LactMed.

references.label: WHO. Treatment of drug-resistant TB, 2020 update.
Bedaquiline exposure in pregnancy and breastfeeding (RR-TB). PMC9296589.

oneLiner: Avoid in pregnancy where possible — animal teratogen (metabolised to fluorouracil); reserve for life-threatening systemic mycosis (e.g. cryptococcal meningitis) with amphotericin. No milk data — caution in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Flucytosine is teratogenic in animals and is partly metabolised to fluorouracil (a known teratogen), so it is avoided in pregnancy where possible. However, in life-threatening invasive mycoses — notably cryptococcal meningitis — it is used in combination with amphotericin B because the maternal benefit outweighs the risk; specialist management is essential.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Reserve for severe systemic fungal infection (with amphotericin B). Monitor blood counts and drug levels. Specialist infectious-disease input.
pregnancy.data: Animal teratogenicity; fluorouracil metabolite.

lactation.riskSummary: No information on flucytosine in human milk; given conversion to fluorouracil and bone-marrow toxicity, use with caution and monitor the infant, or avoid where feasible.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant blood counts if used; discuss feeding with specialists.

oneLiner: Avoid in pregnancy where possible — animal embryotoxicity, limited human data; reserve for serious invasive fungal infection. Minimal expected milk exposure — caution in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Echinocandins, including caspofungin, show embryotoxicity/skeletal effects in animals and have limited human pregnancy data. Use with caution and reserve for serious invasive candidiasis/aspergillosis where benefit outweighs risk and safer azoles are unsuitable or unavailable.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist management for invasive mycoses. Limited human data.
pregnancy.data: Animal embryotoxicity; limited human data.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited milk data; as a large molecule given intravenously, oral infant absorption is likely poor, but data are sparse — use with caution and monitor the infant.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant; poor expected oral bioavailability.
lactation.data: Sparse milk data; poor oral absorption expected per LactMed.

oneLiner: PREFERRED systemic antifungal for serious invasive mycoses in pregnancy — long record without clear teratogenicity. Minimal expected milk exposure; acceptable in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Amphotericin B has the longest record of any systemic antifungal in pregnancy without a clear teratogenic signal and is the preferred agent for serious invasive fungal infections in pregnancy (e.g. invasive candidiasis, cryptococcosis, severe histoplasmosis) when azoles are contraindicated or inadequate. Liposomal formulations reduce nephrotoxicity.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor renal function and electrolytes (potassium, magnesium). Preferred over azoles for systemic mycoses in the first trimester.
pregnancy.data: Long clinical experience; reassuring.

lactation.riskSummary: Acceptable. Amphotericin B is poorly absorbed orally and given intravenously; milk transfer and infant absorption are expected to be minimal. Limited specific data but considered low risk.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant; low expected exposure.
lactation.data: Poor oral bioavailability; minimal expected milk exposure per LactMed.

oneLiner: Rarely relevant in pregnancy; limited data — use only if clearly needed. No milk data — caution in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: A cholinesterase inhibitor for dementia; pregnancy is uncommon in the typical patient population, and human data are very limited. Animal studies show some adverse effects at high doses. Use only when there is a clear indication and no suitable alternative.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Rarely indicated in women of childbearing age; specialist input if needed.
pregnancy.data: Very limited human data.

lactation.riskSummary: No information on donepezil in human milk; use with caution and monitor the infant. Generally a non-urgent therapy that can be reconsidered while breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant; weigh necessity.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy for Parkinson's disease/dopa-responsive dystonia when needed — limited but reassuring data. Caution in breastfeeding (may suppress prolactin/milk supply).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Levodopa/carbidopa has limited but largely reassuring human pregnancy data and is used when Parkinson's disease or dopa-responsive dystonia requires treatment in pregnancy. No consistent teratogenic signal has emerged. Maintaining maternal mobility/function is important.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist neurology input; use lowest effective dose. Monitor blood pressure (orthostasis).
pregnancy.data: Limited but reassuring pregnancy reports.

lactation.riskSummary: Use with caution. Levodopa is a dopaminergic agent and can suppress prolactin, potentially reducing milk supply; data on infant exposure are limited. If used, monitor milk supply and the infant.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Watch maternal milk supply; monitor infant.

oneLiner: Rarely used in women; sometimes used as medical expulsive therapy for ureteric stones in pregnancy — limited data, use with caution. Not relevant to maternal use in lactation.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Tamsulosin is principally a men's BPH drug, but alpha-blockers are sometimes used off-label as medical expulsive therapy for ureteric (kidney) stones, including in pregnancy. Human pregnancy data are limited; no clear teratogenic signal, but use with caution and a clear indication, monitoring maternal blood pressure.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Off-label use for symptomatic ureteric stones; monitor maternal blood pressure. Limited data.
pregnancy.data: Limited human pregnancy data.

lactation.riskSummary: Not indicated in women generally; no lactation data. Avoid where possible and prefer agents with data if alpha-blockade is needed while breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Not typically used in breastfeeding women.

oneLiner: PREFERRED in pregnancy for hypocalcaemia, magnesium-toxicity reversal, and hyperkalaemia cardioprotection. Compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Calcium gluconate is used in pregnancy for symptomatic hypocalcaemia, as the antidote for magnesium-sulphate toxicity (a common obstetric scenario in pre-eclampsia/eclampsia management), and for myocardial protection in severe hyperkalaemia. Calcium is a normal physiological requirement; therapeutic use is appropriate and not teratogenic.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Keep available when giving magnesium sulphate. Give slowly with cardiac monitoring for acute indications.
pregnancy.data: Standard emergency/obstetric use.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Calcium is a normal milk constituent; therapeutic use does not adversely affect the breastfed infant.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: No specific monitoring required.

oneLiner: PREFERRED — used to treat/prevent B12 deficiency in pregnancy and lactation; also the antidote for cyanide poisoning. Compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Hydroxocobalamin treats and prevents vitamin B12 deficiency, which is important in pregnancy for maternal haematology and fetal neurodevelopment; replacement is safe and recommended when deficient. High-dose hydroxocobalamin is also the antidote of choice for cyanide poisoning (e.g. smoke inhalation) and should not be withheld in that emergency.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Replace documented deficiency. For cyanide poisoning, treat the mother as the priority.
pregnancy.data: Essential vitamin; standard replacement and antidotal use.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Vitamin B12 is a normal milk constituent; maternal supplementation supports adequate milk B12, important for the infant (especially with maternal deficiency/vegan diet).
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Ensure adequate maternal B12 to maintain milk levels.

oneLiner: Use with caution in pregnancy (animal teratogenicity at high doses; limited human data) — used for idiopathic intracranial hypertension, glaucoma, altitude. Compatible with breastfeeding (low milk transfer).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor with animal teratogenicity (limb defects) at high doses and limited but largely reassuring human data. It is used in pregnancy for idiopathic intracranial hypertension (to protect vision), glaucoma and occasionally other indications, generally avoided in the first trimester where possible. Weigh benefit (e.g. sight-threatening IIH) against uncertainty.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Prefer to avoid in the first trimester; use lowest effective dose. Monitor electrolytes/acid-base. Specialist (neurology/ophthalmology) input.
pregnancy.data: Animal teratogenicity at high dose; limited reassuring human data.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Acetazolamide passes into milk in small amounts (low relative infant dose); no adverse effects reported in breastfed infants.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant; generally well tolerated.
lactation.data: Low relative infant dose per LactMed.

oneLiner: Use with caution in pregnancy (limited data; neonatal withdrawal reported, especially with intrathecal use) — for spasticity when needed. Compatible with breastfeeding (low milk transfer at oral doses).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Baclofen is used for spasticity; human pregnancy data are limited and no clear major teratogenic signal has emerged, but neonatal withdrawal (irritability, seizures) has been reported, particularly after intrathecal baclofen. Use when needed for significant spasticity, anticipating possible neonatal withdrawal; avoid abrupt maternal discontinuation (withdrawal risk to mother).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Do not stop abruptly. Inform the neonatal team to monitor for withdrawal, especially with high-dose/intrathecal therapy.
pregnancy.data: Limited human data; neonatal withdrawal reports.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible at oral doses. Baclofen passes into milk in small amounts (low relative infant dose); monitor the infant for drowsiness/poor feeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for sedation; low expected exposure at oral doses.
lactation.data: Low relative infant dose per LactMed.

oneLiner: Use with caution in pregnancy (limited data; theoretical effects on fetal growth/glucose) — for acromegaly, variceal/GI bleeding, other endocrine indications. Limited milk data — caution in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Somatostatin analogue used for acromegaly, neuroendocrine tumours, and acute variceal/GI bleeding. Human pregnancy data are limited; most reported pregnancies (e.g. in acromegaly) have had normal outcomes, but octreotide can affect maternal glucose and theoretically fetal growth/blood flow. Use with caution for clear indications. In acute life-threatening variceal bleeding it should not be withheld.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist management. Monitor maternal glucose. For acromegaly, some centres pause therapy in pregnancy if disease permits.
pregnancy.data: Limited human pregnancy data; mostly reassuring case reports.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited information on octreotide in milk; as a peptide it is likely poorly absorbed orally by the infant, but data are sparse — use with caution and monitor the infant.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant; poor expected oral bioavailability.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy for leprosy and drug-resistant TB when indicated — long use without clear teratogenicity; causes reversible skin pigmentation (including the neonate). Compatible with breastfeeding (infant skin discolouration possible).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Clofazimine is used for leprosy (and increasingly for MDR-TB regimens). Long experience in leprosy has not shown a clear teratogenic signal. It crosses the placenta and causes reversible reddish-brown skin pigmentation in the mother and exposed neonate (cosmetic, reversible). Treating maternal leprosy/MDR-TB is important and should not be withheld.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Counsel about reversible neonatal/maternal skin pigmentation. Specialist TB/leprosy management.
pregnancy.data: Long leprosy experience; reversible pigmentation.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Clofazimine passes into milk and may cause reversible reddish skin discolouration in the breastfed infant; no other adverse effects are established. Treating maternal disease takes priority.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Counsel about reversible infant skin discolouration; otherwise breastfeeding may continue.
lactation.data: Milk transfer with reversible pigmentation per LactMed.

oneLiner: Use with caution in pregnancy — limited data, animal toxicity; reserve for serious infection (e.g. PCP) when first-line agents unsuitable; inhaled form has low systemic exposure. Limited milk data — caution in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Pentamidine is used for Pneumocystis pneumonia (treatment/prophylaxis) and certain protozoal infections. Human pregnancy data are limited and animal studies show embryotoxicity; systemic pentamidine carries maternal toxicity (hypoglycaemia, nephrotoxicity, dysrhythmia). Reserve for serious infection where preferred agents (e.g. co-trimoxazole for PCP) are unsuitable. Inhaled pentamidine has low systemic absorption and lower fetal exposure.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Prefer co-trimoxazole for PCP in pregnancy where tolerated. Monitor maternal glucose, renal function, ECG with systemic use.
pregnancy.data: Limited human data; animal embryotoxicity.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited information in human milk; systemic pentamidine has notable toxicity, so use with caution and monitor the infant. Inhaled use produces low systemic exposure.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant; prefer better-studied agents where possible.

oneLiner: PREFERRED first-trimester treatment to reduce mother-to-child transmission of toxoplasmosis (does not readily cross the placenta). Compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Spiramycin is a macrolide used specifically in pregnancy to reduce mother-to-child transmission of acute toxoplasmosis; it concentrates in the placenta and is given when maternal infection is diagnosed but fetal infection is not yet confirmed (it does not reliably cross to treat established fetal infection — for which pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine is used after the first trimester). No teratogenic signal.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Start promptly on diagnosis of maternal toxoplasmosis; switch to pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine (plus folinic acid) if fetal infection is confirmed after the first trimester. Specialist/fetal-medicine input.
pregnancy.data: Established toxoplasmosis-in-pregnancy practice.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Macrolide with limited specific milk data but expected low infant risk; no adverse effects established.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for GI upset.
lactation.data: Macrolide class; limited milk data per LactMed.

oneLiner: Avoid in the first trimester (folate antagonist — teratogenic potential); used after the first trimester with sulfadiazine and folinic acid for fetal toxoplasmosis. Caution in breastfeeding (G6PD/folate).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Pyrimethamine is a folate antagonist with teratogenic potential (neural tube and other defects in animals and theoretically in humans), so it is avoided in the first trimester. After the first trimester it is used WITH sulfadiazine and folinic acid (leucovorin) to treat confirmed fetal toxoplasmosis and for some other indications. Folinic acid co-administration mitigates the antifolate effect.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Always co-prescribe folinic acid. Avoid first-trimester use; specialist/fetal-medicine guidance. Monitor maternal blood counts.
pregnancy.data: Folate-antagonist teratogenicity; established second/third-trimester toxoplasmosis use.

trimesterNotes.note: Avoid (folate antagonist); use spiramycin instead.
Used with sulfadiazine + folinic acid for confirmed fetal toxoplasmosis.
Used with sulfadiazine + folinic acid for confirmed fetal toxoplasmosis.

lactation.riskSummary: Use with caution. Pyrimethamine passes into milk; theoretical concerns include folate antagonism and haemolysis in G6PD-deficient infants. Monitor the infant; ensure adequate folate.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant; consider G6PD status. Co-administer maternal folinic acid.
lactation.data: Milk transfer documented; antifolate/G6PD concerns per LactMed.

oneLiner: Avoid near term (sulfonamide — neonatal kernicterus risk) and in G6PD deficiency; used with pyrimethamine for fetal toxoplasmosis after the first trimester. AVOID in early breastfeeding (jaundiced/preterm/G6PD-deficient infants).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Sulfadiazine (a sulfonamide) is used with pyrimethamine and folinic acid to treat confirmed fetal toxoplasmosis after the first trimester. Sulfonamides are avoided near term because they displace bilirubin and can cause neonatal kernicterus, and they may cause haemolysis in G6PD deficiency. Folate antagonism is also a consideration with co-administered pyrimethamine.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Avoid in the final weeks of pregnancy (kernicterus risk). Co-administer folinic acid with pyrimethamine. Specialist guidance.
pregnancy.data: Sulfonamide kernicterus risk near term; established toxoplasmosis use earlier.

lactation.riskSummary: Avoid in the early neonatal period and in jaundiced, ill, premature or G6PD-deficient infants because of bilirubin-displacement (kernicterus) and haemolysis risks. In healthy older infants short courses are generally tolerated; use with caution and monitor.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Avoid while nursing a newborn/preterm/jaundiced/G6PD-deficient infant; monitor infant for jaundice.

oneLiner: PREFERRED anticoagulant in pregnancy — does not cross the placenta (high molecular weight). Compatible with breastfeeding. Often used peripartum (short half-life, reversible) or when rapid control/reversal needed.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Unfractionated heparin does not cross the placenta (too large) and is not teratogenic; it is a preferred anticoagulant in pregnancy. LMWH is generally favoured for routine prophylaxis/treatment (more predictable, once/twice daily, lower HIT/osteoporosis risk), but unfractionated heparin is valued peripartum and around neuraxial anaesthesia because of its short half-life and reversibility (protamine), and in renal failure.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Long-term use carries maternal risks (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, osteoporosis) — LMWH preferred for prolonged therapy. Often used to bridge around delivery. Monitor APTT (therapeutic IV) and platelets.
pregnancy.data: No transplacental passage; established anticoagulant of choice with LMWH.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Heparin is a large molecule not secreted into milk in meaningful amounts and would be digested in the infant gut (not orally bioavailable).
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: No monitoring of the infant required.
lactation.data: Not orally bioavailable; safe in breastfeeding per LactMed.

references.label: Bates SM et al. VTE and pregnancy. CHEST 2012.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy — DOACs cross the placenta and have inadequate safety data; switch to LMWH preconception. AVOID in breastfeeding (limited data; switch to warfarin/LMWH).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Direct oral anticoagulants (edoxaban, apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran) are small molecules that cross the placenta; human pregnancy data are limited and registry signals raise concern about fetal risk. They are not recommended in pregnancy — switch women of childbearing potential to LMWH preconception or at the first positive pregnancy test.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Switch to LMWH (e.g. enoxaparin) preconception/early pregnancy. Counsel on contraception while on a DOAC if pregnancy is not desired.
pregnancy.data: Limited human data; placental transfer expected. Expert consensus advises against DOACs in pregnancy.

lactation.riskSummary: DOACs in lactation: safety unknown with limited data; expert consensus advises against DOAC use in breastfeeding. Use warfarin or LMWH instead, both of which are compatible.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Switch to warfarin or LMWH while breastfeeding.
lactation.data: Inadequate milk data per LactMed; alternatives preferred.

reproductive.contraception: Effective contraception while on a DOAC if pregnancy is not desired.

oneLiner: Avoid in pregnancy — limited data; prefer agents with more experience (low-dose aspirin +/- clopidogrel) under cardiology guidance. No milk data — avoid in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Ticagrelor has very limited human pregnancy data and animal toxicity at high doses; it is generally avoided in pregnancy. Where dual antiplatelet therapy is essential (e.g. recent coronary stent), agents with more pregnancy experience (low-dose aspirin, and clopidogrel where needed) are preferred under specialist cardiology guidance.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist cardiology/obstetric input for the underlying indication. Antiplatelet therapy near delivery raises bleeding/neuraxial-anaesthesia considerations.
pregnancy.data: Very limited human data.

lactation.riskSummary: No information on ticagrelor in human milk; avoid during breastfeeding and prefer an alternative if antiplatelet therapy is required.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Discuss alternatives with cardiology if breastfeeding.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy for asthma/COPD bronchospasm — poorly absorbed quaternary antimuscarinic. Compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Inhaled/nebulised ipratropium is a quaternary antimuscarinic with low systemic absorption and no clear teratogenic signal; it is used as an add-on bronchodilator in acute asthma and in COPD during pregnancy. Maintaining respiratory control benefits mother and fetus.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Used with inhaled beta-agonists/corticosteroids for control. Low systemic exposure.
pregnancy.data: Low systemic absorption; reassuring use.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Minimal systemic absorption and negligible milk transfer; not expected to affect the infant or (at inhaled doses) milk supply.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Continue as needed for respiratory control.

oneLiner: CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy — folate-antagonist teratogen/abortifacient (methotrexate embryopathy). Stop at least 1-3 months before conception. AVOID in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Methotrexate is a folate antagonist that is teratogenic and an abortifacient; even low weekly doses (rheumatology/dermatology) can cause methotrexate embryopathy (facial dysmorphism, craniosynostosis, limb and cardiac defects, growth restriction) and pregnancy loss. It is contraindicated in pregnancy. Discontinue before conception (commonly advised at least 1-3 months beforehand) and ensure adequate folate; effective contraception is mandatory during therapy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Switch to a pregnancy-compatible DMARD (e.g. hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, certain anti-TNFs) preconception. Co-prescribe folic acid. Mandatory contraception during treatment.
pregnancy.data: Methotrexate embryopathy well described; UKTIS guidance.

lactation.riskSummary: Avoid during breastfeeding. Methotrexate passes into milk and can accumulate in neonatal tissues; given its toxicity (immunosuppression, GI, marrow), it is contraindicated/avoided in lactation. (Some sources allow consideration of low weekly doses with timing/monitoring, but most advise avoidance.)
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Use a lactation-compatible DMARD instead.
lactation.data: Milk transfer with potential accumulation; avoidance advised per LactMed.

reproductive.contraception: Mandatory effective contraception during methotrexate therapy.
reproductive.pregnancyTesting: Confirm non-pregnant status before initiating in patients of childbearing potential.

references.label: UKTIS. Use of methotrexate in pregnancy. https://uktis.org/monographs/use-of-methotrexate-in-pregnancy/

oneLiner: CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy — potent teratogen/abortifacient (used to treat ectopic pregnancy). AVOID in breastfeeding around dosing.

pregnancy.riskSummary: High-dose methotrexate is a potent teratogen and abortifacient and is itself used to medically treat ectopic (and certain other) pregnancies. It is contraindicated in a desired intrauterine pregnancy — exposure causes pregnancy loss and methotrexate embryopathy. Effective contraception is mandatory; conception should be deferred after therapy per oncology guidance.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Confirm pregnancy status and ensure contraception before chemotherapy use. After methotrexate treatment of ectopic pregnancy, delay subsequent conception per guidance (e.g. to allow folate recovery).
pregnancy.data: Established teratogen/abortifacient.

lactation.riskSummary: Avoid breastfeeding around high-dose methotrexate. It passes into milk and can accumulate in infant tissues; with single-dose ectopic-pregnancy treatment, temporary interruption with pumping-and-discarding is commonly advised, and with chemotherapy regimens breastfeeding is generally avoided.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Interrupt/avoid breastfeeding per regimen; seek specialist advice on timing.
lactation.data: Milk transfer/accumulation; avoidance advised per LactMed.

reproductive.contraception: Mandatory effective contraception during therapy.

oneLiner: CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy — mycophenolate embryopathy (ear/facial, cleft, limb, cardiac defects) and first-trimester loss; FDA REMS. Switch to a pregnancy-compatible agent preconception. AVOID in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Mycophenolate is a recognised human teratogen causing a characteristic embryopathy (external-ear and facial malformations, cleft lip/palate, distal-limb, cardiac, oesophageal, renal and CNS anomalies) and an increased risk of first-trimester pregnancy loss. It is contraindicated in pregnancy and subject to an FDA REMS. Switch to a pregnancy-compatible immunosuppressant (e.g. azathioprine, tacrolimus, ciclosporin, hydroxychloroquine) BEFORE conception, allowing a washout per guidance, with effective contraception until then.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Plan pregnancy with the transplant/rheumatology team; switch preconception (commonly at least ~6 weeks before). Two reliable contraceptive methods are advised during therapy.
pregnancy.data: Transplant/rheumatology registries; FDA REMS; mycophenolate embryopathy literature.

lactation.riskSummary: Avoid during breastfeeding. There is little information on mycophenolate in human milk, and given its immunosuppressant/teratogenic profile it should be avoided; use a lactation-compatible immunosuppressant instead.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Use azathioprine/tacrolimus/ciclosporin (lactation-compatible) where appropriate.
lactation.data: Sparse milk data; avoidance advised per LactMed.

reproductive.contraception: Two reliable contraceptive methods during therapy (per REMS).
reproductive.pregnancyTesting: Negative test before initiation and as advised during therapy.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy when needed for active IBD/psoriasis (IgG antibody — transfers across the placenta mainly in late pregnancy); compatible with breastfeeding (low milk levels, infant gut degradation).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Ustekinumab is an IgG1 monoclonal antibody. Accumulating data in inflammatory bowel disease and psoriasis pregnancies have not shown a clear increase in adverse outcomes; active maternal disease (e.g. IBD flare) itself harms pregnancy. As an IgG antibody it crosses the placenta increasingly in the second/third trimester, so live vaccines in the exposed infant are deferred (per local guidance). Continuing therapy to control disease is often appropriate.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Decisions on continuing/timing late-pregnancy dosing are individualised with the specialist. Avoid live vaccines in the infant until cleared (commonly ~6 months) after third-trimester exposure.
pregnancy.data: IBD/dermatology pregnancy registries; reassuring.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Only small amounts appear in milk and the antibody is largely degraded in the infant's gut, so systemic infant exposure is minimal; no adverse effects reported.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Breastfeeding may continue; coordinate infant vaccination schedule with the specialist.
lactation.data: Low milk levels; gut degradation per LactMed.

oneLiner: Avoid in pregnancy — small-molecule JAK inhibitor with animal teratogenicity and limited human data; switch preconception. AVOID in breastfeeding (limited data).

pregnancy.riskSummary: JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, baricitinib, upadacitinib, filgotinib) are small molecules that cross the placenta and show teratogenicity/embryolethality in animals; human pregnancy data are limited. They are avoided in pregnancy — switch to a pregnancy-compatible agent preconception with effective contraception until then.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Switch to a pregnancy-compatible therapy (e.g. certolizumab, azathioprine, hydroxychloroquine as appropriate) preconception. Effective contraception during therapy.
pregnancy.data: Animal teratogenicity; limited human data.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited information in human milk; as a small molecule it may transfer and the safety is unestablished — avoid during breastfeeding and prefer alternatives.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Use a lactation-compatible agent instead.
lactation.data: Sparse milk data per LactMed; avoidance advised.

reproductive.contraception: Effective contraception during therapy if pregnancy is not desired.

oneLiner: Avoid in pregnancy — JAK-inhibitor class (animal teratogenicity; limited human data); switch preconception. AVOID in breastfeeding (limited data).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Upadacitinib is a JAK inhibitor (small molecule) with animal teratogenicity and limited human pregnancy data; the class is avoided in pregnancy. Switch to a pregnancy-compatible agent preconception with effective contraception (per labelling, continued for a period after the last dose).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Switch preconception to a compatible therapy. Effective contraception during and for the labelled interval after therapy.
pregnancy.data: Animal teratogenicity; limited human data.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited milk data; avoid during breastfeeding and prefer an alternative.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Use a lactation-compatible agent instead.
lactation.data: Sparse milk data per LactMed; avoidance advised.

reproductive.contraception: Effective contraception during and after therapy per labelling.

oneLiner: CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy — animal teratogen with long persistence; requires accelerated elimination and verified low plasma levels before conception. AVOID in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Teriflunomide (active metabolite of leflunomide) is teratogenic and embryolethal in animals and persists in plasma for a long time (enterohepatic recirculation). It is contraindicated in pregnancy. Effective contraception is required; before a planned pregnancy (or on accidental pregnancy), an accelerated elimination procedure (cholestyramine or activated charcoal) is used and plasma levels confirmed below the target threshold.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Verify plasma concentration below threshold (with accelerated elimination if needed) before conception. Mandatory effective contraception during therapy. Applies to leflunomide too.
pregnancy.data: Animal teratogenicity; long persistence; labelling/REMS-type controls.

lactation.riskSummary: Avoid during breastfeeding. No adequate human milk data and a significant toxicity profile; do not breastfeed on teriflunomide.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Use a lactation-compatible disease-modifying therapy instead.
lactation.data: No adequate milk data per LactMed; avoidance advised.

reproductive.contraception: Mandatory effective contraception during therapy.
reproductive.pregnancyTesting: Confirm non-pregnant status and acceptable plasma levels before conception.

references.label: FDA label: Teriflunomide (Aubagio). Pregnancy contraindication; accelerated elimination.

oneLiner: Avoid in pregnancy — animal fetal harm (skeletal/dental effects); not for use in women planning pregnancy. AVOID/caution in breastfeeding (limited data; effects on neonatal bone/lactating mammary tissue uncertain).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Denosumab is a RANKL-inhibiting IgG monoclonal antibody. Animal studies show fetal harm (absent lymph nodes, abnormal bone/teeth, reduced postnatal growth). As an IgG it can cross the placenta, increasingly later in pregnancy. It is not recommended in pregnancy; women of childbearing potential should use effective contraception during and for several months after the last dose. Osteoporosis therapy is generally deferrable.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Defer osteoporosis therapy in women planning pregnancy; effective contraception during and for ~5 months after the last dose per labelling. Watch for rebound bone loss/vertebral fractures if discontinued without follow-on therapy.
pregnancy.data: Animal fetal harm; IgG placental transfer.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited human milk data; effects on the neonatal skeleton and on lactating mammary gland are not established. Avoid where possible and prefer agents with data if treatment is needed while breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Defer therapy or use an alternative while breastfeeding where feasible.

reproductive.contraception: Effective contraception during and for ~5 months after the last dose.

oneLiner: Avoid in pregnancy — bisphosphonates persist in bone and cross the placenta (animal skeletal effects); osteoporosis therapy is deferrable. Limited milk data; minimal oral infant absorption — caution in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Bisphosphonates incorporate into bone and persist for years; they cross the placenta and cause skeletal changes in animal studies. Human pregnancy data are limited and have not shown a consistent serious harm, but because osteoporosis treatment is generally deferrable, bisphosphonates are avoided in pregnancy and in women planning pregnancy. The relevant concern can extend to drug retained in bone from prior use.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Defer osteoporosis therapy in women who may become pregnant; counsel about long skeletal retention. Treat hypocalcaemia/vitamin D as needed.
pregnancy.data: Animal skeletal effects; limited human data; precautionary avoidance.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited milk data; bisphosphonates are poorly absorbed orally (also by the infant) and bind milk calcium, so infant systemic exposure is expected to be minimal. Use with caution given sparse data.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant; low expected oral bioavailability. Often deferrable.
lactation.data: Poor oral bioavailability; sparse milk data per LactMed.

oneLiner: Avoid in pregnancy — bisphosphonate with bone persistence and animal fetal effects; therapy generally deferrable. Limited milk data; minimal oral infant absorption — caution in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Intravenous bisphosphonate with long skeletal retention; animal studies show maternal/fetal effects (including hypocalcaemia and skeletal changes). Avoid in pregnancy and in women planning pregnancy; osteoporosis/bone-protection therapy is usually deferrable. Treat acute hypercalcaemia of malignancy on its own merits with specialist input.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Defer in women who may conceive; counsel on long bone retention. Ensure adequate calcium/vitamin D to limit hypocalcaemia.
pregnancy.data: Animal fetal effects; long retention; precautionary avoidance.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited milk data; poor oral bioavailability and calcium binding suggest minimal infant systemic exposure, but data are sparse — use with caution.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant; often deferrable.
lactation.data: Poor oral bioavailability; sparse milk data per LactMed.

oneLiner: CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy — increased risk of major congenital malformations; stop ~2 months before conception. AVOID in breastfeeding. Beware disease rebound on stopping.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Fingolimod (S1P-receptor modulator for MS) is associated with an approximately 2-fold increase in major congenital malformations with in-utero exposure and is contraindicated in pregnancy. It should be stopped about 2 months before a planned pregnancy, with effective contraception until then. Note the risk of severe MS rebound/disease reactivation after discontinuation — plan the switch with neurology.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Stop ~2 months preconception; effective contraception during and for ~2 months after. Plan to manage rebound risk (bridge to a pregnancy-compatible therapy where indicated).
pregnancy.data: Pregnancy registries show increased malformation risk.

lactation.riskSummary: Avoid during breastfeeding. Limited human milk data and a notable toxicity profile; do not breastfeed on fingolimod.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Use a lactation-compatible MS therapy where treatment is needed.
lactation.data: Sparse milk data per LactMed; avoidance advised.

reproductive.contraception: Effective contraception during and for ~2 months after therapy.

references.label: Fingolimod pregnancy registry / EMA labelling: malformation risk.

oneLiner: Limited human pregnancy data — prefer better-studied antidepressants (e.g. sertraline) where possible. No milk data — caution in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Vortioxetine is a newer antidepressant with limited human pregnancy data; animal studies have not shown clear teratogenicity. Because better-characterised antidepressants (e.g. sertraline) exist, prefer those in pregnancy where appropriate. Untreated maternal depression carries its own risks, so do not stop effective treatment without assessment. Late-pregnancy serotonergic exposure can cause transient neonatal adaptation symptoms.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Weigh against better-studied agents; monitor the neonate for transient adaptation symptoms after third-trimester exposure. Individualise with perinatal psychiatry.
pregnancy.data: Limited human data.

lactation.riskSummary: No information on vortioxetine in human milk; use with caution and monitor the infant. Prefer an antidepressant with lactation data (e.g. sertraline) where possible.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for sedation/feeding/irritability.

oneLiner: Limited human pregnancy data — use when needed for serious mental illness; monitor neonate for extrapyramidal/withdrawal symptoms after third-trimester exposure. Limited milk data — caution in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Atypical antipsychotic with limited human pregnancy data and no clear teratogenic signal in available reports. Untreated serious mental illness (e.g. bipolar/schizophrenia) carries major risks, so effective treatment is often continued. Third-trimester antipsychotic exposure can cause neonatal extrapyramidal and withdrawal symptoms (FDA class warning).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Individualise with perinatal psychiatry; monitor the neonate for EPS/withdrawal. Better-studied antipsychotics (e.g. olanzapine, quetiapine) have larger datasets.
pregnancy.data: Limited human data; class neonatal-adaptation warning.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited information on lurasidone in human milk; use with caution and monitor the infant for sedation/feeding/EPS. Prefer an antipsychotic with more lactation data where possible.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for sedation and movement effects.

oneLiner: Use in pregnancy for life-threatening hypotension/shock — maternal resuscitation is the priority (do not withhold), though it reduces uteroplacental flow. Compatible with breastfeeding (short half-life, not orally bioavailable).
