pregnancy.riskSummary: Noradrenaline is a first-line vasopressor for life-threatening hypotension/septic shock. It causes vasoconstriction that can reduce uteroplacental perfusion, but restoring maternal blood pressure and perfusion is essential for both mother and fetus; it should not be withheld in shock. Phenylephrine/ephedrine are preferred for spinal-anaesthesia hypotension, but noradrenaline is used in critical illness.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Treat the underlying cause; titrate to maternal perfusion. Continuous fetal monitoring where viable. Use the lowest effective dose.
pregnancy.data: Standard critical-care/resuscitation use; benefit outweighs theoretical risk.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Very short half-life and not orally bioavailable, so any trace in milk would not affect the infant. Critical-care use does not preclude later breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Resume breastfeeding when the mother is stable.
lactation.data: Short half-life; not orally bioavailable per LactMed.

oneLiner: PREFERRED vasopressor for maternal hypotension during spinal anaesthesia at Caesarean section. Compatible with breastfeeding (parenteral use); oral decongestant use is separate and generally avoided in pregnancy.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Intravenous phenylephrine is a preferred vasopressor for treating/preventing maternal hypotension during spinal anaesthesia for Caesarean delivery, with good maternal and neonatal acid-base outcomes. (Note: ORAL phenylephrine as a decongestant is a separate consideration — its efficacy is doubtful and decongestants are generally avoided, especially in the first trimester.)
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: This entry concerns parenteral obstetric-anaesthesia use. For nasal congestion in pregnancy, prefer saline/non-drug measures.
pregnancy.data: Obstetric-anaesthesia evidence supports IV phenylephrine at Caesarean.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Parenteral phenylephrine has a short duration and poor oral bioavailability, so infant exposure via milk is negligible.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Resume breastfeeding after recovery from anaesthesia.

references.label: Obstetric anaesthesia consensus on vasopressors at Caesarean section.

oneLiner: Acceptable vasopressor for maternal hypotension during spinal anaesthesia at Caesarean (crosses placenta; may cause fetal acidosis at higher doses — phenylephrine often preferred). Compatible with breastfeeding (parenteral use).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Intravenous ephedrine is used to treat maternal hypotension during spinal anaesthesia for Caesarean delivery. It crosses the placenta and at higher doses is associated with lower fetal pH (fetal acidosis) than phenylephrine, so phenylephrine is often preferred; ephedrine remains useful, especially with maternal bradycardia.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Parenteral obstetric-anaesthesia use. Prefer phenylephrine when fetal acid-base is a priority; ephedrine when bradycardia accompanies hypotension.
pregnancy.data: Obstetric-anaesthesia comparative data.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible for parenteral peri-anaesthetic use. (Oral ephedrine, like other stimulant decongestants, may reduce milk supply and cause infant irritability with repeated use, so chronic oral use is less preferred.)
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Resume breastfeeding after recovery; avoid repeated oral stimulant use that could affect supply.
lactation.data: Peri-anaesthetic parenteral use low risk per LactMed.

oneLiner: Use in pregnancy for cardiogenic shock/low-output states when indicated — maternal stabilisation is the priority. Compatible with breastfeeding (short half-life, not orally bioavailable).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Dobutamine is an inotrope used for cardiogenic shock/low cardiac output (e.g. peripartum cardiomyopathy) and as a stress agent. Human pregnancy data are limited but its use in maternal cardiac emergencies is appropriate — maternal haemodynamic stabilisation benefits both mother and fetus. No established teratogenicity at therapeutic short-term use.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Used in critical care for the underlying cardiac condition; continuous monitoring. Short-acting and titratable.
pregnancy.data: Limited data; standard critical-care use.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Very short half-life and not orally bioavailable; any trace in milk would not affect the infant. Critical-care use does not preclude later breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Resume breastfeeding when the mother is stable.
lactation.data: Short half-life; not orally bioavailable per LactMed.

oneLiner: Avoid in pregnancy where possible (limited data; overactive-bladder therapy is deferrable). No milk data; antimuscarinics may reduce supply — caution/avoid in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Antimuscarinic for overactive bladder with limited human pregnancy data; no clear teratogenic signal but experience is sparse. Because overactive-bladder treatment is generally deferrable and conservative measures are first-line in pregnancy, avoid where possible and reserve for clear need.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Prefer bladder training/pelvic-floor measures in pregnancy; defer drug therapy where feasible.
pregnancy.data: Limited human data.

lactation.riskSummary: No information on solifenacin in human milk; antimuscarinics can theoretically reduce milk supply and cause infant antimuscarinic effects. Use with caution; prefer to defer therapy while breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Watch milk supply; monitor infant. Often deferrable.

oneLiner: Avoid in pregnancy where possible (limited data; deferrable indication). No milk data — caution/avoid in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Beta-3 adrenergic agonist for overactive bladder with limited human pregnancy data; animal studies show some fetal effects at high exposures. As the indication is deferrable, avoid where possible and use conservative measures first in pregnancy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Prefer conservative bladder measures; defer drug therapy where feasible. Monitor blood pressure (mirabegron can raise BP).
pregnancy.data: Limited human data.

lactation.riskSummary: No information on mirabegron in human milk; use with caution and prefer to defer therapy while breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Often deferrable; monitor infant if used.

oneLiner: PREFERRED isotonic crystalloid for resuscitation/maintenance in pregnancy (haemorrhage, hypovolaemia). Compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Ringer's lactate (compound sodium lactate) is a balanced isotonic crystalloid used for fluid resuscitation and maintenance in pregnancy, including in obstetric haemorrhage and hypovolaemia. It contains physiological electrolytes and is not teratogenic; appropriate fluid resuscitation is life-saving.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Standard resuscitation/maintenance fluid. Monitor for fluid overload (e.g. in pre-eclampsia, where fluid is restricted/balanced carefully).
pregnancy.data: Standard physiological crystalloid.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. A balanced electrolyte solution with no adverse effect on breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: No specific precautions for breastfeeding.

oneLiner: PREFERRED isotonic crystalloid for resuscitation/maintenance and as a drug diluent in pregnancy. Compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Isotonic sodium chloride 0.9% is used for fluid resuscitation, maintenance and as a diluent in pregnancy. It is a physiological electrolyte solution and is not teratogenic; appropriate fluid resuscitation is essential in obstetric emergencies.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Standard fluid; large volumes can cause hyperchloraemic acidosis (balanced crystalloids may be preferred for large-volume resuscitation). Careful fluid balance in pre-eclampsia.
pregnancy.data: Standard physiological crystalloid.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. No adverse effect on breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: No specific precautions for breastfeeding.

oneLiner: PREFERRED for rehydration in pregnancy and lactation (diarrhoeal illness, mild dehydration). Compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Oral rehydration salts are a glucose-electrolyte solution used to treat/prevent dehydration from diarrhoeal illness in pregnancy. They are physiological and safe; correcting maternal dehydration benefits both mother and fetus.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Use WHO/low-osmolarity ORS; escalate to IV fluids if severe dehydration or persistent vomiting.
pregnancy.data: Standard rehydration therapy.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Safe during breastfeeding; supports maternal hydration. ORS is also given directly to infants for their own dehydration.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Maintain breastfeeding during the mother's diarrhoeal illness; ORS supports hydration.

oneLiner: Cephalosporin (anti-MRSA) considered low-risk in pregnancy by class; limited specific data. Likely compatible with breastfeeding (class effect) — monitor infant.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Ceftaroline is a cephalosporin with anti-MRSA activity. The cephalosporin class has a strong pregnancy safety record without a teratogenic signal; specific human data for ceftaroline are limited, so use for clear indications (e.g. MRSA infection) when needed.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Account for increased renal clearance in pregnancy. Specialist use for resistant gram-positive infection.
pregnancy.data: Class safety; limited drug-specific data.

lactation.riskSummary: Likely compatible based on the cephalosporin class (low milk transfer, minor infant effects such as flora change/thrush); specific data are limited.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for diarrhoea/thrush.

references.label: UKTIS. Use of cephalosporins in pregnancy. https://uktis.org/monographs/use-of-cephalosporins-in-pregnancy/

oneLiner: Cephalosporin/beta-lactamase inhibitor considered low-risk in pregnancy by class; limited specific data. Likely compatible with breastfeeding — monitor infant.

pregnancy.riskSummary: A cephalosporin combined with a beta-lactamase inhibitor for resistant gram-negative infections. The beta-lactam/cephalosporin class is considered safe in pregnancy; specific data are limited, so reserve for serious/resistant infection where benefit is clear.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist use for MDR gram-negative infection; dose for increased renal clearance.
pregnancy.data: Class safety; limited drug-specific data.

lactation.riskSummary: Likely compatible (cephalosporin/beta-lactam class — low milk transfer); specific data limited.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for diarrhoea/thrush.

oneLiner: Cephalosporin/beta-lactamase inhibitor considered low-risk in pregnancy by class; limited specific data. Likely compatible with breastfeeding — monitor infant.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Ceftazidime (a cephalosporin with a long pregnancy record) combined with the beta-lactamase inhibitor avibactam, for resistant gram-negative infections. The cephalosporin component is well established as low-risk; combined-product data are limited. Reserve for serious/resistant infection.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist use for MDR gram-negative infection; dose for increased renal clearance.
pregnancy.data: Ceftazidime class safety; limited combination data.

lactation.riskSummary: Likely compatible (cephalosporin class — low milk transfer); specific combination data limited.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for diarrhoea/thrush.

oneLiner: Carbapenem/beta-lactamase inhibitor considered low-risk in pregnancy by class (meropenem well used); limited specific data. Likely compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Meropenem is a carbapenem with reassuring pregnancy use; combined with vaborbactam for resistant gram-negative infections. Beta-lactams as a class are considered safe in pregnancy; reserve this combination for serious/resistant infection where benefit is clear.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist use; dose for increased renal clearance in pregnancy.
pregnancy.data: Meropenem class safety; limited combination data.

lactation.riskSummary: Likely compatible (carbapenem — low milk transfer, poor infant oral absorption); monitor infant.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for diarrhoea/thrush.

oneLiner: Carbapenem/beta-lactamase inhibitor for resistant infections; beta-lactam class low-risk in pregnancy but limited specific data. Likely compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Imipenem/cilastatin combined with relebactam, for resistant gram-negative infections. Beta-lactams are generally considered safe in pregnancy; however imipenem showed some adverse effects in certain animal studies and human data for this combination are limited, so use with caution and reserve for serious/resistant infection.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist use; dose for increased renal clearance. Meropenem (more pregnancy data) is an alternative carbapenem.
pregnancy.data: Limited combination data; mixed animal data for imipenem.

lactation.riskSummary: Likely compatible (carbapenem — low milk transfer, poor infant oral absorption); monitor infant.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for diarrhoea/thrush.

oneLiner: Avoid in pregnancy where possible — animal embryofetal toxicity, limited human data; reserve for resistant gram-positive infection. Limited milk data — caution in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Oxazolidinone (related to linezolid) for resistant gram-positive infections. Animal studies show embryofetal toxicity and human pregnancy data are limited; use with caution and reserve for serious/resistant infection where preferred agents are unsuitable.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist use. Linezolid has somewhat more experience among oxazolidinones.
pregnancy.data: Animal embryofetal toxicity; limited human data.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited information in human milk; use with caution and monitor the infant. Prefer a better-studied agent where possible.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant for GI upset.

oneLiner: AVOID from the second trimester (tetracycline-class — fetal tooth/bone effects); limited specific data. Caution/avoid in breastfeeding (class concerns).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Omadacycline is an aminomethylcycline (tetracycline-class) antibiotic; the class binds developing teeth and bone, causing permanent dental discolouration and reversible inhibition of bone growth when used from the second trimester onward. Avoid in pregnancy (especially from ~15 weeks); use a non-tetracycline alternative.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Use alternative antibiotics in pregnancy. Inadvertent early exposure not clearly teratogenic but switch and avoid later use.
pregnancy.data: Tetracycline-class fetal tooth/bone effects.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited specific data; tetracycline-class agents transfer into milk but infant absorption is limited by milk calcium chelation. Short courses may be tolerated, but prolonged use is not recommended; prefer a non-tetracycline alternative.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Prefer alternatives for long courses; monitor infant.
lactation.data: Class milk transfer with limited absorption per LactMed.

oneLiner: Avoid in pregnancy where possible — echinocandin animal embryotoxicity, limited human data; reserve for serious invasive mycosis. Minimal expected milk exposure — caution in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Echinocandin with animal embryotoxicity/skeletal effects and limited human pregnancy data. Use with caution and reserve for serious invasive candidiasis where azoles are unsuitable; amphotericin B has the largest pregnancy dataset for systemic mycoses.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist management for invasive mycoses.
pregnancy.data: Animal embryotoxicity; limited human data.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited milk data; as a large molecule given intravenously, oral infant absorption is likely poor — use with caution and monitor the infant.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant; poor expected oral bioavailability.

oneLiner: Avoid in pregnancy where possible — echinocandin animal embryotoxicity, limited human data; reserve for serious invasive mycosis. Minimal expected milk exposure — caution in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Echinocandin with animal embryotoxicity (including visceral abnormalities at high exposure) and limited human pregnancy data. Use with caution; reserve for serious invasive candidiasis where azoles are unsuitable. Amphotericin B has the largest systemic-antifungal pregnancy dataset.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist management for invasive mycoses.
pregnancy.data: Animal embryotoxicity; limited human data.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited milk data; large IV molecule with likely poor infant oral absorption — use with caution and monitor the infant.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant; poor expected oral bioavailability.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy — azole with animal teratogenicity; reserve for life-threatening invasive mycosis. Avoid breastfeeding (no milk data, toxicity concern).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Posaconazole is teratogenic/embryotoxic in animals (as with other systemic azoles); human pregnancy data are very limited. Avoid in pregnancy unless treating a life-threatening invasive fungal infection where no safer alternative exists. Amphotericin B is preferred for systemic mycoses in pregnancy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Effective contraception advised during therapy. Specialist (infectious disease) management.
pregnancy.data: Animal teratogenicity; minimal human data.

lactation.riskSummary: No data on posaconazole in human milk; given its toxicity, avoid during breastfeeding (consistent with advice for voriconazole/posaconazole).
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Discuss feeding alternatives with specialists if treatment is essential.
lactation.data: No milk data per LactMed; avoidance precautionary.

oneLiner: AVOID in pregnancy — azole with animal teratogenicity/embryotoxicity; reserve for life-threatening invasive mycosis. Avoid breastfeeding (no milk data, toxicity concern).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Isavuconazole is teratogenic and embryotoxic in animals; human pregnancy data are very limited. Avoid in pregnancy unless treating a life-threatening invasive mould infection (e.g. aspergillosis, mucormycosis) where no safer option exists. Amphotericin B is the preferred systemic antifungal in pregnancy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Effective contraception during therapy. Specialist management essential.
pregnancy.data: Animal teratogenicity; minimal human data.

lactation.riskSummary: No data on isavuconazole in human milk; given its toxicity, avoid during breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Discuss alternatives with specialists if treatment essential.
lactation.data: No milk data per LactMed; avoidance precautionary.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy and breastfeeding for fungal keratitis — topical ophthalmic use with negligible systemic absorption.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Topical ophthalmic natamycin for fungal keratitis has negligible systemic absorption, so fetal exposure is minimal and systemic azole concerns do not apply. Acceptable for sight-threatening fungal eye infection in pregnancy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Topical ocular use; specialist (ophthalmology) management of fungal keratitis.
pregnancy.data: Negligible systemic absorption.

lactation.riskSummary: Acceptable. Negligible systemic absorption from ophthalmic use means negligible milk transfer.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: No specific monitoring required.

oneLiner: Acceptable NNRTI in pregnancy (PMTCT) with reassuring data where used; breastfeeding follows HIV/PMTCT guidance.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Etravirine is an NNRTI used in treatment-experienced HIV patients. Available pregnancy data are reassuring without a clear teratogenic signal; it achieves adequate exposure in pregnancy. It is used where the regimen is appropriate, though dolutegravir-based regimens are generally first-line.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist HIV management; do not interrupt therapy without advice.
pregnancy.data: Reassuring pregnancy data where used.

lactation.riskSummary: Low milk transfer; breastfeeding in HIV depends on maternal suppression and local PMTCT policy rather than drug toxicity.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Follow local HIV breastfeeding guidance.

oneLiner: Limited human pregnancy data (integrase inhibitor); use individualised with specialist input. Breastfeeding follows HIV/PMTCT guidance.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Cabotegravir is an integrase inhibitor (oral lead-in and long-acting injectable for HIV treatment/PrEP). Human pregnancy data are limited and accumulating; the integrase-inhibitor class (e.g. dolutegravir) is broadly reassuring, but cabotegravir-specific pregnancy experience is smaller, so use is individualised with specialist input. The long-acting injectable persists for many months, a key counselling point for pregnancy planning.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist HIV management; counsel about prolonged drug persistence with the injectable form. Do not interrupt therapy without advice.
pregnancy.data: Limited pregnancy data; integrase class reassuring.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited milk data; breastfeeding in HIV depends on maternal suppression and PMTCT policy. Use with caution.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Follow local HIV breastfeeding guidance.

oneLiner: Integrase-inhibitor single-tablet regimen with accumulating reassuring pregnancy data; bictegravir exposure can fall in late pregnancy (monitor). Breastfeeding follows HIV/PMTCT guidance.

pregnancy.riskSummary: This single-tablet regimen combines bictegravir (integrase inhibitor) with emtricitabine and tenofovir alafenamide. Accumulating data are reassuring without a clear teratogenic signal, but bictegravir plasma exposure can decrease in the second/third trimester, raising a theoretical concern for virological control; some guidelines therefore advise caution or monitoring, while others now consider it acceptable. The TAF/FTC backbone is well regarded in pregnancy.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist HIV management; consider viral-load monitoring given reduced late-pregnancy bictegravir levels. Do not interrupt therapy without advice.
pregnancy.data: Reassuring but evolving pregnancy data; reduced late-pregnancy bictegravir exposure.

lactation.riskSummary: Components transfer into milk in low amounts; breastfeeding in HIV depends on maternal suppression and local PMTCT policy rather than drug toxicity.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Follow local HIV breastfeeding guidance.

oneLiner: No DAA regimen is formally approved in pregnancy, but this ribavirin-free combination lacks animal teratogenicity and has reassuring early human data; use individualised. Limited milk data — caution in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Ledipasvir/sofosbuvir is a ribavirin-free direct-acting antiviral combination for hepatitis C. No DAA regimen is formally established as safe in pregnancy, but animal studies show no teratogenicity and early human pharmacokinetic/safety studies are reassuring. Decisions to treat HCV in pregnancy are individualised; many clinicians defer to postpartum. (Avoid any ribavirin-containing regimen, which is teratogenic.)
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Avoid ribavirin-containing regimens. Consider deferring DAA therapy to postpartum or treating case-by-case with specialist input.
pregnancy.data: No animal teratogenicity; reassuring early human data.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited information in nursing mothers; emerging data for sofosbuvir-based regimens suggest low infant milk exposure. Use with caution pending more data.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Discuss timing of therapy relative to breastfeeding with the specialist.
lactation.data: Low expected milk transfer per LactMed.

oneLiner: Avoid in pregnancy where possible (limited data; lipid-lowering generally deferrable) — reserve for severe hypertriglyceridaemia risking pancreatitis. Limited milk data — caution/avoid in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Fibrate with limited human pregnancy data; routine lipid-lowering is deferrable in pregnancy. The main scenario for use is severe hypertriglyceridaemia threatening pancreatitis, where benefit may outweigh uncertainty; otherwise avoid. Dietary measures and omega-3 are often tried first for gestational hypertriglyceridaemia.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Reserve for severe hypertriglyceridaemia (pancreatitis risk) with specialist input; otherwise defer lipid therapy.
pregnancy.data: Limited human data.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited information in human milk; use with caution and prefer to defer lipid therapy while breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Often deferrable; monitor infant if used.

oneLiner: Use with caution in pregnancy (limited data; monitor for maternal hypotension) — for angina/heart-failure symptoms when needed. Limited milk data — caution in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Long-acting nitrate used for angina and heart-failure symptoms. Human pregnancy data are limited; no clear teratogenic signal, but maternal hypotension could reduce uteroplacental perfusion. Use with caution for clear cardiac indications, monitoring blood pressure. (Short-acting GTN is used acutely in obstetrics.)
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor maternal blood pressure; specialist cardiology input for the underlying condition.
pregnancy.data: Limited human data.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited information in human milk; use with caution and monitor the infant. Brief/acute nitrate use is lower concern than chronic therapy.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant; weigh chronic use.

oneLiner: Use in pregnancy when indicated for aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage (prevention of cerebral vasospasm) — maternal benefit is the priority. Limited milk data — caution in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Nimodipine is a calcium-channel blocker used specifically to reduce cerebral vasospasm and improve outcomes after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage. Human pregnancy data are limited, but in this serious neurological emergency the maternal benefit takes priority; monitor maternal blood pressure (hypotension can reduce cerebral/uteroplacental perfusion).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Used for a specific critical indication (SAH). Monitor maternal blood pressure. Specialist neuro-critical-care management.
pregnancy.data: Limited pregnancy data; established SAH indication.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited information in human milk; calcium-channel blockers as a group transfer in small amounts. Use with caution and monitor the infant.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant; typically a short defined course.

oneLiner: Limited human pregnancy data — use only if clearly needed for ALS. No milk data — caution/avoid in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Riluzole is used for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS); human pregnancy data are very limited and animal studies show some adverse effects. Use only when clearly needed, weighing the maternal benefit against limited safety data, with specialist input.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist neurology management; individualised decision.
pregnancy.data: Very limited human data.

lactation.riskSummary: No information on riluzole in human milk; use with caution and monitor the infant, or avoid where feasible.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant if used.

oneLiner: Avoid in pregnancy where possible — first-trimester case reports of malformations; limited data. AVOID in breastfeeding (may suppress milk supply; infant effects).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Amantadine (used for Parkinson's disease/dyskinesia and historically influenza) has case reports of cardiovascular and other malformations with first-trimester exposure, and limited data overall. Avoid in pregnancy where possible; if Parkinsonian treatment is needed, agents with more data (e.g. levodopa) are generally preferred.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Prefer better-studied agents for Parkinson's in pregnancy; avoid amantadine especially in the first trimester.
pregnancy.data: Limited data; first-trimester malformation case reports.

lactation.riskSummary: Avoid during breastfeeding. Amantadine is excreted into milk, has dopaminergic activity that may suppress prolactin/milk supply, and could cause infant effects (e.g. rash, vomiting, urinary retention). Prefer an alternative.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Avoid; watch milk supply if inadvertently used.
lactation.data: Milk excretion with potential supply suppression per LactMed.

oneLiner: Use with caution in pregnancy (limited data) — for drug-induced parkinsonism/dystonia/acute dystonic reactions when needed. Limited milk data; antimuscarinics may reduce supply — caution in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Antimuscarinic used for drug-induced parkinsonism, dystonia and acute dystonic reactions (e.g. from antipsychotics/antiemetics). Human pregnancy data are limited; no clear teratogenic signal. For an acute dystonic reaction it should not be withheld; for chronic use, weigh against limited data.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Acceptable for acute dystonic reactions in pregnancy; use lowest effective dose for chronic indications.
pregnancy.data: Limited human data.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited information in human milk; antimuscarinics can theoretically reduce milk supply and cause infant antimuscarinic effects. Use with caution and monitor.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Watch milk supply; monitor infant. Brief/acute use lower concern.

oneLiner: Avoid in pregnancy where possible (limited data; deferrable COPD add-on) — animal embryotoxicity. No milk data — avoid/caution in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitor used as an add-on in severe COPD. Animal studies show embryotoxicity/post-implantation loss and human pregnancy data are limited. As it is a deferrable add-on therapy, avoid in pregnancy where possible; optimise inhaled therapy instead.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Prefer inhaled COPD therapy; defer roflumilast where feasible.
pregnancy.data: Animal embryotoxicity; limited human data.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited/no human milk data; use with caution and prefer to defer therapy while breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Often deferrable; monitor infant if used.

oneLiner: Acceptable in pregnancy for cystic fibrosis — inhaled enzyme with negligible systemic absorption; continue for respiratory health. Compatible with breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Inhaled dornase alfa (recombinant DNase) reduces sputum viscosity in cystic fibrosis. It acts locally with negligible systemic absorption and no expected fetal exposure; maintaining CF respiratory health in pregnancy is important and therapy should generally continue.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Continue CF airway-clearance therapy in pregnancy. Negligible systemic exposure.
pregnancy.data: Local action; negligible systemic absorption.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Negligible systemic absorption and no expected milk transfer; continue for CF respiratory care while breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Continue as needed; no specific monitoring.

oneLiner: Use in pregnancy for acute indications (raised intracranial pressure, acute glaucoma) when needed — maternal benefit prioritised; monitor fluid/electrolyte balance. Compatible with breastfeeding (not orally bioavailable).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic used acutely for raised intracranial pressure and acute angle-closure glaucoma. Human pregnancy data are limited; it can shift maternal fluid/electrolytes and theoretically cause fetal fluid shifts, so use with monitoring. In a neurological/ophthalmic emergency the maternal benefit takes priority.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor fluid balance, electrolytes and osmolality. Used for acute, defined emergencies.
pregnancy.data: Limited pregnancy data; emergency use.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Mannitol is not orally bioavailable and is given intravenously; any amount in milk would not be absorbed by the infant.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: No interruption of breastfeeding required after acute use.

oneLiner: Avoid in pregnancy where possible (limited data; angina therapy often deferrable/substitutable). Limited milk data — caution in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Nicorandil (potassium-channel activator with nitrate-like action) is used for angina. Human pregnancy data are limited; no clear teratogenic signal but experience is sparse. Where antianginal therapy is needed in pregnancy, better-characterised agents (e.g. beta-blockers, nitrates as appropriate) are generally preferred. Monitor for maternal hypotension.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Prefer better-studied antianginals; monitor blood pressure. Specialist cardiology input.
pregnancy.data: Limited human data.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited information in human milk; use with caution and monitor the infant, or prefer a better-studied alternative.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant if used.

oneLiner: Avoid in pregnancy where possible (limited data; lipid-lowering generally deferrable). Limited milk data — caution/avoid in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Cholesterol-absorption inhibitor with limited human pregnancy data. As routine lipid-lowering is deferrable in pregnancy, ezetimibe is generally avoided; reserve only for selected very high-risk situations under specialist guidance.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Defer lipid-lowering therapy in most pregnancies; specialist input for high-risk patients.
pregnancy.data: Limited human data.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited information in human milk; use with caution and prefer to defer lipid therapy while breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Often deferrable; monitor infant if used.

oneLiner: Avoid in pregnancy where possible — limited human data, photosensitivity/animal effects; reserve for clear need in progressive fibrosis. No milk data — avoid/caution in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Antifibrotic used for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Human pregnancy data are very limited. Use only when clearly needed for progressive fibrotic lung disease, weighing maternal benefit against limited safety data, with specialist input.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Specialist respiratory management; individualised decision. Photosensitivity is a maternal consideration.
pregnancy.data: Very limited human data.

lactation.riskSummary: No information on pirfenidone in human milk; use with caution and monitor the infant, or avoid where feasible.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant if used.

oneLiner: May be continued in pregnancy for active MS when needed (IgG antibody — late-pregnancy transfer can cause transient neonatal haematological effects); beware severe rebound if stopped. Compatible with breastfeeding (low milk levels, gut degradation).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Natalizumab is an IgG4 monoclonal antibody for highly active multiple sclerosis. Continuation in pregnancy may be appropriate for active disease because stopping can cause severe MS rebound. As an IgG it crosses the placenta increasingly in the third trimester, and third-trimester exposure has caused transient neonatal haematological abnormalities (mild thrombocytopenia, anaemia) — monitor the neonate. Timing of late-pregnancy dosing is individualised.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Individualise late-pregnancy dosing with neurology; monitor the neonate for haematological effects after third-trimester exposure. Defer infant live vaccines per guidance.
pregnancy.data: Pregnancy cohorts; neonatal haematological effects with late exposure.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Only small amounts appear in milk and the antibody is largely degraded in the infant's gut; no adverse effects reported.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Breastfeeding may continue; coordinate infant vaccination with the specialist.
lactation.data: Low milk levels; gut degradation per LactMed.

oneLiner: Avoid late-pregnancy dosing (IgG antibody — placental transfer can deplete neonatal B-cells); plan dosing before conception. Compatible with breastfeeding (low milk levels, gut degradation).

pregnancy.riskSummary: Ocrelizumab is an anti-CD20 IgG1 monoclonal antibody for multiple sclerosis given as infrequent infusions. As an IgG it crosses the placenta (mainly later in pregnancy) and can deplete neonatal B-cells if given in the second/third trimester; its long duration of effect means dosing is generally planned BEFORE conception, with the prolonged B-cell-depleting effect covering early pregnancy. Avoid dosing in late pregnancy; monitor/adjust infant vaccination.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Time the last infusion before conception where possible. Defer neonatal live vaccines if late exposure occurred; consider checking infant B-cells per specialist advice.
pregnancy.data: IgG placental transfer; B-cell-depletion considerations.

lactation.riskSummary: Compatible. Only minimal amounts appear in milk and the antibody is largely degraded in the infant's gut; available data are reassuring.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Breastfeeding may continue; coordinate infant vaccinations with the specialist.
lactation.data: Low milk levels; gut degradation per LactMed.

oneLiner: Use only if clearly needed in pregnancy (limited data; rapidly cleared) — for active MS/psoriasis. Limited milk data — caution in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Dimethyl fumarate (for MS and psoriasis) is rapidly metabolised to monomethyl fumarate and cleared quickly. Human pregnancy data are limited; available registry data have not shown a clear teratogenic signal, but data remain insufficient to call it preferred. Use only when needed for active disease, balancing relapse risk against limited safety data.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Individualise with specialist; the short half-life is relevant to preconception planning. Better-characterised options may be preferred where suitable.
pregnancy.data: Limited registry data; rapid clearance.

lactation.riskSummary: Limited information in human milk; the active metabolite is rapidly cleared and oral infant exposure is expected to be low, but data are sparse — use with caution and monitor the infant.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant; consider timing relative to feeds.

oneLiner: PREFERRED/acceptable systemic antifungal for serious invasive mycoses in pregnancy — long record without clear teratogenicity (liposomal forms reduce nephrotoxicity). Minimal expected milk exposure; acceptable in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: Conventional amphotericin B deoxycholate has the longest record of any systemic antifungal in pregnancy without a clear teratogenic signal and is used for serious invasive fungal infection when azoles are contraindicated/inadequate. The main drawback is maternal nephrotoxicity and infusion reactions (liposomal formulations are better tolerated and often preferred).
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor renal function and electrolytes (potassium, magnesium); premedicate for infusion reactions. Liposomal amphotericin reduces nephrotoxicity.
pregnancy.data: Long clinical experience; reassuring.

lactation.riskSummary: Acceptable. Poorly absorbed orally and given intravenously; milk transfer and infant oral absorption are expected to be minimal. Limited specific data but considered low risk.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant; low expected exposure.

oneLiner: Rarely relevant in pregnancy; limited data — use only if clearly needed. No milk data — caution in breastfeeding.

pregnancy.riskSummary: NMDA-receptor antagonist for dementia; pregnancy is uncommon in the typical population and human data are very limited. Animal studies show some effects at high doses. Use only when there is a clear indication and no suitable alternative.
pregnancy.clinicalConsiderations: Rarely indicated in women of childbearing age; specialist input if needed.
pregnancy.data: Very limited human data.

lactation.riskSummary: No information on memantine in human milk; use with caution and monitor the infant. Generally a non-urgent therapy that can be reconsidered while breastfeeding.
lactation.clinicalConsiderations: Monitor infant; weigh necessity.
